items.e: A burst fracture with neurological deficit scores 8 (4 for column injury + 3 for neurologic + 1 for displacement) mandates surgical treatment; posterior pedicle fixation with decompression is the recommended approach.

items.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of a hanging‑type thoracolumbar fracture‑dislocation?
o: Transverse fracture line across the vertebral body
Displacement of the superior fragment posteriorly over the pedicle
Lateral shift of the entire vertebral body
Alar facet fracture with no involvement of the pedicle
items.e: In a hanging‑type fracture‑dislocation, the superior fragment drapes posteriorly over the pedicle, creating a 'flap‑leg' appearance.

items.q: The most reliable single imaging finding that predicts non‑union in a displaced thoracolumbar burst fracture is:
o: Presence of a posterior wall fragment larger than 5 mm
A canal compromise of >50% on CT
Deformity of the pedicle on AP view
items.e: A posterior wall fragment >5 mm indicates incomplete healing potential and correlates strongly with non‑union.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old office worker develops chronic lower back pain after a lumbar MRI shows a grade 1 spondylolisthesis at L4‑L5. Which of the following is NOT a contraindication for a minimally invasive transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion (MIS‑TLIF) at this level?
o: Spinal canal stenosis with >30 % diameter reduction
Presence of a well‑demarcated disc herniation at L4‑L5
items.e: A well‑demarcated disc herniation is actually an indication for TLIF, not a contraindication.

items.q: During a retrospective review, surgeons noted that patients undergoing posterior short‑segment fixation for T12‑L1 burst fractures had a higher incidence of cement‑augmented pedicle screws if they had:
items.e: Low BMD (T‑score <−2.0) increases screw loosening; cement augmentation mitigates this risk.

items.q: In a thoracolumbar fracture with an ISCORE of 3 (low), the recommended initial management is:
o: Halo‑vest traction for 3 weeks followed by surgery
Conservative treatment with bracing and close imaging follow‑up
items.e: An ISCORE of 3 indicates a stable injury; conservative management with bracing and serial imaging is the standard approach.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old male presents with chronic back pain after a fall from 3 m. The CT shows a vertebral body comminution at L2‑L3 with a posterior wall fragment of 18 mm. Which of the following statements best describes the risk of future kyphotic deformity?
o: It is low because the posterior wall fragment will heal spontaneously
The risk is significant if the fragment is >15 mm and the anterior height loss is >20 %
Kyphosis develops only if the facet joints are injured
The presence of a disc herniation above the fracture protects against deformity
items.e: A posterior fragment >15 mm and >20 % anterior height loss predict progressive kyphosis in thoracolumbar fractures.

items.q: A 64-year-old diabetic has 6 weeks of worsening low back pain, night pain and a raised CRP. Plain radiographs are normal. Which imaging investigation is most sensitive and specific for early pyogenic spondylodiscitis?
items.e: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the investigation of choice: disc and end-plate T2 hyperintensity, marrow oedema and enhancement appear within days, long before radiographic change, and it also shows epidural or paravertebral abscess.

items.q: Twelve months after an instrumented posterolateral L4–S1 fusion, a patient has persistent back pain and pseudarthrosis is suspected. Which is the most accurate non-invasive investigation to assess the fusion?
o: Fine-cut CT with sagittal and coronal reconstructions
items.e: Thin-slice CT with multiplanar reconstruction best shows continuous trabecular bridging or a pseudarthrosis cleft and screw lucency; flexion–extension films are insensitive across rigid instrumentation and MRI is degraded by metal artefact.

items.q: A 66-year-old with a previous L2–S1 instrumented fusion is planned for THA. On standing and sitting lateral spinopelvic radiographs, which finding best identifies a 'stiff' spinopelvic unit with a higher risk of dislocation?
o: Change in sacral slope of less than 10° between standing and sitting
items.e: Normally the pelvis tilts posteriorly on sitting and sacral slope falls by about 20° or more; a change below 10° indicates a stiff spinopelvic unit, which increases impingement and instability after THA and favours dual-mobility or adjusted cup positioning.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a closed, isolated, minimally displaced transverse midshaft tibial fracture with an intact fibula after a fall. Soft tissues and neurovascular status are normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Closed reduction if needed and an above-knee cast
items.e: Most closed paediatric tibial shaft fractures heal well with closed treatment in a long-leg cast; because an intact fibula tends to make the tibia drift into varus, alignment is checked with serial radiographs in the first weeks.

items.q: After closed reduction and percutaneous pinning of a Gartland III extension supracondylar humerus fracture in a 6-year-old, the radial pulse is not palpable but the hand is warm and pink with brisk capillary refill and an audible Doppler signal. Nerve function is intact. What is the next step?
o: Immediate open exploration of the brachial artery
Admit with the elbow in about 30–40° of flexion and monitor perfusion closely
Formal angiography before any further intervention
Remove the pins and immobilise in hyperflexion
items.e: A perfused (pink) but pulseless hand after satisfactory reduction is usually observed closely in hospital, as collateral flow is adequate; exploration is indicated if the hand becomes cold or white, perfusion worsens, or there is median nerve palsy or compartment syndrome.

items.q: An 8-year-old boy weighing 28 kg has a closed, length-stable transverse midshaft femoral fracture. The usual treatment of choice is:
o: Skin traction for 6 weeks followed by a cast
items.e: Flexible titanium elastic nails are the usual treatment for length-stable diaphyseal femoral fractures in children of about 5–11 years who weigh under about 45–50 kg; piriformis-entry rigid nails risk femoral head avascular necrosis in the skeletally immature, and spica casting is preferred under about 5 years.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman notices her foot flattening over a year. Viewed from behind, more lateral toes are visible on the affected side, and on single-limb heel rise the heel fails to invert and she cannot rise fully. The deformity corrects passively. Most likely diagnosis?
o: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (progressive collapsing foot deformity)
items.e: The 'too many toes' sign and failure of heel inversion on single heel rise in an adult with an acquired, flexible flatfoot are classic for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction; tarsal coalition causes a rigid flatfoot, usually presenting in adolescence.

items.q: A 15-year-old has a distal femoral metaphyseal lesion with a sunburst periosteal reaction, suspicious for osteosarcoma. Before biopsy, which investigation best defines local extent (marrow involvement, skip lesions, soft-tissue mass and neurovascular relations) for limb-salvage planning?
o: MRI of the entire femur including the adjacent joints
items.e: MRI of the whole involved bone defines intramedullary extent, skip metastases, soft-tissue extension and neurovascular involvement, and is ideally done before biopsy so post-biopsy oedema does not confound it; chest CT and bone scan or PET-CT stage distant disease.

items.q: A 5-year-old has a fever of 39.3 °C, a hot swollen left knee, pain on any passive movement, refuses to bear weight and has an ESR of 55 mm/h. Radiographs show only an effusion. What is the most important next investigation?
o: Joint aspiration for cell count, Gram stain and culture
items.e: Suspected septic arthritis needs urgent aspiration: synovial white cell count, Gram stain and culture confirm the diagnosis and guide antibiotics, and further imaging should not delay it; MRI is added if adjacent osteomyelitis is suspected.

items.q: In a zone II flexor digitorum profundus repair intended for early active motion, which factor contributes most to the tensile strength of the repair?
o: Placing the core suture purchase about 2 mm from the cut tendon ends
Relying on a running epitendinous suture alone
The number of core suture strands crossing the repair site
items.e: Repair strength rises roughly in proportion to the number of core strands crossing the repair, so 4- to 6-strand repairs are used to allow early active motion; thicker suture, core purchase of about 7–10 mm and an epitendinous suture add further strength.

items.q: A 12-year-old has an eccentric, expansile, lytic metaphyseal lesion of the proximal tibia. MRI shows multiple fluid–fluid levels separated by thin, smoothly enhancing septa with no solid or nodular enhancing component. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Fluid–fluid levels with thin, uniformly enhancing septa and no solid component favour a primary aneurysmal bone cyst; thick nodular enhancing septa or a solid mass suggest telangiectatic osteosarcoma, and a simple bone cyst is central and usually has a single fluid level only after fracture.

items.q: A 24-year-old man has an isolated posterior wall fracture of the acetabulum after a dashboard injury; the hip is unstable on examination under anaesthesia. The surgical approach of choice for fixation is:
items.e: Posterior wall and posterior column fractures are reached through the Kocher–Langenbeck approach, which exposes the retroacetabular surface for lag-screw and buttress-plate fixation. The ilioinguinal, Stoppa and Smith-Petersen approaches give access to the anterior column and wall.

items.q: The Tubiana staging of Dupuytren disease is based on:
o: The number of digital rays involved
The thickness of the cord on ultrasound
The presence of ectopic deposits (knuckle pads, Ledderhose, Peyronie)
The total flexion deformity of the affected ray (MCP + PIP + DIP)
items.e: Tubiana stages each ray by the sum of the flexion deformities at the MCP, PIP and DIP joints (stage 1: 0–45°, 2: 45–90°, 3: 90–135°, 4: >135°). Ectopic deposits indicate Dupuytren diathesis but are not part of this staging.

items.q: In the combined task force (NASS/ASSR/ASNR) lumbar disc nomenclature, displaced disc material that has completely lost continuity with the parent disc is termed:
items.e: A sequestration is a subtype of extrusion in which the displaced fragment has no continuity with the disc of origin. In a protrusion the base is wider than the displaced material, while an extrusion has a narrower neck but remains attached; a bulge involves more than 25% of the disc circumference.

items.q: A 17-year-old has a permeative diaphyseal lesion of the femur with a large soft-tissue mass. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with membranous CD99 positivity and an EWSR1–FLI1 fusion. The standard systemic chemotherapy is:
o: Vincristine, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide alternating with ifosfamide and etoposide (VDC/IE)
items.e: EWSR1–FLI1 [t(11;22)] with CD99 positivity confirms Ewing sarcoma, for which interval-compressed VDC alternating with IE is the standard regimen. MAP is used for osteosarcoma and imatinib for GIST and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans.

items.q: For staging a newly diagnosed high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma of the thigh, the investigation of choice to detect pulmonary metastases is:
items.e: The lung is the commonest site of metastasis from high-grade soft-tissue sarcoma, and CT of the chest is the standard staging test because it detects nodules too small for a chest radiograph. PET-CT is less sensitive than thin-section CT for small pulmonary nodules.

items.q: A 38-year-old man with chronic alcohol use has groin pain and normal hip radiographs. The most sensitive investigation to detect early osteonecrosis of the femoral head is:
items.e: MRI is the most sensitive and specific test for early (pre-collapse, Ficat I) osteonecrosis, showing a band-like lesion or the double-line sign before radiographs change. Bone scan is less sensitive and non-specific, and CT shows changes only later.

items.q: A 32-year-old has 3 months of back pain, night sweats and weight loss. MRI shows paradiscal involvement of T11–T12 with a subligamentous abscess spanning several levels; he is neurologically intact. Before starting definitive treatment, the most appropriate next step is:
o: Empirical antitubercular therapy for 12 months without tissue diagnosis
Anterior radical debridement and strut grafting
CT-guided biopsy for histopathology, culture and GeneXpert (CBNAAT)
items.e: Tissue diagnosis by image-guided biopsy confirms tuberculosis, excludes pyogenic infection and malignancy, and allows rapid detection of rifampicin resistance with GeneXpert, so the correct drug regimen can be chosen. Surgery is reserved for neurological deficit, instability, progressive kyphosis or failure of medical treatment.

items.q: The most common organism causing pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis in adults is:
items.e: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) causes about half of pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis. Gram-negative organisms such as E. coli follow urinary infection, and Pseudomonas is associated with intravenous drug use.

items.q: In supine hip arthroscopy, the anterior portal places which structure at greatest risk?
items.e: The anterior portal passes closest to the branches of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (within a few millimetres), and the femoral neurovascular bundle lies more medially. The anterolateral portal endangers the superior gluteal nerve and the posterolateral portal the sciatic nerve.

items.q: A 3-month-old girl has a dislocated hip that reduces with a clunk on the Ortolani manoeuvre. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
o: Observation with repeat ultrasound at 6 weeks
Closed reduction under anaesthesia and hip spica
Open reduction through a medial approach
items.e: A dislocated but reducible (Ortolani-positive) hip in an infant under 6 months is treated with a Pavlik harness, with ultrasound to confirm reduction. Closed reduction and spica is used if the harness fails or the child is older (about 6–18 months).

items.q: In the sample-size calculation for a randomised trial, the investigators set the power at 80%. Power is the probability of:
o: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true (type I error)
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is false (type II error)
Correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when a true difference exists
Obtaining a p-value below 0.05 when the null hypothesis is true
items.e: Power equals 1 − β, the probability of detecting a true effect of the specified size. With 80% power there is a 20% chance of a type II error; α (usually 0.05) is the type I error rate.

items.q: In lamellar bone formation, hydroxyapatite crystals are first deposited mainly:
o: Within the cytoplasm of mature osteocytes
In the hole (gap) zones between staggered type I collagen molecules
By free precipitation in the interstitial fluid of the Haversian canal
Within proteoglycan aggregates of the cement line
items.e: Primary mineralisation of osteoid begins extracellularly, with calcium phosphate nucleating in the gap (hole) zones of the quarter-staggered type I collagen fibrils, aided by osteoblast-derived matrix vesicles. Crystals then grow along and between the fibrils during secondary mineralisation.

items.q: After successful Ponseti correction of idiopathic clubfoot, the most important risk factor for relapse is:
o: The number of casts needed to achieve correction
Incomplete correction of cavus in the first cast
Non-compliance with the foot abduction brace
items.e: Poor adherence to the foot abduction brace is the strongest and commonest cause of relapse after Ponseti treatment, increasing relapse risk several-fold. Tenotomy is a routine part of the method, and the number of casts is not a major independent predictor.

items.q: In the Gould modification of the Broström procedure for chronic lateral ankle instability, the anatomical repair of the ATFL and CFL is reinforced with the:
items.e: The modified Broström–Gould procedure imbricates the ATFL and CFL and advances the lateral limb of the inferior extensor retinaculum to the fibula, which reinforces the repair and limits subtalar inversion. Peroneus brevis is sacrificed in non-anatomical tenodeses such as Evans, Watson-Jones and Chrisman–Snook.

items.q: The characteristic biochemical change in the collagen of Dupuytren cords, compared with normal palmar fascia, is:
o: Replacement of type I collagen by type II collagen
An increased proportion of type III collagen relative to type I
Loss of all type I collagen
items.e: Normal palmar fascia is almost entirely type I collagen; in Dupuytren disease myofibroblasts lay down excess type III collagen, raising the type III:I ratio. Type II is cartilage collagen and type IV forms basement membranes.

items.q: On histology of a central cartilage tumour of the femur, which feature most reliably indicates an atypical cartilaginous tumour/grade 1 chondrosarcoma rather than an enchondroma?
o: Permeation of the medullary cavity with entrapment of host lamellar bone trabeculae
Encasement of cartilage lobules by a rim of lamellar bone
items.e: Infiltrative growth with permeation of marrow spaces and entrapment of pre-existing host trabeculae is the key histological criterion of malignancy in low-grade cartilage tumours. Enchondromas form discrete lobules encased by reactive lamellar bone, and cytological atypia alone is unreliable.

items.q: A 25-year-old has an upper trunk (C5–C6) brachial plexus avulsion with intact C7–T1 function, 3 months after injury. The standard nerve transfer to restore shoulder abduction and external rotation is:
o: Ulnar nerve fascicle to the biceps branch of the musculocutaneous nerve (Oberlin)
Spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve
Medial pectoral nerve to the musculocutaneous nerve
Anterior interosseous nerve to the ulnar motor branch
items.e: Transferring the distal spinal accessory nerve to the suprascapular nerve reinnervates supraspinatus and infraspinatus, often combined with a triceps branch to axillary nerve transfer for deltoid. The Oberlin transfer restores elbow flexion, not shoulder function.

items.q: In the Enneking (MSTS) surgical staging system for malignant bone tumours, stage III denotes:
o: A tumour of any grade or extent with regional or distant metastasis
A high-grade tumour with extracompartmental extension
A low-grade tumour with extracompartmental extension
A high-grade tumour confined to its compartment
items.e: Enneking stage III is defined by metastasis (M1), regardless of grade (G) or compartmental status (T). Stage I is low grade and stage II high grade, each subdivided into A (intracompartmental) and B (extracompartmental).

items.q: A meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing two fixation methods reports an I² statistic of 70%. This indicates:
o: Publication bias among the included trials
That 70% of patients benefited from the intervention
Substantial heterogeneity between the study results
That the pooled effect is statistically significant
items.e: I² estimates the percentage of total variation across studies due to true heterogeneity rather than chance; values above about 50% (Cochrane: 50–90%) indicate substantial heterogeneity, which should be explored and usually calls for a random-effects model. It says nothing about publication bias or significance.

items.q: The principal mechanosensory cells that detect loading of bone and orchestrate remodelling are:
items.e: Osteocytes, embedded in lacunae and connected by dendritic processes through canaliculi, sense load-induced interstitial fluid flow and signal to osteoblasts and osteoclasts (e.g. via sclerostin and RANKL). Unloading raises sclerostin and favours resorption.

items.q: An adult has drug-sensitive tuberculosis of the dorsolumbar spine. The regimen recommended by the Indian INDEX-TB guidelines is:
o: 2 months HRZE followed by 4 months HRE (6 months)
2 months HRZE followed by 10 months HRE (12 months)
2 months HRZES, 1 month HRZE, then 5 months HRE
Isoniazid and rifampicin alone for 18 months
items.e: INDEX-TB advises 12 months of treatment for osteoarticular, including spinal, tuberculosis: an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then 10 months of isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol. The streptomycin-containing retreatment regimen has been discontinued.

items.q: The most common site of skeletal tuberculosis is the:
items.e: The spine accounts for about half of osteoarticular tuberculosis, usually the thoracolumbar region with paradiscal involvement. The hip and knee are the next most common sites.

items.q: A 62-year-old man with metastatic disease to the thoracic spine has a revised Tokuhashi score of 7. His predicted survival, which favours conservative or palliative treatment, is:
items.e: In the revised Tokuhashi score (0–15), 0–8 predicts survival under 6 months, 9–11 at least 6 months and 12–15 at least a year; a score of 0–8 favours conservative or palliative care.

items.q: A patient with spinal metastasis has a Tomita prognostic score of 9. The treatment goal recommended by Tomita for this score is:
o: Wide or marginal excision for long-term local control
Marginal or intralesional excision for middle-term control
items.e: Tomita scores of 2–3 suggest wide/marginal excision, 4–5 marginal/intralesional excision, 6–7 palliative surgery and 8–10 non-operative supportive care.

items.q: On MRI of a metastatic thoracic lesion, epidural tumour compresses the spinal cord but CSF is still visible around the cord. The Bilsky epidural spinal cord compression (ESCC) grade is:
items.e: Bilsky grade 2 is cord compression with CSF still visible around the cord; grade 3 is cord compression with no CSF visible. Grades 2 and 3 are high-grade ESCC; 1c abuts the cord without compressing it.

items.q: The landmark randomised trial by Patchell et al. (Lancet 2005) compared direct decompressive surgery plus radiotherapy with radiotherapy alone for metastatic spinal cord compression. Its principal finding was that surgery improved:
o: Local tumour control on MRI only
The ability to walk after treatment
Overall survival only in radiosensitive tumours
items.e: Patchell showed that significantly more patients were ambulatory after surgery plus radiotherapy (84%) than after radiotherapy alone (57%), and surgery also helped non-ambulatory patients regain walking.

items.q: Under the NOMS framework, a neurologically intact patient with a stable spine and high-grade epidural cord compression can be treated with conventional external beam radiotherapy alone if the metastasis is from:
items.e: Lymphoma, myeloma and seminoma are radiosensitive to conventional radiotherapy even with high-grade ESCC. Radioresistant tumours such as renal cell carcinoma, melanoma and NSCLC with high-grade ESCC need separation surgery followed by stereotactic radiosurgery.

items.q: A 14-year-old boy has a painful, rapidly developing scoliosis with night pain relieved by NSAIDs. CT shows a 1 cm lesion with a central nidus in the pedicle on the concave side at the apex of the curve. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Osteoid osteoma is the commonest cause of painful scoliosis in adolescents; it lies in the posterior elements on the concavity of the curve, has a nidus under 1.5–2 cm and classically responds to NSAIDs.

items.q: The Weinstein–Boriani–Biagini (WBB) staging system for primary spinal tumours divides the vertebra in the axial plane into:
items.e: WBB divides the vertebra into 12 clock-face radiating zones and 5 concentric layers (A extraosseous paravertebral to E dural involvement) to plan en bloc resection.

items.q: When planning correction of adult spinal deformity using the SRS–Schwab targets, the lumbar lordosis should be restored so that the pelvic incidence minus lumbar lordosis (PI–LL) mismatch is within about:
items.e: The commonly used realignment goals are PI–LL within about 10°, pelvic tilt under 20° and sagittal vertical axis under 5 cm, which correlate with better health-related quality of life.

items.q: In the Roussouly classification of sagittal lumbar shape, a sacral slope greater than 45° with a long, curved lordosis is type:
items.e: Roussouly types 1 and 2 have sacral slope under 35°, type 3 has 35–45°, and type 4 has more than 45° with a hyperlordotic lumbar spine, predisposing to posterior element and facet overload.

items.q: A 66-year-old diabetic man has 4 weeks of severe back pain and raised CRP. MRI shows L3–L4 spondylodiscitis without abscess; he is afebrile, haemodynamically stable and neurologically intact. Blood cultures are pending. The best next step is:
o: Await blood cultures and, if negative, obtain CT-guided biopsy before antibiotics
items.e: In a stable, neurologically intact patient (IDSA 2015 guideline), antibiotics are withheld until a microbiological diagnosis is made from blood cultures or image-guided biopsy; empirical treatment is started at once only for sepsis or neurological compromise.

items.q: A randomised trial (Bernard et al., Lancet 2015) of antibiotic duration for pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis showed that compared with 12 weeks, a total duration of:
items.e: Six weeks of antibiotics was non-inferior to 12 weeks for cure at one year in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, so 6 weeks is the standard duration for most patients.

items.q: Two years after instrumented posterior lumbar fusion a patient presents with indolent pain and loosening around pedicle screws but no wound problems. The low-virulence organism most associated with such delayed infection, which requires prolonged culture incubation, is:
items.e: Delayed or late spinal implant infections are often due to low-virulence skin flora such as Cutibacterium acnes and coagulase-negative staphylococci; cultures should be held for about 14 days.

items.q: In Hodgson's classification of Pott paraplegia, late-onset paraplegia appearing years after healed thoracic tuberculosis with severe kyphosis is most often due to:
o: Reactivation with a large cold abscess
Stretching of the cord over an internal gibbus or bony ridge
Spinal artery thrombosis from active vasculitis
items.e: Late-onset paraplegia in healed disease usually results from mechanical compression by the internal salient (gibbus) or fibrosis, and carries a poorer prognosis than early-onset paraplegia of active disease, which is mainly due to abscess, granulation tissue or sequestra.

items.q: A 7-year-old with thoracic tuberculosis is assessed with Rajasekaran's 'spine-at-risk' radiological signs to predict progressive kyphosis. Which of the following is one of these signs?
o: Loss of disc height at the involved level
items.e: The four spine-at-risk signs are separation of the facet joints, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation and toppling of the superior vertebra; two or more predict severe kyphosis progression in children.

items.q: In Rajasekaran and Shanmugasundaram's formula for predicting final kyphosis in spinal tuberculosis (Y = a + bX), X is the initial loss of vertebral body height. The value of b is:
items.e: The formula is Y = 5.5 + 30.5X, where Y is the final angle of kyphosis and X is the initial loss of vertebral body height expressed in vertebral body units.

items.q: A farmer who consumes unpasteurised milk has low back pain and fever. Radiographs show an erosion of the anterosuperior corner of the L4 body with adjacent osteophyte formation and relative preservation of the vertebral body. This 'Pedro Pons' sign suggests:
items.e: Brucellosis typically causes anterosuperior epiphysitis of the lower lumbar spine (Pedro Pons sign) with early sclerosis and osteophytes, little vertebral collapse and rare large abscesses, in contrast to tuberculosis.

items.q: Using the 2018 International Consensus Meeting (ICM) preoperative minor criteria for periprosthetic joint infection, a total score that classifies the joint as infected is:
items.e: In the 2018 ICM/Parvizi criteria a weighted minor-criteria score of 6 or more indicates infection, 2–5 is possibly infected (consider intraoperative findings) and 0–1 not infected; one major criterion alone is diagnostic.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM definition of periprosthetic joint infection, the serum D-dimer threshold counted as a minor criterion is:
items.e: The serum minor criteria are CRP above 1 mg/dL (2 points), D-dimer above 860 ng/mL (2 points) and ESR above 30 mm/h (1 point).

items.q: On contrast MRI of a thoracolumbar spinal infection, which feature favours tuberculous over pyogenic spondylitis?
o: Diffuse homogeneous enhancement of a single vertebral body with early disc destruction
A well-defined paraspinal abscess with a thin, smooth enhancing wall and subligamentous spread over several levels
Involvement limited to the disc and adjacent endplates of one level
items.e: Tuberculous spondylitis typically shows thin, smooth-walled, well-defined paraspinal abscesses, subligamentous spread across multiple levels, heterogeneous vertebral enhancement and relative disc preservation; pyogenic infection gives thick irregular abscess walls and early disc destruction.

items.q: The cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (Xpert MTB/RIF) performed on pus from a tuberculous psoas abscess detects rifampicin resistance by identifying mutations in the:
items.e: Xpert MTB/RIF detects mutations in the 81-bp rifampicin-resistance–determining region of rpoB, which accounts for about 95% of rifampicin resistance; katG and inhA mutations confer isoniazid resistance.

items.q: In 'separation surgery' for radioresistant metastatic epidural spinal cord compression, followed by stereotactic radiosurgery, the aim of decompression is to:
o: Create a gap of about 2–3 mm between the tumour and the spinal cord
Achieve en bloc resection of the involved vertebra
Resect all paraspinal tumour to obtain negative margins
Remove the posterior elements only without addressing ventral tumour
items.e: Separation surgery is a posterolateral circumferential decompression with stabilisation that clears tumour from the dura to leave a margin of roughly 2–3 mm, allowing high-dose SRS to the residual tumour without exceeding spinal cord tolerance.

items.q: A 70-year-old with progressive loss of lumbar lordosis tries to stay upright by compensating through the pelvis. Which change in pelvic parameters occurs?
o: Pelvic tilt increases and sacral slope decreases
Pelvic tilt decreases and sacral slope increases
Pelvic tilt and sacral slope both increase
items.e: Pelvic retroversion is the main pelvic compensation for sagittal imbalance: pelvic tilt rises and sacral slope falls by the same amount, while pelvic incidence stays constant (PI = PT + SS).

items.q: In cervical sagittal alignment, a C2–C7 sagittal vertical axis greater than about which value correlates with worse neck disability after posterior cervical fusion?
items.e: A C2–C7 SVA above about 40 mm correlates with higher Neck Disability Index scores (Tang et al. 2012) and is used as the threshold for cervical sagittal malalignment in the Ames classification.

items.q: A randomised trial (CAFE, Berenson et al. 2011) in patients with cancer and painful vertebral compression fractures showed that balloon kyphoplasty, compared with non-surgical care, led to:
o: Higher rates of symptomatic cement leakage than benefit
No difference in function at one month
Better back-specific function (Roland–Morris score) at one month
items.e: In CAFE, kyphoplasty improved Roland–Morris disability scores, pain and quality of life at one month compared with non-surgical management in cancer-related painful vertebral fractures, with few serious complications.

items.q: In suspected spinal tuberculosis, MRI of the whole spine rather than only the symptomatic region is advised mainly to detect:
items.e: Multifocal non-contiguous (skip) lesions occur in a notable minority of spinal tuberculosis cases and may be clinically silent, so whole-spine screening sequences are recommended.

items.q: Eight months after an uncemented THA, a 58-year-old woman has groin pain on active hip flexion and on climbing into a car, with pain on resisted straight-leg raise. Infection markers are normal and the cross-table lateral CT shows the anterior rim of the cup projecting beyond the anterior acetabular wall. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Anterior cup overhang (often from a retroverted, oversized or lateralised cup) irritates the iliopsoas tendon, giving groin pain on active flexion; it is treated with image-guided injection, iliopsoas tenotomy or cup revision.

items.q: A well-fixed TKA with acute haematogenous Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-sensitive) infection is treated by debridement, antibiotics and implant retention with polyethylene exchange. The antibiotic added to the regimen for its activity against biofilm on the retained implant is:
o: Rifampicin, always combined with another active agent
items.e: Rifampicin penetrates biofilm and kills adherent, slow-growing staphylococci (Zimmerli et al. 1998), improving cure with implant retention; it must be combined with a partner drug such as a fluoroquinolone because resistance emerges rapidly with monotherapy.

items.q: Fourteen months after TKA a 70-year-old has a chronic patellar tendon rupture with a 30° extensor lag and retracted, poor-quality tendon. The most reliable treatment is:
o: Reconstruction with a synthetic (polypropylene) mesh or extensor mechanism allograft
Primary end-to-end suture repair of the tendon
Revision of the femoral component to a hinged prosthesis
items.e: Primary repair of chronic extensor mechanism disruption after TKA has a high failure rate; reconstruction with Marlex synthetic mesh (Hanssen technique) or a whole extensor mechanism allograft tensioned in full extension gives better results.

items.q: In a posterior-stabilised total knee prosthesis, femoral rollback during deep flexion is produced by:
o: Increased posterior slope of the tibial cut alone
A highly conforming medial pivot insert
Engagement of the femoral cam against the tibial post
items.e: In PS designs the PCL is sacrificed and the femoral cam contacts the tibial polyethylene post from mid-flexion, forcing the femur posteriorly on the tibia (rollback) to improve flexion and quadriceps lever arm.

items.q: To reduce dislocation and impingement after THA, the combined anteversion of the cup and femoral stem (Dorr's 'combined anteversion' concept) is generally targeted at about:
items.e: Dorr recommended a combined (cup plus stem) anteversion of roughly 25°–50°, with stem version adjusted to the cup; too little risks posterior dislocation and too much anterior dislocation.

items.q: A patient with a dual-mobility THA has a 'dislocation' on radiographs in which the femoral head is eccentric within the shell without a dislocated liner shadow, after years of wear. This complication unique to dual-mobility bearings is:
items.e: Intraprosthetic dislocation occurs when wear of the polyethylene retentive rim (or an iatrogenic closed reduction) lets the small head escape the mobile liner and articulate directly with the metal shell; it needs early revision.

items.q: With modern onlay patellofemoral arthroplasty for isolated patellofemoral arthritis, the most common cause of failure requiring revision is:
o: Aseptic loosening of the trochlear component
items.e: Older inlay designs failed mainly from maltracking; with onlay trochlear components, progression of tibiofemoral osteoarthritis is the commonest reason for conversion to TKA.

items.q: During medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy, a lateral hinge fracture is seen to exit distal to the proximal tibiofibular joint. In the Takeuchi classification this is:
o: Type III, intra-articular into the lateral plateau
Type IV, involving the tibial tubercle
items.e: Takeuchi type I reaches the proximal tibiofibular joint and is relatively stable; type II exits distal to it and type III extends into the lateral tibial plateau, both unstable and associated with loss of correction and delayed union.

items.q: On axial CT of an arthritic shoulder, the glenoid shows posterior erosion creating a distinct posterior neoglenoid alongside the original anterior paleoglenoid. In the Walch classification this glenoid is type:
items.e: Walch B2 is a biconcave glenoid with posterior erosion and humeral head subluxation; B1 has posterior joint-space narrowing without erosion, and type C is dysplastic retroversion over 25°.

items.q: Dislocation after a reverse total shoulder arthroplasty most often occurs anteriorly with the arm in which position?
items.e: Reverse prostheses typically dislocate anteriorly in extension, adduction and internal rotation (for example pushing up from a chair or tucking in a shirt), with risk increased by subscapularis deficiency and inadequate soft-tissue tension.

items.q: A 38-year-old manual worker has isolated lateral compartment osteoarthritis with 9° of valgus; the deformity arises from the femur (low mechanical lateral distal femoral angle). The most appropriate joint-preserving operation is:
items.e: Valgus deformity of femoral origin in a young active patient is corrected at its source by a lateral opening-wedge or medial closing-wedge distal femoral osteotomy; a tibial osteotomy would create joint-line obliquity.

items.q: Under UK MHRA guidance for patients with metal-on-metal hip implants, a blood cobalt or chromium level above which value suggests possible soft-tissue reaction and warrants further investigation such as MARS MRI?
items.e: The MHRA threshold of 7 ppb (7 µg/L) of cobalt or chromium indicates potential for adverse local tissue reaction and prompts cross-sectional imaging and closer follow-up.

items.q: A 40-year-old woman with developmental hip dysplasia is being planned for THA. The femoral head has migrated proximally by 80% of its own vertical height. Her Crowe class is:
items.e: Crowe grades proximal migration as a proportion of femoral head height (or 20% of pelvic height): I under 50%, II 50–75%, III 75–100% and IV more than 100% (high dislocation).

items.q: Radiolucent lines around a cemented acetabular component on an AP pelvic radiograph are described using DeLee and Charnley zones. These divide the bone–cement interface into:
items.e: DeLee and Charnley described three acetabular zones (I superolateral, II medial, III inferomedial); the femoral side uses the seven Gruen zones on the AP view.

items.q: In TKA, the 'Akagi line' used to set rotational alignment of the tibial component runs from the centre of the PCL insertion to the:
o: Lateral border of the tibial tubercle
Medial border of the patellar tendon at the tibial tubercle
items.e: The Akagi line joins the middle of the PCL tibial attachment to the medial border of the patellar tendon at its insertion and approximates the AP axis of the tibia; internal tibial rotation causes patellar maltracking and pain.

items.q: Six weeks after primary TKA a compliant patient has only 70° of flexion despite physiotherapy, with no infection or component malposition. Manipulation under anaesthesia is most likely to succeed if performed within about:
items.e: MUA for postoperative stiffness gives the best gains when done early, generally within about 12 weeks (ideally 6–8 weeks), before arthrofibrosis matures; later stiffness usually needs arthroscopic or open arthrolysis or revision.

items.q: The CRISTAL cluster-randomised trial (JAMA 2022) compared aspirin with enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis after hip and knee arthroplasty. Its main finding was that aspirin:
o: Was non-inferior to enoxaparin for symptomatic VTE
Reduced pulmonary embolism compared with enoxaparin
Resulted in a significantly higher rate of symptomatic VTE at 90 days, mainly below-knee DVT
items.e: In CRISTAL, symptomatic VTE within 90 days was about 3.5% with aspirin against 1.8% with enoxaparin, driven by below-knee DVT, so aspirin did not meet non-inferiority; bleeding and mortality were similar.

items.q: The TOPKAT randomised trial (Lancet 2019) of patients with medial compartment knee arthritis eligible for either operation found that, compared with total knee replacement, unicompartmental replacement:
o: Had similar Oxford Knee Scores at 5 years and was more cost-effective
Had significantly worse Oxford Knee Scores at 5 years
Had a significantly higher reoperation rate at 5 years
items.e: TOPKAT showed no significant difference in Oxford Knee Score at 5 years, with similar reoperation rates, and partial knee replacement was more cost-effective, supporting UKA when the patient is suitable for both.

items.q: The HEALTH trial (NEJM 2019) compared total hip arthroplasty with hemiarthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures in ambulatory older patients. The primary outcome result was:
o: THA significantly reduced unplanned secondary procedures at 24 months
THA had a significantly lower dislocation rate
There was no significant difference in unplanned secondary procedures at 24 months
items.e: Secondary procedures within 24 months were similar (about 8% in each group); THA gave small, possibly unimportant improvements in function and quality of life but more dislocations.

items.q: Fourth-generation ceramic femoral heads (for example BIOLOX delta) have a much lower fracture rate than earlier pure alumina heads mainly because they are:
o: An alumina matrix toughened with zirconia particles and strontium-based platelets
items.e: Zirconia-toughened alumina composites gain fracture toughness from transformation toughening of dispersed zirconia and crack deflection by platelets, while retaining the hardness and wear resistance of alumina.

items.q: An oxidised zirconium (Oxinium) femoral head is best described as:
o: A zirconium–niobium alloy whose surface is converted to zirconium oxide by thermal oxidation
A cobalt–chromium head with a sprayed ceramic coating
A titanium head with a titanium nitride surface
items.e: Thermal oxidation transforms the surface of a Zr–2.5Nb alloy into a few-micron ceramic oxide layer that is not a coating; it resists scratching but can be damaged if the head dislocates against the metal shell, causing rapid polyethylene wear.

items.q: When resurfacing the patella during TKA, to reduce the risk of patellar fracture the residual bony patella should usually be at least about:
items.e: Leaving at least about 12 mm of bone (and restoring the original composite thickness) reduces patellar fracture risk without overstuffing the patellofemoral joint.

items.q: In revision TKA, the 'zones of fixation' concept (epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis) recommends that durable component fixation should be achieved in at least:
o: The diaphysis only, with cemented stems
All three zones on both femur and tibia
items.e: Morgan-Jones and colleagues proposed that stable revision fixation needs at least two of the three zones; metaphyseal cones or sleeves are a key way of obtaining zone 2 fixation when the epiphysis is deficient.

items.q: Two years after an uneventful TKA, a patient develops a hot swollen knee three days after a dental abscess. In the Tsukayama classification of prosthetic joint infection this is type:
items.e: Tsukayama type III is acute haematogenous infection of a previously well-functioning prosthesis; types II (early postoperative, within about 4 weeks) and III with short symptom duration and a stable implant are the candidates for DAIR.

items.q: The classic Kozinn and Scott selection criteria for unicompartmental knee arthroplasty include which of the following?
o: Age under 50 years and high activity level
Coronal deformity up to 25° that is not passively correctable
Flexion contracture of less than 5° and range of motion of at least 90°
items.e: Kozinn and Scott (1989) advised UKA for patients over 60, under 82 kg, of low activity, with flexion contracture under 5°, flexion arc of at least 90° and an angular deformity under 15° correctable to neutral; modern Oxford criteria are less restrictive.

items.q: During anatomical ACL reconstruction, the 'resident's ridge' on the medial wall of the lateral femoral condyle is a key landmark because it:
o: Separates the anteromedial and posterolateral bundle footprints
Marks the posterior border of the lateral condyle articular cartilage
Forms the anterior (upper, in the arthroscopic view) border of the ACL femoral footprint
Marks the origin of the popliteus tendon
items.e: The lateral intercondylar (resident's) ridge forms the anterior boundary of the ACL femoral attachment, with ACL fibres lying posterior to it; the bifurcate ridge separates the AM and PL bundle footprints.

items.q: Which bundle of the native ACL is tight near full extension and contributes most to rotational stability, being the main target of the pivot-shift?
items.e: The posterolateral bundle is tight in extension and controls rotational laxity, while the anteromedial bundle tightens in flexion and is the main restraint to anterior translation tested by the anterior drawer.

items.q: The anterolateral bundle of the PCL, the larger of its two bundles and the usual target of single-bundle reconstruction, is tight in:
items.e: The anterolateral bundle of the PCL is tight in flexion and the posteromedial bundle in extension; single-bundle reconstruction therefore reproduces the AL bundle and is tensioned in about 90° of flexion.

items.q: After a knee injury, the AP radiograph shows a small avulsion from the medial tibial plateau at the tibial attachment of the deep MCL (a 'reverse Segond' fracture). This most strongly suggests an associated tear of the:
items.e: The reverse Segond fracture is associated with PCL tears and medial meniscal injury, whereas the classic lateral Segond avulsion is associated with ACL rupture.

items.q: The classic 'kissing' bone bruise pattern on MRI after an acute non-contact ACL rupture involves the:
o: Medial femoral condyle and medial tibial plateau
Lateral femoral condyle near the sulcus terminalis and the posterolateral tibial plateau
Anterior tibial plateau and anterior femoral condyles
items.e: During the pivot-shift mechanism the lateral femoral condyle impacts the posterolateral tibial plateau, producing bruises in both; patella and lateral trochlea bruises suggest lateral patellar dislocation.

items.q: On a lateral knee radiograph, a 'deep lateral femoral notch sign' strongly suggesting an ACL tear is a depression of the lateral condylopatellar sulcus deeper than about:
items.e: A lateral femoral notch deeper than about 1.5 mm reflects an impaction injury from anterior tibial subluxation and is a specific indirect sign of ACL rupture.

items.q: According to Arnoczky and Warren, the peripheral vascularised portion of the adult medial meniscus is approximately:
items.e: Branches of the genicular arteries supply about the outer 10–30% of the medial meniscus (10–25% laterally); tears in this red–red zone have the best healing potential after repair.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a painful snapping knee. Arthroscopy shows a lateral meniscus of normal shape that is hypermobile because it lacks posterior meniscotibial (coronary) attachments and is held only by the ligament of Wrisberg. The best treatment is:
o: Partial meniscectomy of the posterior horn only
Saucerisation if needed with peripheral repair to stabilise the posterior horn
items.e: The Wrisberg variant of discoid meniscus is unstable because of absent posterior capsular attachment; treatment is stabilisation of the posterior horn by peripheral repair (with saucerisation if discoid), avoiding meniscectomy.

items.q: After ACL reconstruction, a patient cannot achieve full extension. The graft impinges on the anterior intercondylar notch roof in extension. The most likely technical error is:
o: A tibial tunnel placed too anteriorly
A femoral tunnel placed too posteriorly
Graft fixed with the knee in full extension
A tibial tunnel placed too posteriorly
items.e: An anteriorly placed tibial tunnel makes the graft impinge on the notch roof in extension, causing loss of extension, effusion and graft failure; a posterior tibial tunnel produces a vertical graft with poor rotational control.

items.q: The KANON randomised trial (Frobell et al., NEJM 2010) in young active adults with acute ACL tears compared structured rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction with rehabilitation and optional delayed reconstruction. At 2 years:
o: Early reconstruction gave significantly better KOOS scores
There was no significant difference in KOOS scores
Delayed reconstruction led to more meniscal surgery and worse KOOS
items.e: KANON found no difference in the KOOS4 between the strategies at 2 and 5 years, and about 60% of the rehabilitation group avoided reconstruction, though meniscal procedures were somewhat more frequent with delayed surgery.

items.q: The FIDELITY trial (Sihvonen et al., NEJM 2013) of patients aged 35–65 with degenerative medial meniscal tears and no knee osteoarthritis compared arthroscopic partial meniscectomy with:
o: Sham surgery, finding no difference in outcomes
items.e: FIDELITY showed that arthroscopic partial meniscectomy was no better than sham arthroscopy for knee pain and function at 12 months in degenerative non-obstructive tears.

items.q: The METEOR trial (Katz et al., NEJM 2013) of patients with a symptomatic meniscal tear and mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis found that, compared with arthroscopic partial meniscectomy, physical therapy:
o: Gave similar functional improvement at 6 months, although about 30% crossed over to surgery
items.e: In METEOR, WOMAC function improved similarly in both groups at 6 months, with about 30% of the physical therapy group crossing over to surgery, supporting an initial trial of physiotherapy.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a 6 cm² osteochondral defect of the medial femoral condyle with 8 mm of subchondral bone loss after failed fixation of an osteochondral fragment. The most appropriate cartilage procedure is:
items.e: Large defects with significant subchondral bone loss are best treated with fresh osteochondral allograft, which restores both bone and hyaline cartilage; microfracture suits small lesions and ACI alone does not replace bone loss.

items.q: In the LaPrade classification of meniscal root tears, the most common type is:
o: Type 3 – bucket-handle tear with root detachment
Type 2 – complete radial tear within 9 mm of the root attachment
Type 5 – bony avulsion of the root
items.e: Type 2 complete radial tears within 9 mm of the bony root attachment (subdivided 2A–2C by distance) are the most common; root tears are functionally equivalent to total meniscectomy and are repaired, for example by transtibial pull-out.

items.q: A 19-year-old footballer with an acute ACL tear is most likely to have an associated root tear of the:
o: Posterior root of the medial meniscus
Anterior root of the medial meniscus
Anterior root of the lateral meniscus
Posterior root of the lateral meniscus
items.e: Posterior lateral meniscal root tears occur acutely with ACL injuries in young patients, whereas posterior medial root tears are usually degenerative in middle-aged, often female, patients.

items.q: In a revision ACL reconstruction after two graft failures, the lateral radiograph shows a posterior tibial slope of 15°. The additional procedure most likely to protect the new graft is:
o: Medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy that increases slope
items.e: A posterior tibial slope above about 12° increases anterior tibial translation and ACL graft force; slope-reducing anterior closing-wedge osteotomy is recommended in revision cases.

items.q: Numbness over the anterolateral aspect of the proximal leg and knee after hamstring tendon harvest for ACL reconstruction is due to injury to the:
o: Infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve
items.e: The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve crosses the anteromedial tibia near the harvest site and is commonly injured, giving numbness lateral and inferior to the incision; an oblique incision reduces the risk.

items.q: With the patient supine, the knee flexed to 90° and the foot held on the couch, contraction of the quadriceps causes the tibia to shift anteriorly from a posteriorly subluxed position. This positive test indicates deficiency of the:
items.e: In the quadriceps active test (Daniel), the PCL-deficient tibia sags posteriorly at 90° and is pulled forward by the patellar tendon when the quadriceps contracts.

items.q: In prospective studies of female athletes (Hewett et al.), the biomechanical factor that best predicted later non-contact ACL injury was:
o: Increased dynamic knee valgus (knee abduction moment) on landing
items.e: Greater knee abduction angles and moments during drop-jump landing predicted ACL injury in female athletes; neuromuscular training programmes aim to reduce dynamic valgus and increase hamstring activation.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a firm, tender swelling at the lateral joint line of the knee that is more prominent in extension. MRI shows a multiloculated cyst adjacent to the lateral meniscus. The associated meniscal tear is most likely:
o: Radial tear of the posterior root
items.e: Parameniscal cysts, most common laterally, form when synovial fluid is pumped through a horizontal cleavage tear; treatment is arthroscopic decompression with partial meniscectomy or repair.

items.q: In the ICRS classification of cartilage lesions, a defect extending deeper than 50% of the cartilage thickness down to the calcified layer, but not through the subchondral bone, is grade:
items.e: ICRS grade 1 is superficial, grade 2 under 50% depth, grade 3 over 50% depth (to calcified cartilage or subchondral plate) and grade 4 extends through the subchondral bone.

items.q: In conventional polyethylene acetabular liners, periprosthetic osteolysis becomes common when the linear wear rate exceeds about:
items.e: Osteolysis is uncommon below about 0.05 mm per year and increasingly frequent above 0.1 mm per year (Dumbleton et al.), reflecting the burden of submicron wear particles.

items.q: Infusing or blending vitamin E into highly cross-linked polyethylene is designed to:
o: Neutralise residual free radicals without remelting, preserving mechanical properties
Increase the crystallinity and hardness of the polymer
items.e: Vitamin E (α-tocopherol) acts as an antioxidant that stabilises free radicals after irradiation, avoiding the loss of fatigue strength and toughness caused by remelting.

items.q: Retrieved tibial polyethylene inserts from older TKAs show a subsurface white band and delamination. This was mainly caused by:
o: Gamma irradiation sterilisation in air with oxidation during shelf storage
Direct compression moulding of the insert
items.e: Gamma sterilisation in air creates free radicals that combine with oxygen, causing oxidative embrittlement on the shelf and in vivo; the subsurface oxidation band leads to fatigue delamination, so sterilisation is now done in inert gas or vacuum packaging.

items.q: In anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty, compared with keeled cemented glenoid components, pegged cemented glenoid components have been shown to have:
o: Higher rates of early radiolucent lines
Lower rates of radiolucent lines and better seating
items.e: Randomised trials (for example Gartsman et al.) found fewer radiolucent lines with pegged than keeled cemented glenoid components, which is why pegged designs are widely preferred.

items.q: The commonest cause of anterior instability after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty is:
items.e: Subscapularis insufficiency, from failure of tenotomy or peel repair or lesser tuberosity osteotomy non-union, is the leading cause of anterior instability after anatomic TSA; anterior component malposition contributes.

items.q: In shoulder hemiarthroplasty or anatomic TSA, the top of the humeral head component should normally sit how far above the top of the greater tuberosity?
items.e: Restoring a head-to-tuberosity height of about 5–8 mm preserves rotator cuff tension and avoids impingement (too low) or overstuffing and cuff overload (too high).

items.q: A 46-year-old labourer has painful medial compartment osteoarthritis, a functionally intact ACL, full range of motion and 8° of varus from the tibia (medial proximal tibial angle 83°). The most appropriate surgery is:
items.e: Young, active patients with medial compartment arthritis and a varus deformity of tibial (metaphyseal) origin are best treated with high tibial osteotomy, which corrects the deformity at its source and preserves the joint.

items.q: An 18-month-old child with a recent upper respiratory infection has a painful swollen knee, temperature 38.1 °C and CRP 30 mg/L. Aspiration yields turbid fluid with 60,000 WBC/mm³ (85% neutrophils), but Gram stain and routine cultures are negative at 48 hours. Which organism is most likely?
items.e: Kingella kingae is the commonest cause of osteoarticular infection between 6 months and 4 years; it is fastidious, often culture-negative on routine media, and is best detected by inoculating blood-culture bottles or by PCR.

items.q: A previously healthy child has fever and localised metaphyseal tenderness of the distal femur for 3 days; plain radiographs are normal. Which investigation best confirms early acute osteomyelitis?
items.e: MRI shows marrow oedema and subperiosteal abscess within days of onset, well before the 10–14 days needed for radiographic changes, and guides any surgical drainage.

items.q: A 3-year-old has a painless fusiform swelling of the proximal phalanx of the index finger. Radiographs show an expanded diaphysis with a cyst-like lytic cavity and thin cortices ('ballooned' bone) with minimal periosteal reaction. Most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Spina ventosa is tuberculous dactylitis of the short tubular bones in young children, producing a spindle-shaped expanded diaphysis; sickle dactylitis is usually bilateral, acute and painful in infants.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a classification of distal radius fractures?
items.e: Schatzker classifies tibial plateau fractures; Frykman, Fernandez (mechanism-based) and Melone (four-part articular) are distal radius classifications.

items.q: A 22-year-old cricketer has a bony mallet injury of the ring finger. Lateral radiograph shows a dorsal fragment involving 40% of the articular surface with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx. Best management?
o: Stack splint in extension for 6 weeks
items.e: Volar subluxation of the distal phalanx (usually with a fragment >30% of the joint) is the accepted indication for operative treatment, commonly by extension-block pinning; non-subluxed bony mallets do well with splinting.

items.q: Compared with open repair of an acute Achilles tendon rupture, percutaneous repair carries a significantly higher risk of which complication?
items.e: Percutaneous techniques reduce wound complications but the sural nerve, crossing the lateral border of the tendon about 10 cm above the calcaneus, is at risk from blind suture passage.

items.q: A 6-year-old has an expansile, eccentric lytic lesion of the femoral neck suspected to be an aneurysmal bone cyst. Which investigation best demonstrates the characteristic fluid–fluid levels?
items.e: MRI (and to a lesser extent CT) shows the multiloculated cavities with fluid–fluid levels from layering blood products; they are not pathognomonic, as telangiectatic osteosarcoma can mimic ABC, so biopsy remains essential.

items.q: Which statement about giant cell tumour of bone is FALSE?
o: It typically arises in the epiphysis of a long bone after physeal closure
Recurrence after simple curettage alone is about 25–50%
It is more common in males than in females
Benign pulmonary metastases occur in about 2–5% of cases
items.e: GCT has a slight female predominance; it is epiphyseal-metaphyseal in skeletally mature patients, recurs frequently after curettage without adjuvants, and can produce 'benign' lung metastases in a small proportion.

items.q: A 32-year-old has a Campanacci grade II giant cell tumour of the distal femoral epiphysis-metaphysis with an intact articular surface. Most appropriate treatment?
o: Extended curettage with high-speed burr, local adjuvant and PMMA cementation
items.e: Joint-preserving extended intralesional curettage with burring, adjuvants (phenol, hydrogen peroxide, argon/liquid nitrogen) and cement gives local control near 85–90%; resection is reserved for unsalvageable joints.

items.q: After complete axonal transection of a peripheral nerve, when do fibrillation potentials first appear on needle EMG of the denervated muscles?
items.e: Fibrillations and positive sharp waves indicate denervation and appear after Wallerian degeneration reaches the muscle, typically 2–3 weeks after injury (earlier in proximal muscles); EMG before this can be falsely reassuring.

items.q: Which muscle is the principal antagonist of iliopsoas at the hip joint?
items.e: Iliopsoas is the chief hip flexor; gluteus maximus is the chief hip extensor and therefore its main antagonist, while rectus femoris is a synergist.

items.q: During repair of a massive retracted rotator cuff tear, lateral advancement of the supraspinatus by more than about 3 cm places which nerve at risk of traction injury?
items.e: The suprascapular nerve is tethered at the suprascapular notch and supplies supraspinatus from its deep surface, so excessive lateral advancement (>3 cm) can stretch its motor branches.

items.q: The maximum isometric force a skeletal muscle can generate is directly proportional to its:
items.e: Force is proportional to physiological cross-sectional area (increased by pennation, which packs more fibres), whereas fibre length determines excursion and contraction velocity.

items.q: A 66-year-old man with CKD (eGFR 25 mL/min) and a recent bleeding peptic ulcer has an acute monoarticular gout flare of the knee; septic arthritis has been excluded. Most appropriate treatment?
items.e: NSAIDs are contraindicated by CKD and ulcer, colchicine needs dose reduction in severe renal impairment; intra-articular steroid is safe and effective for a single large joint. Allopurinol is urate-lowering, not flare treatment, and starts low in CKD.

items.q: Which statement about crystal identification under compensated polarised light microscopy is FALSE?
o: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent
Positively birefringent rhomboid crystals are diagnostic of gout
Crystals can be identified in synovial fluid even between attacks
items.e: Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (CPPD, pseudogout); gout shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent urate crystals.

items.q: Which radiographic finding is most characteristic of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease?
o: Subchondral cysts in the femoral head
Chondrocalcinosis of the knee menisci and triangular fibrocartilage
items.e: Linear or punctate calcification of hyaline and fibrocartilage (menisci, TFCC, pubic symphysis) is the hallmark of CPPD; overhanging-edge erosions suggest gout.

items.q: A 24-year-old has an isolated posterior wall acetabular fracture involving about 15% of the wall on CT. The joint is congruent and the hip is stable on dynamic fluoroscopic examination under anaesthesia. Best management?
o: Non-operative treatment with protected weight bearing
items.e: Small posterior wall fractures (<20–25%) with a stable, congruent hip on EUA can be treated non-operatively; wall fragments >40–50% or instability require ORIF.

items.q: In a young adult with a high-energy pelvic ring injury, which imaging modality best defines associated sacral fractures for planning fixation?
o: CT of the pelvis with reconstructions
items.e: Thin-slice CT with multiplanar reconstructions defines sacral fracture lines, foraminal involvement and dysmorphism and is essential before iliosacral screw placement; plain films miss many sacral fractures.

items.q: Which acetabular fracture pattern is most commonly associated with a traumatic posterior hip dislocation?
items.e: A dashboard force on the flexed, adducted hip drives the head posteriorly and most often shears off the posterior wall; it is also the most common acetabular fracture overall.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman has a displaced anterior column acetabular fracture extending to the pubic ramus. Which surgical approach is classically used for its fixation?
items.e: The ilioinguinal approach (or the intrapelvic modified Stoppa) gives access to the whole anterior column from the SI joint to the symphysis; Kocher–Langenbeck accesses the posterior column and wall.

items.q: Which clinical feature best predicts a good outcome after microdiscectomy for a single-level lumbar disc herniation?
o: Back pain dominant over leg pain
Leg pain dominant over back pain with a positive straight-leg raise
items.e: Radicular leg pain exceeding back pain, a positive tension sign and concordant imaging predict success; back-dominant pain, long duration and compensation claims predict poorer outcomes.

items.q: In the SPORT trial of lumbar spinal stenosis without spondylolisthesis, the as-treated analysis showed:
o: Greater improvement in pain and function with surgery, maintained through 4 years
No difference between surgery and non-operative care at any time
Better outcomes with non-operative care at 2 years
Surgical benefit at 6 weeks that disappeared by 1 year
items.e: SPORT's as-treated analysis showed significantly greater improvement in pain and function after decompression compared with non-operative care, persisting through 4 years; intention-to-treat comparisons were diluted by crossover.

items.q: During lumbar decompression, which intraoperative neuromonitoring modality is most sensitive for real-time detection of nerve root irritation?
items.e: Free-run EMG detects neurotonic discharges from mechanical irritation of individual roots in real time; SSEPs are slow, averaged and mainly reflect dorsal column function, and are insensitive to single-root injury.

items.q: Revision THA: radiographs show a loose cup that has migrated superolaterally more than 3 cm above the superior obturator line, with an intact Köhler's line, moderate ischial osteolysis and partial teardrop loss. Paprosky type?
items.e: Paprosky IIIA is 'up and out': superolateral migration >3 cm with Köhler's line intact; IIIB is 'up and in' with Köhler's line breached, severe ischial lysis and teardrop obliteration, often with pelvic discontinuity.

items.q: Which intraoperative measure has most consistently been shown to reduce dislocation after primary THA through the posterior approach?
o: Use of a smaller (22 mm) femoral head
Repair of the posterior capsule and short external rotators
items.e: Enhanced posterior soft-tissue repair lowers dislocation after the posterior approach from roughly 4–5% to about 1%; larger heads also help, whereas steep cups and retroverted stems increase instability.

items.q: A 27-year-old footballer has groin pain with a positive FADIR test; radiographs suggest cam morphology. Which investigation best maps the three-dimensional extent of the cam lesion and femoral version for planning arthroscopic osteoplasty?
items.e: CT with 3-D reconstruction precisely localises the cam and pincer morphology and allows femoral version measurement, guiding resection; MR arthrography is preferred for labral and chondral assessment.

items.q: Which nerve is most at risk during creation of the anterior portal in hip arthroscopy?
items.e: Branches of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve lie within a few millimetres of the anterior portal; the femoral nerve is about 3–4 cm medial, and the sciatic nerve is at risk with the posterolateral portal.

items.q: A symptomatic young adult hip has an alpha angle of 68° measured on radial MRI at the anterosuperior head–neck junction. This finding indicates:
items.e: An alpha angle above about 50–55° indicates loss of femoral head–neck offset (cam morphology); pincer and dysplasia are acetabular parameters assessed by centre-edge angle, crossover sign and Tönnis angle.

items.q: After full Ponseti correction including percutaneous tenotomy, what is the recommended foot abduction brace protocol?
o: Full time (about 23 h/day) for 3 months, then nights and naps until 4–5 years of age
Bracing only if the deformity recurs
items.e: The brace holds the feet in 60–70° external rotation; non-compliance with bracing is the main cause of recurrence after Ponseti treatment.

items.q: In post-polio residual paralysis, isolated paralysis of the triceps surae with functioning dorsiflexors produces which foot deformity?
items.e: Unopposed dorsiflexors pull the calcaneus into dorsiflexion, while intact intrinsic and long toe flexors raise the arch, producing a calcaneocavus foot; deformity results from muscle imbalance during growth.

items.q: In chronic scapholunate dissociation, which finding is characteristic on the lateral wrist radiograph?
o: Scapholunate angle below 30° with a volar-flexed lunate (VISI)
Scapholunate angle above 70° with a dorsally tilted lunate (DISI)
items.e: SL ligament failure lets the scaphoid flex and the lunate extend with the triquetrum, giving DISI with an SL angle >60–70°; on the AP view look for SL gap >3 mm and the cortical ring sign.

items.q: Why do proximal pole scaphoid fractures carry the highest risk of avascular necrosis?
o: The main blood supply enters the dorsal ridge distally and flows retrograde to the proximal pole
The proximal pole is supplied only by the ulnar artery
The scaphoid has no intraosseous anastomoses distally
Synovial fluid inhibits fracture healing only at the proximal pole
items.e: About 70–80% of scaphoid blood supply comes from dorsal ridge branches of the radial artery entering at or distal to the waist; a proximal fracture cuts off this retrograde flow, so AVN rates rise to 30% or more.

items.q: Which primary malignancy most commonly produces osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone metastases in men?
items.e: Prostate metastases are classically blastic; renal and thyroid metastases are purely lytic and highly vascular, so preoperative embolisation is advised before fixation.

items.q: A woman with breast cancer has a purely lytic lesion in the femoral diaphysis involving more than two-thirds of the cortical width, with mild pain. What is the Mirels score and management?
o: 9 – prophylactic fixation with a long cephalomedullary nail, then radiotherapy
items.e: Lower limb 2 + mild pain 1 + lytic 3 + >2/3 width 3 = 9; a score of 9 or more carries about a 33% fracture risk, so prophylactic fixation (protecting the whole bone) is followed by radiotherapy.

items.q: As part of multimodal analgesia for TKA, which regional technique best preserves quadriceps strength for early mobilisation?
items.e: The adductor canal block targets the saphenous and articular branches and largely spares motor fibres to the quadriceps, reducing fall risk compared with femoral nerve block while giving similar analgesia.

items.q: An 80-year-old on warfarin (INR 2.8) has a displaced femoral neck fracture and is otherwise fit for surgery. Best approach to anticoagulation?
o: Stop warfarin and wait 5 days for the INR to normalise
Routine FFP transfusion regardless of INR
Proceed immediately with spinal anaesthesia at INR 2.8
Give intravenous vitamin K and proceed when the INR is acceptable, avoiding delay beyond 36 hours
items.e: Low-dose IV vitamin K normalises the INR within 12–24 h and allows surgery within the recommended 36 hours; neuraxial anaesthesia needs an INR around ≤1.5, and delay increases mortality.

items.q: For routine elective shoulder arthroscopy in a patient without additional thromboembolic risk factors, which VTE prophylaxis is recommended?
o: Early mobilisation only, without routine pharmacological prophylaxis
items.e: VTE is rare after upper-limb arthroscopy, so guidelines (e.g. NICE) do not recommend routine chemoprophylaxis; it is reserved for patients with significant individual risk factors.

items.q: Phemister's triad of tuberculous arthritis on radiographs comprises:
o: Subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes and early joint-space loss
Juxta-articular osteoporosis, peripheral osseous erosions and gradual joint-space narrowing
Periosteal reaction, rapid joint-space loss and early ankylosis
items.e: Tuberculous synovitis preserves cartilage for a long time, so joint-space loss is slow, unlike pyogenic arthritis; marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia dominate.

items.q: A 68-year-old independent, cognitively intact woman who walks unaided outdoors has a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. Preferred treatment per NICE guidance?
items.e: NICE recommends THA for displaced intracapsular fractures in patients who walk independently outdoors with no more than a stick, are not cognitively impaired and are fit for surgery; fixation has high failure rates in this age group.

items.q: A 45-year-old man has a reverse-oblique intertrochanteric fracture (AO/OTA 31A3). Most appropriate fixation?
items.e: In reverse-oblique fractures the fracture line parallels the sliding axis of a DHS, so the shaft displaces medially and fixation fails; an intramedullary nail acts as a buttress and has much lower failure rates.

items.q: A 23-year-old female distance runner has activity-related groin pain. MRI shows a femoral neck stress fracture with a fracture line on the superolateral (tension) side of the neck. Best management?
o: Urgent internal fixation with cannulated screws
Protected weight bearing on crutches for 6 weeks
items.e: Tension-side stress fractures are prone to displacement and AVN and need prompt fixation; compression-side (inferomedial) fractures involving <50% of the neck can usually be treated with protected weight bearing. Screen for the female athlete triad (RED-S).

items.q: A 35-year-old has a displaced vertical (Pauwels III) femoral neck fracture after a fall from height. Which construct is biomechanically superior to three parallel cannulated screws for this pattern?
o: Fixed-angle device such as a sliding hip screw with an anti-rotation screw
items.e: Vertical shear forces in Pauwels III fractures cause varus collapse with parallel screws; a fixed-angle device (sliding hip screw with derotation screw, or a medial buttress plate) resists shear better, while arthroplasty is avoided in young patients.

items.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive man has chronic back pain. MRI shows paradiscal enhancement with a paravertebral abscess at L4–L5 and no neurological deficit. Most appropriate initial step?
o: CT-guided biopsy/aspiration for histology, GeneXpert and culture, then ATT
Start anti-tubercular therapy without tissue diagnosis
items.e: Tissue diagnosis (histopathology, CBNAAT/GeneXpert for rifampicin resistance, and culture) should precede ATT, particularly in HIV where atypical organisms, lymphoma and drug resistance are more frequent; a neurologically intact patient rarely needs surgery first.

items.q: Which classification of spinal tuberculosis uses MRI findings (anterior lesion, kyphosis, posterior element involvement) to recommend anterior, posterior or combined surgical stabilisation?
items.e: Mehta and Bhojraj grouped thoracic TB into four MRI-based groups to choose the surgical approach; Frankel grades neurological deficit, Denis is a trauma classification, and Tuli's middle path is a management philosophy.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT, by itself, an indication for surgery in spinal tuberculosis?
o: Neurological deficit not improving after 3–4 weeks of ATT
Spinal instability or 'spine-at-risk' signs predicting severe kyphosis
items.e: HIV co-infection modifies drug interactions and monitoring but is not a surgical indication; failure of neural recovery on ATT, instability or progressive kyphosis, and diagnostic uncertainty are accepted indications.

items.q: A 60-year-old diabetic has fever, back pain and new left foot drop. CT shows a paravertebral abscess from T9 to T11. Which imaging best defines epidural extension and the full extent of disease before debridement?
o: Contrast CT of the involved levels
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine
items.e: Gadolinium MRI shows marrow, disc, epidural and paraspinal involvement, and whole-spine imaging detects skip lesions in up to 10–15% of spinal infections.

items.q: Why is the wear advantage of highly cross-linked polyethylene less clear-cut in TKA than in THA?
o: Knee bearings have much lower contact stresses than hips
TKA wear is dominated by fatigue (pitting, delamination) and cross-linking reduces fatigue and fracture resistance
HXLPE cannot be manufactured in tibial insert shapes
Cobalt-chrome femoral components release ions that degrade HXLPE
items.e: Hip wear is mainly adhesive/abrasive, which cross-linking greatly reduces; non-conforming knee bearings have high cyclic contact stresses, so fatigue failure matters and the reduced toughness of HXLPE limits its benefit.

items.q: Seven years after a TKA with a cobalt-chrome on polyethylene bearing, an expanding osteolytic cyst appears beneath the tibial tray. What is the key pathogenic mechanism?
o: Type IV hypersensitivity to cobalt ions
Stress shielding beneath the tibial tray
Macrophage phagocytosis of submicron polyethylene particles releasing cytokines that activate osteoclasts via RANKL
items.e: Particles of about 0.1–1 µm are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 and PGE2, upregulating RANKL and osteoclastic resorption; stress shielding causes diffuse bone loss, not expansile cysts.

items.q: On the WADA Prohibited List, which category is prohibited at all times (both in- and out-of-competition)?
items.e: Anabolic agents, peptide hormones, beta-2 agonists, hormone and metabolic modulators, diuretics/masking agents and prohibited methods including gene and cell doping are banned at all times; stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids and glucocorticoids are banned in competition only.

items.q: Indirect detection of autologous blood doping in elite sport currently relies mainly on:
o: A direct urine test for autologous red cells
The haematological module of the Athlete Biological Passport
items.e: Autologous transfusion cannot be detected directly; longitudinal monitoring of haemoglobin, reticulocyte percentage and the OFF-score in the Athlete Biological Passport identifies abnormal variations.

items.q: Which is NOT a radiographic feature of nutritional rickets in a 2-year-old?
o: Dense metaphyseal bands from excessive mineralisation
Cupping and fraying of the metaphyses
items.e: Rickets is a failure of mineralisation at the physis, giving widened physes, cupped and frayed metaphyses and bowing; dense metaphyseal bands suggest lead poisoning or healing rickets, not active disease.

items.q: A 4-year-old with bowed legs has premature loss of deciduous teeth with intact roots, and a very low serum alkaline phosphatase. Deficiency of which enzyme causes this condition?
items.e: Hypophosphatasia results from ALPL mutations; accumulated pyrophosphate inhibits mineralisation. It is treated with enzyme replacement (asfotase alfa), and low ALP distinguishes it from other forms of rickets.

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has progressive erosions of the hand joints despite an adequate dose of methotrexate. Next step in medical management?
o: Add a biological DMARD such as a TNF inhibitor
