items.e: Treat-to-target guidance (EULAR/ACR) escalates to a biological or targeted synthetic DMARD (e.g. TNF inhibitor) when methotrexate fails to control disease; NSAIDs and steroids do not halt erosive progression.

items.q: Which procedure for Dupuytren disease has the lowest recurrence rate?
items.e: Replacing the involved palmar skin with a graft (firebreak) gives the lowest recurrence; needle fasciotomy and collagenase are less invasive but recur in roughly half of patients within 5 years.

items.q: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has end-stage ankle arthritis with 25° valgus deformity and collapse of the talar body. Most appropriate surgery?
items.e: Total ankle arthroplasty is relatively contraindicated by coronal deformity above about 15–20°, talar collapse or AVN and poor bone stock; arthrodesis gives durable pain relief. Synovectomy and osteotomy are for earlier disease.

items.q: What is the most common long-term complication of a displaced talar neck fracture?
o: Avascular necrosis of the talar body
items.e: Post-traumatic arthritis, most often subtalar, occurs in more than half of patients and is more common than AVN; malunion (usually varus) further increases the risk.

items.q: A 12-year-old has a slowly enlarging painless hard swelling above the knee. Radiographs show a pedunculated bony projection pointing away from the joint, whose cortex and medulla are continuous with those of the distal femoral metaphysis. Most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Corticomedullary continuity with the host bone is diagnostic of osteochondroma; parosteal osteosarcoma is attached to the cortex with a cleavage plane, and myositis ossificans matures from the periphery inwards.

items.q: Which statement about chondroblastoma is FALSE?
o: It usually arises in the epiphysis of skeletally immature patients
It shows marked nuclear pleomorphism with atypical mitoses, indicating a high-grade malignancy
It is usually treated by curettage and bone grafting
items.e: Chondroblastoma is a benign epiphyseal tumour of adolescents with polygonal chondroblasts, grooved 'coffee-bean' nuclei and chicken-wire calcification; it does not show high-grade atypia, though recurrence and rare benign lung metastases occur.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has a 5-cm destructive juxtacortical lesion of the distal femur with chaotic mineralisation on radiographs. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: MRI of the whole femur before biopsy
items.e: Local staging with MRI of the entire bone (showing marrow extent and skip lesions) precedes biopsy, which should then be a core biopsy planned along the definitive resection tract at the treating sarcoma centre.

items.q: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman is started on raloxifene for osteoporosis. What is its most important serious adverse effect?
items.e: Raloxifene raises the risk of DVT and PE roughly two- to three-fold and causes hot flushes and leg cramps; unlike tamoxifen it does not stimulate the endometrium, and it reduces invasive breast cancer risk.

items.q: An adult with spinal deformity has PI–LL mismatch 25°, SVA 7 cm and pelvic tilt 28°. What are the SRS–Schwab sagittal modifiers?
items.e: Thresholds: PI–LL <10° = 0, 10–20° = +, >20° = ++; SVA <4 cm = 0, 4–9.5 cm = +, >9.5 cm = ++; PT <20° = 0, 20–30° = +, >30° = ++. These modifiers correlate with disability (ODI).

items.q: A 60-year-old with an osteoporotic L3 fracture has PI 70°, PT 20°, SS 50° and lumbar lordosis 30° on standing films. Which mechanism does the pelvis mainly use to compensate for sagittal imbalance?
o: Anteversion, with an increase in sacral slope
Retroversion, with an increase in pelvic tilt
items.e: Pelvic incidence is a fixed morphological parameter (PI = PT + SS); the pelvis compensates by retroverting, raising PT and lowering SS, along with knee flexion and reduced thoracic kyphosis.

items.q: After a long posterior thoracolumbar fusion, proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) is most commonly defined radiographically as a proximal junctional angle of:
o: ≥10° and at least 10° greater than the preoperative value
≥30° measured from the UIV to the sacrum
items.e: The Glattes definition measures the angle between the UIV inferior endplate and the endplate two levels above; PJK is ≥10° and ≥10° greater than before surgery. Proximal junctional failure adds fracture, instability or neurological compromise.

items.q: Six years after a metal-on-metal THA, a patient has hip pain. Synovial alpha-defensin is positive, but cultures, synovial WBC and CRP are normal and the fluid is dark grey. The most likely explanation for the alpha-defensin result is:
o: False positive due to metallosis / adverse local tissue reaction
items.e: Alpha-defensin is highly specific for PJI, but false positives occur with metallosis and adverse local tissue reactions; interpret it alongside the full ICM criteria.

items.q: The CRIME80 score (COPD, CRP >150 mg/L, rheumatoid arthritis, index arthroplasty for femoral neck fracture, male sex, exchange of modular components not done, age >80) predicts failure of DAIR in:
o: Chronic PJI with a sinus tract
items.e: CRIME80 was developed for late acute haematogenous PJI, whereas the KLIC score predicts DAIR failure in early acute postoperative PJI.

items.q: During the posterior approach to the hip, brisk bleeding is encountered while dividing the quadratus femoris. Which vessel is responsible?
o: Ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery
Ascending branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery
items.e: The ascending branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery runs deep to quadratus femoris toward the trochanteric fossa; it is also the main head supply preserved in the Ganz surgical dislocation.

items.q: Patellar clunk syndrome after TKA is caused by:
o: A fibrous nodule at the junction of the quadriceps tendon and superior pole of the patella catching in the femoral box
Lateral patellar subluxation from an internally rotated femoral component
items.e: It is typical of posterior-stabilised designs: the suprapatellar fibrous nodule enters the intercondylar box in flexion and clunks out at 30–45° during extension; treatment is arthroscopic or open excision.

items.q: During TKA for a fixed valgus knee, which lateral structure is tight mainly in flexion?
items.e: The iliotibial band and posterolateral capsule are tight in extension, the popliteus in flexion, and the LCL in both; releases are chosen according to which gap is tight.

items.q: On the first postoperative day after TKA for a 25° valgus deformity with a 20° flexion contracture, the patient develops foot drop. Immediate management?
o: Immediate exploration and neurolysis of the common peroneal nerve
Ankle–foot orthosis and review at 3 months only
Remove constrictive dressings and flex the knee to about 20–30°
Nerve conduction studies before any intervention
items.e: Correcting combined valgus and flexion deformity stretches the common peroneal nerve; releasing dressings and flexing the knee relieves tension, and most palsies recover partially or completely.

items.q: Two years after posterior-stabilised TKA, a patient has recurrent effusions, difficulty climbing stairs and anteroposterior laxity at 90° of flexion, with a stable knee in full extension. Best definitive treatment?
o: Isolated exchange to a thicker polyethylene insert
Revision to restore the flexion gap, e.g. a larger femoral component or posterior femoral augments
items.e: This is flexion instability: a thicker insert would also tighten the balanced extension gap and cause a flexion contracture, so the flexion gap must be selectively filled at revision.

items.q: A patient has groin pain on active hip flexion and straight-leg raise 6 months after THA, relieved by a diagnostic iliopsoas sheath injection. The most common implant-related cause is:
o: Anterior overhang of a retroverted or lateralised acetabular cup
items.e: An anteriorly prominent cup rim (overhang >8–12 mm on CT) irritates the iliopsoas tendon; options include arthroscopic iliopsoas tenotomy or cup revision if malposition is gross.

items.q: For prophylaxis against heterotopic ossification after THA in a high-risk patient, single-dose radiotherapy (about 7–8 Gy) should be given:
o: Within 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery
Only after radiographic HO is seen
items.e: Radiation must be given in the narrow window around surgery, before mesenchymal cells differentiate into osteoblasts; NSAIDs such as indomethacin are the main alternative.

items.q: Instability after a reverse shoulder arthroplasty most commonly occurs in which arm position?
items.e: Reverse prostheses usually dislocate anteriorly in extension, adduction and internal rotation (e.g. pushing up from a chair); subscapularis deficiency and loss of deltoid tension are risk factors.

items.q: When performing a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy in a varus knee with chronic ACL deficiency, the posterior tibial slope should be:
o: Increased, to unload the medial compartment
Decreased, to reduce anterior tibial translation
items.e: Higher slope increases anterior tibial translation and stress on the ACL (graft); in ACL deficiency the slope is reduced, whereas in PCL deficiency it may be increased.

items.q: Internal rotation of the femoral component in TKA most commonly results in:
o: Lateral patellar maltracking and a tight medial flexion gap
items.e: The femoral component should be parallel to the surgical transepicondylar axis (roughly 3° external to the posterior condylar axis); internal rotation shifts the trochlea medially, causing patellar tilt or subluxation and an asymmetric flexion gap.

items.q: On radiographs of a shoulder with cuff tear arthropathy, the acromiohumeral interval is 4 mm with no acetabularisation of the acromion and a preserved glenohumeral joint space. Hamada grade?
items.e: Hamada: 1 AHI >6 mm; 2 AHI ≤5 mm; 3 acetabularisation of the acromion; 4 glenohumeral narrowing (4A without, 4B with acetabularisation); 5 humeral head collapse.

items.q: Anterior instability after anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty is most commonly due to:
items.e: Subscapularis tenotomy, peel or lesser tuberosity osteotomy must heal; its failure leads to anterior instability, whereas posterior instability is related to glenoid retroversion and posterior erosion.

items.q: The 'French paradox' in cemented hip arthroplasty refers to:
o: Better results with cementless than cemented stems in the elderly
Higher dislocation with larger femoral heads
Cement failure in Dorr C femurs
Good long-term results with canal-filling stems using a thin or incomplete cement mantle
items.e: Line-to-line canal-filling stems (e.g. Kerboull, Charnley-Kerboull) achieved excellent survival despite thin mantles, contradicting the teaching that a uniform 2 mm mantle is essential.

items.q: In hemiarthroplasty for a four-part proximal humerus fracture, the most important determinant of functional outcome is:
o: Anatomical healing of the greater and lesser tuberosities
Humeral head size exactly matching the native head
items.e: Tuberosity malposition or non-union (which occurs often in elderly osteoporotic bone) causes poor elevation; this is why reverse arthroplasty, which depends less on tuberosity healing, is preferred in the elderly.

items.q: According to large joint registries, the most common cause of revision within the first 2 years after primary TKA is:
items.e: Infection dominates early revisions, followed by instability; aseptic loosening and wear are more typical causes of late failure.

items.q: Before elective joint arthroplasty, a patient is a nasal Staphylococcus aureus carrier. The recommended preoperative measure is:
o: Postponing surgery until three negative swabs
Nasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine body washes (decolonisation)
items.e: Short-course decolonisation with intranasal mupirocin (or povidone-iodine) and chlorhexidine washing reduces surgical site infection in S. aureus carriers.

items.q: After primary TKA, persistent wound drainage beyond about 5–7 days despite local measures should be managed by:
o: Repeated aspiration of the knee every 48 hours
Return to theatre for irrigation and debridement with polyethylene exchange
items.e: Persistent drainage is a risk factor for deep infection; ICM consensus recommends surgical washout with modular exchange (and deep cultures) rather than antibiotic suppression.

items.q: After transtibial ACL reconstruction, a patient has a stable Lachman but a persistent pivot shift. Radiographs show the femoral tunnel high in the notch at the 12 o'clock position. Explanation?
o: A vertical, non-anatomic graft controls anterior translation but not rotational instability
Graft impingement causing a cyclops lesion
items.e: A vertical femoral tunnel places the graft near the axis of rotation, leaving rotatory laxity; anatomic low femoral tunnels (via anteromedial portal or outside-in drilling) better restore rotational control.

items.q: The STABILITY 1 randomised trial (Getgood et al., 2020) in young, high-risk patients showed that adding a lateral extra-articular tenodesis to hamstring ACL reconstruction:
o: Increased lateral compartment arthritis at 2 years
Significantly reduced graft rupture and persistent rotatory laxity
Made no difference to graft failure
Increased graft failure because of overconstraint
items.e: Adding a modified Lemaire LET reduced clinical failure from 40% to 25% and graft rupture from 11% to 4% at 2 years, with only small early increases in pain.

items.q: Which suture configuration is biomechanically strongest for repairing a vertical longitudinal meniscal tear?
items.e: Vertical sutures capture the strong circumferential collagen fibres of the meniscus, giving greater load to failure than horizontal sutures or rigid absorbable devices.

items.q: How is the Caton–Deschamps index calculated, and what value indicates patella alta?
o: Patellar tendon length divided by patellar length; >1.2
Patellar length divided by tendon length; <0.8
Distance from the tibial tubercle to the trochlear groove; >20 mm
Distance from the inferior edge of the patellar articular surface to the anterosuperior tibial plateau divided by the patellar articular surface length; >1.2
items.e: The Caton–Deschamps index uses the articular surface and is independent of tubercle position, making it useful after tubercle osteotomy; >1.2 is alta and <0.6 baja. Option B describes Insall–Salvati.

items.q: Dejour type D trochlear dysplasia is characterised by:
o: Crossing sign, supratrochlear spur and double contour with a cliff-shaped trochlea
Crossing sign only with a shallow but symmetrical trochlea
Flat trochlea with crossing sign but no spur
Hypoplastic medial facet only, without crossing sign
items.e: All Dejour types have the crossing sign; A shallow trochlea, B flat trochlea with spur, C asymmetric facets with double contour, D adds a vertical cliff between facets with spur and double contour.

items.q: Under the Instability Severity Index Score (Balg & Boileau), a score above 6 in a patient with recurrent anterior shoulder instability favours:
o: Bone block (Latarjet) procedure rather than arthroscopic Bankart repair
items.e: ISIS includes age <20, competitive and contact/overhead sport, hyperlaxity, Hill–Sachs and glenoid contour loss on AP radiographs; scores >6 had about 70% recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart repair.

items.q: A 24-year-old has recurrent anterior shoulder instability. MR arthrography shows the anterior labrum intact, but the inferior glenohumeral ligament has torn from its humeral attachment, turning the axillary pouch from a U-shape into a 'J' shape. Diagnosis?
items.e: Humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (J-sign on MRA) is a cause of failed Bankart repair if missed and needs open or arthroscopic repair of the IGHL to the humeral neck.

items.q: How does an ALPSA lesion differ from a classic Bankart lesion?
o: The labroligamentous complex is displaced medially and inferiorly on the scapular neck with an intact periosteal sleeve
The labrum is torn but remains in its anatomical position
There is a glenoid rim fracture
The IGHL is avulsed from the humerus
items.e: In anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion the complex heals medially on the neck; it must be mobilised and repaired back to the articular margin, otherwise recurrence is higher. A Perthes lesion is non-displaced with stripped periosteum.

items.q: Goutallier grade 3 fatty infiltration of the supraspinatus means:
o: Equal amounts of fat and muscle
items.e: Goutallier (CT, adapted to MRI): 0 normal, 1 some fatty streaks, 2 fat < muscle, 3 fat = muscle, 4 fat > muscle; grade ≥3 predicts poor healing and function after repair because fatty infiltration is irreversible.

items.q: In the Patte classification of rotator cuff tear retraction (coronal plane), stage 3 means the tendon stump has retracted to:
o: The level of the humeral head
items.e: Patte stage 1: stump near the footprint; stage 2: at the level of the humeral head; stage 3: at the glenoid. Greater retraction predicts a harder, less reliable repair.

items.q: Which clinical test is most sensitive for detecting a tear of the upper portion of the subscapularis?
items.e: Barth et al. found the bear-hug test the most sensitive for subscapularis tears, particularly partial upper-border tears; lift-off detects larger tears involving the lower part and needs adequate internal rotation.

items.q: A baseball pitcher has posterosuperior shoulder pain in late cocking with a 30° loss of internal rotation compared with the other side, and a reduced total arc of motion. First-line management?
o: Posterior capsular (sleeper) stretching and scapular rehabilitation
items.e: This is glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) from posteroinferior capsular contracture, which shifts the humeral head posterosuperiorly and causes internal impingement; most improve with sleeper and cross-body stretching.

items.q: The medial patellofemoral ligament is the primary restraint to lateral patellar translation in which range of knee flexion?
items.e: MPFL provides about 50–60% of the restraint to lateral displacement near extension; beyond about 30° the patella engages the trochlea, which becomes the main stabiliser.

items.q: A prepubescent 10-year-old (Tanner 1) has a complete ACL tear with recurrent instability. Which reconstruction avoids drilling across both physes?
o: Physeal-sparing combined intra- and extra-articular iliotibial band reconstruction (Micheli–Kocher)
Standard transphyseal reconstruction with bone–patellar tendon–bone graft
Primary ACL repair with suture anchors alone
Transtibial reconstruction with interference screws across the physis
items.e: In children with substantial growth remaining, physeal-sparing ITB (or all-epiphyseal) techniques reduce the risk of growth arrest and angular deformity; bone plugs and screws across the physis are avoided.

items.q: In an acute ACL injury, which meniscus is most commonly torn?
o: Neither, as meniscal tears occur only in chronic ACL deficiency
items.e: The pivot-shift mechanism injures the lateral meniscus in acute ACL tears, whereas in chronic ACL deficiency repeated anterior translation makes medial meniscal (posterior horn) tears more common.

items.q: Regarding the two bundles of the PCL, which statement is correct?
o: The anterolateral bundle is tight in extension and the posteromedial bundle is tight in flexion
Both bundles are tight in full extension only
The anterolateral bundle is tight in flexion and the posteromedial bundle is tight in extension
The posteromedial bundle is larger and stronger
items.e: The larger anterolateral bundle tightens in flexion and is the focus of single-bundle reconstruction (tensioned at about 90°); the posteromedial bundle tightens in extension.

items.q: A 55-year-old has an irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear with good pain-free passive motion, Hamada grade 1 and no glenohumeral arthritis. Which arthroscopic reconstruction restores superior stability?
items.e: Superior capsular reconstruction (graft from superior glenoid to greater tuberosity) restores the superior restraint and acts as a depressor of the humeral head in younger patients without arthritis; RSA is preferred for older patients or arthropathy.

items.q: To minimise arthrofibrosis after an acute ACL tear, reconstruction is best performed when:
o: The knee has regained full extension and minimal effusion, rather than after a fixed time interval
Exactly 6 weeks after injury regardless of knee status
Only after 6 months of failed rehabilitation
items.e: Arthrofibrosis is linked to operating on an inflamed, stiff knee; 'prehabilitation' to restore full extension and quadriceps control matters more than a fixed delay.

items.q: A neonate after a difficult shoulder-dystocia delivery holds the arm adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder, with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed; grasp is intact. Which deficit best explains this posture?
o: Paralysis of shoulder abduction and external rotation and of elbow flexion (C5–C6 upper trunk)
Paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and finger flexors (C8–T1 lower trunk)
Isolated radial nerve palsy from humeral shaft fracture
Complete flail arm from total plexus (C5–T1) avulsion
items.e: This is the 'waiter's tip' posture of Erb's palsy: loss of deltoid, supraspinatus/infraspinatus and biceps/brachialis (C5–C6), with C7 involvement adding wrist flexion. Preserved grasp excludes Klumpke (C8–T1) and total plexus palsy.

items.q: In an adult with a traction brachial plexus injury, which investigation has traditionally been regarded as the gold standard for demonstrating preganglionic root avulsion (pseudomeningocele, absent rootlets)?
o: Plain radiograph of the cervical spine
items.e: CT myelography shows pseudomeningoceles and absent ventral/dorsal rootlets and remains the reference standard, although high-resolution MRI is increasingly used as a non-invasive alternative. Ultrasound images the postganglionic plexus, not the intradural rootlets.

items.q: A 55-year-old man with varus ankle osteoarthritis has weight-bearing radiographs showing obliteration of the joint space in the medial gutter, while the tibiotalar joint space at the plafond is preserved. What is his Takakura stage?
items.e: Takakura: stage 1 no narrowing (sclerosis/osteophytes), 2 narrowing of the medial joint space, 3a obliteration limited to the medial gutter, 3b obliteration extending to the roof of the talar dome, 4 obliteration of the whole joint. Stage 3a is the classic indication for a low tibial (supramalleolar) osteotomy.

items.q: During ankle arthroscopy for a medial talar dome osteochondral lesion, the standard anteromedial portal is established. Where is it placed, and which structure is most at risk?
o: Lateral to peroneus tertius; superficial peroneal nerve
Between EHL and EDL; dorsalis pedis artery
Just medial to tibialis anterior at the joint line; saphenous vein and nerve
Posterior to the medial malleolus; posterior tibial neurovascular bundle
items.e: The anteromedial portal lies just medial to tibialis anterior at the joint line, with the great saphenous vein and saphenous nerve at risk. The anterocentral portal (between EHL and EDL) is avoided because of the dorsalis pedis artery and deep peroneal nerve.

items.q: A 28-year-old runner rolls his foot into plantarflexion and inversion and has anterolateral ankle swelling and tenderness anterior to the lateral malleolus. Anterior drawer test is positive with a negative talar tilt. Which ligament is injured?
items.e: The ATFL is taut in plantarflexion, is the first and most commonly torn lateral ligament, and is tested by the anterior drawer. A positive talar tilt (inversion stress in neutral) would indicate additional CFL injury.

items.q: All of the following statements about ankle arthritis are true EXCEPT:
o: Post-traumatic arthritis is the commonest cause of ankle arthritis
Ankle arthrodesis is ideally positioned in neutral dorsiflexion, about 5° of hindfoot valgus and external rotation matching the opposite limb
Primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis is the commonest cause of ankle arthritis
Ankle arthrodesis increases stress and late degeneration in the adjacent subtalar and midfoot joints
items.e: Unlike the hip and knee, the ankle rarely develops primary OA; about 70–80% of ankle arthritis is post-traumatic (rotational fractures, pilon fractures, recurrent instability). The other statements are true.

items.q: A 45-year-old man has a 9 cm deep, enlarging mass in the posterior thigh. Core-needle biopsy shows high-grade undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma and staging CT of the chest is clear. What is the standard local treatment?
o: Wide resection with negative margins combined with (neo)adjuvant radiotherapy
items.e: For a large, deep, high-grade extremity soft-tissue sarcoma, limb-salvage wide resection plus pre- or postoperative radiotherapy gives local control comparable to amputation. Marginal excision alone has an unacceptable local recurrence rate.

items.q: The FNCLCC (French) histological grading system for soft-tissue sarcoma is based on all of the following EXCEPT:
items.e: FNCLCC grade sums scores for differentiation (1–3), mitotic count per 10 HPF (1–3) and necrosis (0–2). Size is a staging (AJCC T) variable, not part of histological grade.

items.q: What is the most common site of distant metastasis of a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)?
items.e: Like most soft-tissue sarcomas, MPNST (half of which arise in NF1) spreads haematogenously, chiefly to the lungs; nodal spread is uncommon.

items.q: Beam-hardening (streak and cupping) artefact around a metal implant on CT arises fundamentally because:
o: The X-ray beam is polychromatic and lower-energy photons are preferentially absorbed
Partial-volume averaging occurs across thick slices
items.e: A polychromatic beam loses its low-energy photons as it passes through dense material, so its mean energy rises ('hardens') and attenuation is underestimated, producing dark streaks. Higher kVp, filtration and metal-artefact-reduction algorithms reduce it.

items.q: Which change reduces image noise on a CT scan without increasing radiation dose or reducing slice thickness?
items.e: Iterative reconstruction models noise statistically and lowers noise at a given dose. Raising kVp increases dose, thinner slices increase noise and lowering mAs increases noise.

items.q: A 32-year-old man on long-term oral steroids for severe asthma develops right groin pain with a limp. Hip radiographs are normal. Which investigation is most sensitive for early osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: MRI has about 99% sensitivity for early ONFH, showing the double-line sign before radiographic change; it also screens the asymptomatic contralateral hip, which is commonly involved in steroid-associated disease.

items.q: In the Ficat–Arlet staging of osteonecrosis of the femoral head, the radiographic crescent sign (subchondral fracture) indicates which stage?
items.e: Ficat stage I: normal radiographs; II: sclerosis/cysts with a spherical head; III: crescent sign and/or subchondral collapse; IV: joint-space narrowing and acetabular changes (secondary OA).

items.q: Which of the following is NOT an established risk factor for non-traumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: Corticosteroids, alcohol and haemoglobinopathies (with SLE, Gaucher disease, caisson disease and coagulopathies) are recognised causes; vitamin D deficiency is not.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman has painful atraumatic osteonecrosis of the humeral head with sclerosis but a preserved spherical head and no collapse (Cruess stage II). Non-operative measures have failed. Which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: Core decompression is indicated for pre-collapse (Cruess I–II) humeral head osteonecrosis. Arthroplasty is reserved for collapse (stage III onwards), with hemiarthroplasty if the glenoid is intact and TSA if it is involved.

items.q: Which MRI finding is regarded as virtually pathognomonic of osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
o: Diffuse bone-marrow oedema extending into the intertrochanteric region
items.e: The double-line sign is a low-signal outer rim (sclerotic reactive interface) with a high-signal inner band (hypervascular granulation tissue) on T2. Diffuse marrow oedema is non-specific and is typical of transient osteoporosis of the hip.

items.q: A multicentre randomised controlled trial (Chen et al., 2012) of alendronate versus placebo in pre-collapse (Steinberg II–III) osteonecrosis of the femoral head found that alendronate:
o: Significantly reduced collapse and need for THA
Produced no significant difference in collapse or progression to THA
Doubled the rate of atypical femoral fractures
items.e: In the double-blind RCT by Chen et al. (Arthritis Rheum 2012) alendronate did not prevent collapse, reduce the need for THA or improve symptoms at 2 years; earlier favourable reports were uncontrolled or small, so bisphosphonates are not established disease-modifying therapy.

items.q: A 23-year-old motorcyclist has a displaced medial tibial plateau split fracture (Schatzker IV) with 5 mm articular step-off and a mild varus deformity. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Long-leg hinged brace with early motion
Open reduction and medial/posteromedial buttress plating
items.e: Schatzker IV fractures are high-energy, unstable shear injuries (a fracture-dislocation equivalent) that need anatomical reduction and medial buttress (antiglide) plating. A lateral locking plate alone cannot buttress a medial shear fragment, and vascular and ligamentous injury must be excluded.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has a Schatzker VI bicondylar tibial plateau fracture with a comminuted lateral plateau and a displaced posteromedial coronal-plane fragment. Soft tissues have settled after a spanning external fixator. What is the preferred fixation?
o: Dual plating through separate anterolateral and posteromedial approaches
Single midline incision with extensive stripping for dual plates
items.e: A posteromedial coronal fragment cannot be reliably captured by lateral locking screws and needs a posteromedial buttress plate; dual incisions with a full-thickness skin bridge give lower wound complications than a single midline incision.

items.q: In a bicondylar tibial plateau fracture, failure to reduce and buttress a displaced posterior (posteromedial) column fragment most commonly leads to:
o: Delayed union of the tibial shaft
Loss of reduction with posterior subsidence and later post-traumatic arthritis
items.e: An unbuttressed posterior shear fragment subsides under flexion loading, producing articular incongruity, increased posterior slope/instability and post-traumatic osteoarthritis.

items.q: A 40-year-old has a high-energy comminuted pilon fracture treated initially with a spanning external fixator. Which imaging best plans definitive articular fixation?
o: Plain AP and lateral radiographs only
CT with 3-D reconstruction obtained after the spanning external fixator
items.e: CT after length has been restored by ligamentotaxis shows the classic fragments (medial, anterolateral/Chaput, posterolateral/Volkmann) and impaction far better than pre-traction imaging, guiding approach selection in the staged protocol.

items.q: According to the GATA (Oguz) classification of spinal tuberculosis, single-level disc degeneration with vertebral involvement but no collapse, abscess or neurological deficit is classified as:
items.e: GATA IA: early lesion without collapse, abscess or deficit — biopsy and antitubercular therapy. IB adds abscess (debridement); II has collapse/kyphosis but is stable (anterior debridement and fusion); III has severe kyphosis/instability (anterior plus posterior instrumentation).

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with known pulmonary tuberculosis develops fever, severe neck pain and new hand weakness. Cervical epidural abscess is suspected. What is the investigation of choice?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the cervical spine
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the cervical spine
Plain radiographs of the cervical spine
items.e: Contrast MRI shows the extent of epidural and paravertebral abscess, cord compression and skip lesions, and distinguishes abscess from granulation tissue; it has replaced CT myelography.

items.q: A 6-year-old child with dorsal spinal tuberculosis is under follow-up. Which radiological 'spine at risk' sign (Rajasekaran) predicts progressive kyphosis even after the infection heals?
items.e: Rajasekaran's four spine-at-risk signs are separation of the facet joints, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation and toppling. Children with two or more signs are at high risk of progressive kyphosis during growth and may need early surgery.

items.q: According to Tuli's 'middle path' regimen for spinal tuberculosis, all of the following are indications for surgery EXCEPT:
o: Neurological deficit that has not started recovering after 3–4 weeks of antitubercular therapy
Recurrence of neurological deficit or worsening despite treatment
Single-level vertebral destruction with preserved alignment and no deficit
items.e: Uncomplicated, stable disease without deficit is treated with antitubercular drugs and rest. Surgery is indicated for non-recovering or worsening deficit, instability/progressive kyphosis, diagnostic doubt and failure of medical therapy.

items.q: A 58-year-old diabetic man has MRSA L4–L5 spondylodiscitis with an epidural abscess. Despite 10 days of appropriate IV antibiotics his quadriceps and ankle dorsiflexion weakness is progressing and there is endplate destruction with segmental instability. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue IV antibiotics and repeat MRI in 2 weeks
Posterior decompression, debridement and instrumented fusion
CT-guided aspiration of the disc space
items.e: Progressive deficit, abscess and instability despite antibiotics are indications for surgery. Debridement with instrumentation is safe in active pyogenic infection (titanium implants), whereas laminectomy alone in a destabilised segment risks progressive kyphosis.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman has a painful THA 6 months after surgery with raised ESR and CRP. Her family doctor started oral antibiotics 1 week ago. What is the most appropriate next step in investigating suspected periprosthetic joint infection?
o: Aspirate the hip immediately while on antibiotics
Stop antibiotics for at least 2 weeks, then aspirate with extended (up to 14-day) culture incubation
items.e: ICM guidance is to withhold antibiotics for at least 2 weeks before aspiration (unless septic) to avoid culture-negative PJI, and to extend incubation to detect low-virulence organisms such as Cutibacterium.

items.q: A 66-year-old has a painful, swollen knee 3 weeks after primary TKA. According to the 2018 ICM definition, which synovial fluid thresholds suggest acute periprosthetic joint infection (within 6 weeks of surgery)?
items.e: Early postoperative haemarthrosis and inflammation raise synovial counts, so acute PJI thresholds are higher (WBC >10,000/µL, PMN >90%) than for chronic PJI (WBC >3,000/µL, PMN >80%). Serum CRP threshold is also higher early (about 100 mg/L).

items.q: A 60-year-old man has knee pain 12 weeks after TKA. Serum CRP is 35 mg/L and ESR 55 mm/h; aspiration shows 9,000 WBC/µL with 45% neutrophils. Cultures are pending. Using the 2018 ICM preoperative scoring system, how is he classified?
o: Cannot be classified until cultures result
items.e: Scores: raised CRP 2 + raised ESR 1 + synovial WBC >3,000/µL 3 = 6, which meets the 'infected' threshold even though PMN% is below 80% (which would have added 2).

items.q: A 27-year-old sprinter has an acute grade II lateral ankle sprain. According to the 2018 international clinical practice guideline on lateral ankle sprains (Vuurberg et al.), what is the preferred management?
o: Functional treatment: semi-rigid brace or tape with early weight-bearing and exercise therapy
Primary surgical repair of the ATFL
Rest without weight-bearing until pain resolves
items.e: Functional treatment with external support and supervised exercise gives faster return to sport and less instability than prolonged immobilisation; a short period (<10 days) of rigid support may be used for severe pain, and surgery is reserved for selected chronic instability.

items.q: In a 22-year-old with recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation, which investigation best quantifies the size of the Hill–Sachs lesion and glenoid bone loss to determine whether the lesion is 'on-track' or 'off-track'?
items.e: 3-D CT measures glenoid width/bone loss (best-fit circle) and the Hill–Sachs interval, allowing glenoid-track calculation (Di Giacomo); MR arthrography is an alternative that also shows labral injury.

items.q: A 12-year-old has a symptomatic, complete discoid lateral meniscus with a stable peripheral rim. What is the arthroscopic treatment of choice?
o: Saucerisation leaving a 6–8 mm peripheral rim
items.e: Saucerisation reshapes the meniscus to a normal width while preserving hoop stresses; any peripheral instability (e.g. Wrisberg variant) is repaired. Total meniscectomy leads to early lateral compartment arthritis and valgus.

items.q: A 19-year-old female distance runner has amenorrhoea for 8 months and a second tibial stress fracture this year. What is the fundamental underlying abnormality in the female athlete triad / relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S)?
items.e: Low energy availability (intake insufficient for training expenditure) suppresses the hypothalamic–pituitary–ovarian axis, causing functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea and low bone mineral density with stress fractures. Treatment centres on restoring energy availability.

items.q: In a child with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy, a dynamic equinovarus foot deformity is most often due to overactivity of:
o: Tibialis posterior (with or without tibialis anterior)
items.e: Spastic equinovarus in hemiplegia results from overactive triceps surae with tibialis posterior and/or tibialis anterior; dynamic EMG guides split transfer or lengthening. In spastic diplegia the typical foot deformity is equinoplanovalgus.

items.q: A 10-year-old with spastic diplegia develops progressive crouch gait (excessive knee flexion and ankle dorsiflexion in stance) after an earlier surgery. Which previous procedure is the classic iatrogenic cause?
items.e: Isolated overlengthening of the Achilles tendon weakens the plantarflexion–knee extension couple, allowing the tibia to collapse forward into crouch. Multilevel surgery addressing hamstrings, lever-arm dysfunction and the calf together avoids this.

items.q: A 32-year-old recreational jogger feels a sudden 'kick' in the back of his heel while pushing off, with an audible pop. There is a palpable gap 4 cm above the calcaneal insertion and squeezing the calf produces no ankle plantarflexion. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: A positive Simmonds–Thompson test, palpable gap in the watershed zone (2–6 cm above insertion) and sudden pop are diagnostic of rupture. Matles test (loss of resting equinus with the knee flexed prone) is also abnormal.

items.q: A neglected Achilles tendon rupture has a 5 cm gap after debridement of the tendon ends. According to the Kuwada classification, what type is this and what reconstruction is typically recommended?
o: Type III; gastrocnemius recession/V–Y advancement or tendon flap
items.e: Kuwada: I partial tear (cast), II complete with defect ≤3 cm (end-to-end repair), III defect 3–6 cm (tendon graft flap/V–Y), IV defect >6 cm (recession, free tendon graft or synthetic). FHL transfer is a common augment in chronic cases.

items.q: When non-operative treatment of an acute Achilles rupture is being considered, which investigation best assesses tendon-end apposition with the ankle in plantarflexion?
o: Plain lateral radiograph of the ankle
items.e: Dynamic ultrasound is quick and cheap and shows the gap and whether the ends appose in equinus; a large gap in plantarflexion is a relative indication for repair. MRI is reserved for chronic or diagnostically unclear cases.

items.q: A 28-year-old presents within 48 hours of an acute Achilles tendon rupture. Based on recent RCTs (e.g. Willits 2010, UKSTAR 2020), which statement about functional non-operative treatment with early weight-bearing in an equinus orthosis is correct?
o: It has a several-fold higher re-rupture rate than surgery
Re-rupture rates are similar to surgery, with fewer wound complications
It is contraindicated in patients under 40
It requires non-weight-bearing casting in full plantarflexion for 8 weeks
items.e: With accelerated functional rehabilitation, re-rupture rates approach those of operative repair, which carries wound and sural nerve complications; UKSTAR showed no difference in Achilles Tendon Rupture Score at 9 months.

items.q: For local staging of a suspected high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femur, what is the investigation of choice?
o: MRI of the entire femur including the hip and knee joints
items.e: MRI defines intramedullary extent, soft-tissue mass, physeal/epiphyseal and joint involvement and neurovascular proximity; imaging the whole bone detects skip metastases. Staging is completed with chest CT and bone scan or PET-CT, and biopsy is done last, along the planned incision.

items.q: A 25-year-old has a Campanacci grade II giant cell tumour of the distal femoral epiphysis extending to subchondral bone with no joint breach. What is the standard surgical treatment?
o: Extended intralesional curettage with high-speed burr, local adjuvant and filling with cement or graft
items.e: Extended curettage through a large cortical window, high-speed burring and adjuvants (phenol, cryotherapy, argon beam) with PMMA gives recurrence rates of about 10–15% while preserving the joint. Resection is reserved for Campanacci III lesions with joint or extensive cortical destruction or pathological fracture.

items.q: Which molecular finding most helps distinguish low-grade central osteosarcoma from fibrous dysplasia on biopsy?
items.e: Low-grade central and parosteal osteosarcomas show MDM2/CDK4 amplification (12q13–15). GNAS mutation characterises fibrous dysplasia, H3F3A G34W giant cell tumour, and IDH1/2 enchondroma and chondrosarcoma.

items.q: A large giant cell tumour of the distal radius is treated with several months of neoadjuvant denosumab followed by curettage. What is the main recognised drawback of this strategy?
o: Rapid malignant transformation in most patients
Increased local recurrence after curettage because tumour cells persist within the newly formed bone and cortical rim
items.e: Denosumab (anti-RANKL) eliminates giant cells and induces ossification, but neoplastic stromal cells persist and the new bone obscures tumour margins, so recurrence after curettage is higher. Hypocalcaemia and osteonecrosis of the jaw are its systemic adverse effects.

items.q: A 28-year-old has an isolated partial-thickness articular cartilage defect of the femoral condyle that does not breach the tidemark or subchondral bone. What is the expected natural healing response?
o: Fill with fibrocartilage from marrow-derived mesenchymal cells
Little or no repair, as adjacent chondrocytes proliferate only briefly and cannot migrate into the defect
items.e: Cartilage is avascular, so a superficial defect elicits no inflammatory or marrow response and does not heal. Full-thickness defects that penetrate subchondral bone (or microfracture) fill with type I collagen-rich fibrocartilage.

items.q: In rheumatoid arthritis, the invasive pannus that erodes cartilage and bone at the joint margins is driven chiefly by which synovial cell?
items.e: Activated fibroblast-like synoviocytes proliferate, resist apoptosis and secrete MMPs and cathepsins that invade cartilage, while RANKL-driven osteoclasts produce marginal erosions. Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-derived and act mainly through cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6).

items.q: Which zone of articular cartilage has the highest water content, the lowest proteoglycan content, flattened chondrocytes and collagen fibres oriented parallel to the surface?
items.e: The superficial zone resists shear and secretes lubricin (PRG4). The middle zone has oblique fibres; the deep zone has perpendicular fibres, the highest proteoglycan content and columnar chondrocytes; the calcified zone lies below the tidemark.

items.q: A 10-year-old boy has genu varum, widened wrists and a rachitic rosary. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 8 ng/mL with raised alkaline phosphatase. According to the 2016 Global Consensus on nutritional rickets, what is the appropriate treatment?
o: Oral vitamin D 3000–6000 IU daily for at least 12 weeks plus calcium about 500 mg/day
items.e: Nutritional rickets is treated with vitamin D (daily dosing, or a single 'stoss' dose of up to 300,000 IU in older children) together with calcium. Calcitriol is for hypophosphataemic or 1α-hydroxylase-deficient rickets, and most bowing remodels without surgery.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman with vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia has bone pain, proximal myopathy and Looser zones on radiographs. Which laboratory abnormality is the most consistent finding?
items.e: Alkaline phosphatase is raised in over 90% of cases. Calcium is low or low-normal, phosphate low and PTH raised (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which drives phosphaturia.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical clinical feature of nutritional rickets?
items.e: Acanthosis nigricans reflects insulin resistance. Rickets causes metaphyseal widening, rachitic rosary, Harrison's sulcus, delayed fontanelle closure and dentition, hypotonia/proximal myopathy and leg bowing.

items.q: A 26-year-old has an isolated Weber B lateral malleolar fracture with medial tenderness. On a gravity stress radiograph the medial clear space widens to 6 mm. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Below-knee cast for 6 weeks without stress review
Open reduction and internal fixation of the fibula
items.e: Medial clear space ≥5 mm (or greater than the superior clear space) on stress views indicates deep deltoid incompetence, i.e. an unstable bimalleolar-equivalent injury needing fibular fixation to restore the mortise. A stable Weber B with a normal stress view can be treated in a boot.

items.q: An ankle fracture has a fibular fracture proximal to the syndesmosis with a medial malleolar fracture. What is its AO/OTA classification?
items.e: AO/OTA 44 (malleolar) follows Danis–Weber: 44-A infrasyndesmotic, 44-B transsyndesmotic, 44-C suprasyndesmotic (with syndesmotic disruption). 43 denotes distal tibial (pilon) fractures.

items.q: All of the following are indications for operative fixation of an ankle fracture EXCEPT:
o: Lateral talar shift with medial clear space widening
Syndesmotic instability on intraoperative stress testing
Isolated undisplaced Weber B fibular fracture with a congruent mortise on stress views
items.e: An isolated Weber B fracture with a stable mortise on stress radiographs does well with functional treatment. Talar shift (1 mm reduces tibiotalar contact by about 40%), open fractures and syndesmotic instability require fixation.

items.q: A distal fibular fracture treated non-operatively remains painful at 9 months and radiographs are equivocal. What is the best investigation to confirm non-union?
items.e: CT shows bridging trabeculae and cortical continuity across the fracture in multiple planes and is the investigation of choice when radiographs are inconclusive; a bone scan may stay positive long after union.

items.q: A 22-year-old footballer has a 1.5 cm vertical longitudinal tear of the medial meniscus 2 mm from the meniscocapsular junction on MRI. Which statement is correct?
o: Partial meniscectomy is preferred regardless of location
The tear lies in the red–red zone and should be repaired
Repair is contraindicated in patients under 25
Most such tears need meniscal allograft transplantation
items.e: Peripheral (red–red, within 3 mm of the capsule) vertical longitudinal tears in young patients have the best healing potential and should be repaired; healing rates are further improved when performed with ACL reconstruction.

items.q: During arthroscopy of a locked knee in a 24-year-old, a displaced bucket-handle tear of the lateral meniscus is found in the notch. The tissue is of good quality and the tear is peripheral. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reduction of the fragment and meniscal repair
Leave the fragment displaced and start rehabilitation
Open meniscectomy through a posterolateral approach
items.e: Repairable bucket-handle tears in young patients should be reduced and repaired (inside-out or all-inside) to preserve hoop function; total lateral meniscectomy rapidly leads to lateral compartment arthritis. Irreparable fragments are excised.

items.q: Screening ultrasound in a 6-week-old girl with a family history of DDH shows an alpha angle of 54° and a beta angle of 70°. What is the Graf classification and usual plan?
o: Type IIa; repeat ultrasound at about 12 weeks
Type IV; closed reduction under anaesthesia
items.e: Graf type IIa is an alpha angle of 50–59° in an infant under 3 months (physiologically immature) and is usually re-scanned; the same angle after 3 months is IIb and is treated. IIc has alpha 43–49°, and type IV is a decentred hip.

items.q: A 45-year-old electrician has nocturnal tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers relieved by shaking the hand, with a positive Durkan compression test. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis and grades severity before surgery?
items.e: Nerve conduction studies show prolonged distal motor and sensory latencies of the median nerve across the wrist and grade severity (with EMG for denervation of APB). Ultrasound measuring median nerve cross-sectional area is a useful adjunct.

items.q: All of the following may be found in ulnar nerve compression in Guyon's canal EXCEPT:
o: Sensory loss on the volar little finger
Weakness of thumb adduction (positive Froment sign)
Tinel sign over the hook of hamate
Sensory loss over the dorsoulnar aspect of the hand
items.e: The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve leaves about 5–8 cm proximal to the wrist, so dorsoulnar sensation is spared in Guyon canal lesions; its loss localises the lesion proximally, e.g. to the cubital tunnel.

items.q: All of the following are accepted indications for a Lapidus procedure (first tarsometatarsal arthrodesis) EXCEPT:
o: Moderate to severe hallux valgus with first-ray hypermobility
Recurrent hallux valgus after a failed distal osteotomy
Isolated hallux rigidus with dorsal first MTP osteophytes
items.e: The Lapidus corrects metatarsus primus varus at its apex and stabilises a hypermobile or arthritic first TMT joint. Hallux rigidus is a first MTP problem treated by cheilectomy, Moberg osteotomy or MTP arthrodesis.

items.q: A 12-year-old has a painful swelling of the tibial diaphysis with fever and raised ESR. Radiographs show a permeative lesion with lamellated 'onion-skin' periosteal reaction, and biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. Which immunohistochemical marker is most characteristic?
items.e: Ewing sarcoma shows diffuse membranous CD99 and nuclear NKX2.2 positivity, confirmed by EWSR1 rearrangement (usually EWSR1–FLI1). Desmin suggests rhabdomyosarcoma and S-100/HMB-45 melanocytic tumours.

items.q: Which radiographic finding is most characteristic of conventional high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femoral metaphysis in an adolescent?
o: Well-defined lytic lesion with a sclerotic margin
Sunburst periosteal reaction with Codman triangle and cloud-like osteoid matrix
Epiphyseal lytic lesion with chicken-wire calcification
Ground-glass lesion with a rind of sclerosis
items.e: Aggressive periosteal reaction (sunburst, Codman triangle) with mixed lytic–sclerotic, fluffy osteoid matrix and soft-tissue extension is typical. A sclerotic margin suggests a benign, slow lesion; ground glass suggests fibrous dysplasia.

items.q: A 14-year-old has shoulder pain. Radiographs show a well-defined lytic lesion with a sclerotic rim in the proximal humeral epiphysis. Biopsy shows polygonal cells with grooved nuclei, scattered giant cells and 'chicken-wire' pericellular calcification. What is the treatment of choice?
items.e: This is chondroblastoma (H3F3B K36M mutation), a benign epiphyseal tumour treated by extended curettage and grafting, taking care of the physis and joint; recurrence is about 10–20%.

items.q: A meta-analysis reports a pooled odds ratio of 0.32 (95% CI 0.20–0.51) for dislocation after THA with dual-mobility cups compared with standard cups. Which interpretation is correct?
o: The odds of dislocation are reduced by 32% with dual-mobility cups
The odds of dislocation are about 68% lower with dual-mobility cups, and the result is statistically significant
Dual-mobility cups increase the odds of dislocation by 32%
The absolute risk of dislocation falls by 68 percentage points
items.e: An OR of 0.32 means the odds in the dual-mobility group are 32% of those with standard cups, a 68% relative reduction in odds; the CI excludes 1, so it is significant. ORs are relative measures and say nothing directly about absolute risk.

items.q: A meta-analysis of RCTs comparing hip arthroscopy with physiotherapy for FAI reports a mean difference in iHOT-33 of 5.2 points (95% CI 2.8 to 7.6) favouring surgery. Which conclusion is correct?
o: The difference is statistically significant, but clinical importance depends on whether it exceeds the minimal clinically important difference
The result is not significant because the CI is wide
The CI crosses zero, so the benefit is uncertain
Heterogeneity must be excessive because the CI is wide
items.e: A 95% CI of a mean difference that excludes zero indicates statistical significance. Whether 5 points matters to patients depends on the MCID (about 6–10 points for iHOT-33), so statistical and clinical significance must be judged separately.

items.q: A 68-year-old with active Paget disease of the hemipelvis and proximal femur (raised alkaline phosphatase) is listed for THA. Which preoperative measure best reduces intraoperative bleeding and heterotopic bone problems?
o: A course of bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronate) to suppress disease activity
items.e: Pagetic bone is hypervascular; bisphosphonate pretreatment lowers turnover and blood loss. Teriparatide is contraindicated in Paget disease because of the osteosarcoma risk.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman has a lytic expansile lesion of a phalanx; biopsy shows haemosiderin-laden giant-cell-rich fibrous tissue (brown tumour). Which biochemical pattern is expected if this is due to primary hyperparathyroidism?
o: Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
Normal calcium, low ALP, low PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, raised PTH
High calcium, high phosphate, suppressed PTH
items.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism gives hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia (phosphaturia) and inappropriately raised PTH with raised ALP. Secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal failure gives low/normal calcium and high phosphate, while suppressed PTH points to malignancy or vitamin D excess.

items.q: Which histological feature is classic for the sclerotic phase of Paget disease of bone?
o: 'Chinese letter' woven trabeculae without osteoblastic rimming
Mosaic pattern of lamellar bone with irregular cement lines
Lace-like osteoid laid down directly by malignant cells
items.e: Chaotic alternating resorption and formation leaves a jigsaw (mosaic) pattern of cement lines with fibrovascular marrow. Chinese letters suggest fibrous dysplasia, tunnelling resorption hyperparathyroidism, and lace-like osteoid osteosarcoma.

items.q: A 70-year-old osteoporotic woman has a displaced 3-part proximal humerus fracture fixed with a locking plate. Which technical factor most reduces the risk of postoperative varus collapse and screw cut-out?
o: Placing the plate high, above the greater tuberosity
Restoring medial support with inferomedial calcar screws (and medial cortical contact)
Using only short screws to avoid joint penetration
items.e: Loss of medial column support is the main cause of varus failure; inferomedial calcar screws (Gardner), anatomical medial reduction or a fibular strut provide it. A high plate causes subacromial impingement, and cuff sutures neutralise tuberosity pull.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a locked posterior shoulder dislocation after a seizure; CT shows an anteromedial humeral head impaction defect (reverse Hill–Sachs) involving about 30% of the articular surface. After reduction, what is the most appropriate procedure?
o: Modified McLaughlin procedure (lesser tuberosity transfer into the defect)
items.e: Defects of about 20–40% are filled by transferring subscapularis or the lesser tuberosity into the defect (modified McLaughlin) or by allograft reconstruction; larger defects or old dislocations may need arthroplasty. Remplissage and Latarjet address anterior instability.

items.q: In a thoracolumbar burst fracture, which CT parameter correlates best with the presence of neurological deficit (e.g. Hashimoto thresholds of about 35% at T11–12, 45% at L1 and 55% at L2 and below)?
o: Percentage of anterior vertebral body height loss
Percentage of spinal canal compromise by retropulsed fragments
items.e: Hashimoto et al. found canal compromise of ≥35% at T11–T12, ≥45% at L1 and ≥55% at L2 or below significantly associated with neurological injury, reflecting the decreasing vulnerability from conus to cauda equina.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has an L2–L3 unilateral facet dislocation after a fall. Which investigation best delineates the posterior ligamentous complex and disc injury?
o: MRI of the lumbar spine (including STIR/fat-suppressed sequences)
items.e: MRI shows disruption of the supraspinous/interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum and disc and any epidural haematoma or disc herniation, while CT best defines bony anatomy of the dislocation.

items.q: A patient with an L3 burst fracture and a laminar fracture has a traumatic dural tear found at surgery but no neurological deficit. Which statement about this injury is most accurate?
o: A dural tear indicates permanent neurological loss
Primary watertight repair reduces the risk of persistent CSF leak and pseudomeningocele, but the neurological prognosis remains governed by the initial deficit
Dural tears never need repair after trauma
All such patients require 7 days of flat bed-rest in ICU
items.e: Burst fractures with laminar fractures (especially with neurological deficit) are associated with dural tears and entrapped rootlets. Repair prevents CSF fistula and pseudomeningocele; it does not in itself change neurological outcome.

items.q: Two years after a Grammont-type reverse shoulder arthroplasty, radiographs show an erosive defect of the inferior scapular neck that extends over the inferior baseplate screw. What is the Sirveaux grade of scapular notching?
items.e: Sirveaux: grade 1 defect limited to the scapular pillar, 2 reaching the inferior screw, 3 extending over the inferior screw, 4 extending under the baseplate towards the central peg. Inferior placement with inferior tilt and lateralisation reduce notching.

items.q: A 72-year-old woman with primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis and an intact rotator cuff is planned for anatomic shoulder replacement. Which finding is the main contraindication to a stemless humeral component?
o: Poor metaphyseal bone quality (osteoporosis or large metaphyseal cysts)
items.e: Stemless implants rely on metaphyseal cancellous fixation, so osteoporotic or cystic metaphyseal bone (and proximal humeral malunion or fracture) is the key contraindication; a stemmed component is then used.

items.q: Compared with the original medialised Grammont reverse shoulder design, a lateralised (glenoid- or humeral-lateralised) RSA:
o: Has a higher rate of scapular notching
Reduces deltoid moment arm to zero
Reduces scapular notching and improves rotation through better cuff tensioning, at the cost of higher shear on the glenoid baseplate
Cannot be used for cuff tear arthropathy
items.e: Lateralisation keeps the humerus away from the scapular pillar (less notching), tensions the remaining teres minor/infraspinatus (better external rotation) and improves contour, but moves the centre of rotation out, increasing torque and shear at the baseplate–bone interface.

items.q: Five months after an uneventful reverse shoulder arthroplasty, a 76-year-old woman has sudden pain over the top of the shoulder and can no longer actively elevate the arm. The prosthesis is located and there is no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acromial or scapular spine stress fracture
items.e: Increased deltoid tension after RSA can cause acromial or scapular spine stress fractures (Levy types I–III), presenting with acute superior pain and loss of elevation; plain films may be normal and CT confirms. Risk factors include osteoporosis and excessive lateralisation/lengthening.

items.q: During hemiarthroplasty for a four-part proximal humerus fracture, the native anatomy is lost. Which intraoperative landmark is commonly used to restore humeral height?
o: The top of the humeral head lies about 5–6 cm above the upper border of the pectoralis major tendon insertion
The top of the humeral head lies at the level of the deltoid tuberosity
The lesser tuberosity tip marks the top of the head
The surgical neck lies 2 cm below the coracoid
items.e: Murachovsky et al. found the top of the head about 5.6 cm above the upper border of the pectoralis major insertion; correct height and anatomical tuberosity reduction (about 5–8 mm below the head) are key to function and tuberosity healing.

items.q: A standing knee radiograph shows definite osteophytes, definite joint-space narrowing, some subchondral sclerosis and possible deformity of the bone ends, without marked osteophytes or severe narrowing. What is the Kellgren–Lawrence grade?
items.e: Kellgren–Lawrence: 1 doubtful narrowing/possible osteophyte; 2 definite osteophytes, possible narrowing; 3 moderate multiple osteophytes, definite narrowing, some sclerosis, possible deformity; 4 large osteophytes, marked narrowing, severe sclerosis and definite deformity.

items.q: In a medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty for anteromedial osteoarthritis, what is the recommended alignment goal?
o: Overcorrection into 5° of mechanical valgus to offload the prosthesis
Slight undercorrection, leaving the limb in mild varus
Neutral mechanical alignment achieved by releasing the superficial MCL
Correction determined by the lateral compartment insert thickness
items.e: Overcorrection overloads the lateral compartment and accelerates its degeneration, a leading cause of UKA revision. The aim is to restore the medial ligament tension to its pre-disease state (no MCL release), usually leaving mild residual varus.

items.q: A constrained (tripolar or locking) acetabular liner is used for recurrent THA instability with abductor deficiency. What is its most common mode of failure?
o: Dislocation or dissociation at the locking mechanism, usually after component impingement
Accelerated adhesive wear of the outer bearing
items.e: Constraint reduces range of motion and transfers impingement forces to the locking ring and fixation interface, so failures are dislocation/liner dissociation and acetabular loosening. Dual-mobility bearings are increasingly preferred where the abductors are partly functional.

items.q: A 66-year-old has primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis with an intact, functioning rotator cuff and a Walch A1 glenoid with adequate bone stock. Compared with hemiarthroplasty, anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty:
o: Is contraindicated because of glenoid loosening
Gives better pain relief and function with a lower revision rate in the medium term
Requires a reverse prosthesis if the cuff is intact
items.e: Randomised trials and meta-analyses favour TSA over hemiarthroplasty for primary OA with an intact cuff, as progressive glenoid erosion causes pain after hemiarthroplasty. Glenoid loosening is the long-term weak point of TSA.

items.q: After TKA for a fixed valgus knee with a 20° flexion contracture, the patient wakes with foot drop. Which immediate step is most appropriate?
o: Release all dressings and flex the knee to reduce tension on the common peroneal nerve
Immediate surgical exploration of the nerve
Apply a long-leg cast in full extension
items.e: Acute correction of valgus–flexion deformity stretches the common peroneal nerve; removing compressive dressings and flexing the knee relieve tension. Most palsies recover partially or fully; exploration is considered only if there is no recovery.

items.q: A 19-year-old has recurrent lateral patellar dislocations with a positive J sign. Imaging shows Dejour type B trochlear dysplasia with a 7 mm supratrochlear spur (bump), TT–TG 14 mm and normal patellar height. In addition to MPFL reconstruction, which procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: High-grade dysplasia (Dejour B or D) with a prominent bump (>5 mm) and maltracking is the indication for trochleoplasty. Tubercle medialisation is for raised TT–TG (>20 mm) and distalisation for patella alta; isolated lateral release is not used for instability.

items.q: After ACL reconstruction with a free tendon autograft, during which period is the graft mechanically weakest because of avascular necrosis and early revascularisation?
items.e: Ligamentisation proceeds through early necrosis, revascularisation/cell repopulation (weakest at roughly 6–12 weeks) and remodelling/maturation over a year or more, which is why aggressive loading early in rehabilitation is avoided.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a complete radial tear of the lateral meniscus extending from the free edge through to the capsule in the mid-body. What is the biomechanical consequence if it is left unrepaired?
o: Minimal effect because the meniscus is intact elsewhere
Loss of hoop-stress transmission, making the meniscus functionally equivalent to a total meniscectomy
Increased load sharing by the meniscus
Isolated loss of the meniscofemoral ligaments
items.e: Circumferential collagen fibres convert axial load into hoop stress; a complete radial tear divides all of them, so contact pressures rise as after total meniscectomy. Such tears in young patients should be repaired (e.g. side-to-side inside-out sutures).

items.q: Osteochondral autograft transfer (mosaicplasty) from the non-weight-bearing trochlea is best suited to which femoral condyle lesion?
o: A 1–2.5 cm² full-thickness lesion in a young, active patient
An uncorrected varus knee with a medial defect
items.e: OAT provides immediate mature hyaline cartilage and bone but is limited by donor-site morbidity, so it is used for small lesions (about ≤2.5–4 cm²). Larger defects suit ACI/MACI or osteochondral allograft, and malalignment must be corrected.

items.q: At the first (arthroscopic) stage of autologous chondrocyte implantation, from where is the cartilage biopsy usually taken?
o: Lesser-loaded areas such as the intercondylar notch or the superomedial trochlear margin
items.e: About 200–300 mg of cartilage is harvested from low-load sites (intercondylar notch or superior trochlear ridge), expanded in culture and implanted weeks later (on a collagen membrane in MACI).

items.q: In patients undergoing arthroscopic Bankart repair, Shaha et al. showed that anterior glenoid bone loss below the classic 20–25% threshold still worsened outcomes. Above what 'subcritical' level was this seen?
items.e: In a military cohort, bone loss above about 13.5% was associated with clinically significant worse WOSI scores despite no recurrent dislocation; many surgeons now consider bony augmentation in high-risk athletes at lower thresholds.

items.q: A 55-year-old manual worker has an irreparable posterosuperior rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus and infraspinatus with Goutallier grade 4), no arthritis and loss of active external rotation. Which tendon transfer is currently favoured for restoring external rotation?
o: Lower trapezius transfer (with tendon graft extension)
items.e: Lower trapezius transfer (Elhassan) has a line of pull in phase with the infraspinatus and gives reliable gains in external rotation; latissimus dorsi transfer is an alternative. Pectoralis major transfer is for irreparable subscapularis tears.

items.q: At arthroscopy, a full-thickness rotator cuff tear measures 4 cm in its greatest dimension. How is it classified according to Cofield?
items.e: Cofield: small <1 cm, medium 1–3 cm, large 3–5 cm and massive >5 cm. Massive tears are alternatively defined (Gerber) as complete tears of two or more tendons.

items.q: At arthroscopy for a subscapularis tear, there is a complete tear of the upper two-thirds of the tendon with a centred humeral head and fatty infiltration below Goutallier grade 3. What is the Lafosse type?
items.e: Lafosse: I partial lesion of the upper third; II complete lesion of the upper third; III complete lesion of the upper two-thirds; IV complete tear with centred head and fatty infiltration ≤ grade 3; V complete tear with eccentric head, coracoid impingement and fatty infiltration ≥ grade 3.

items.q: After hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement, a patient reports perineal numbness and erectile dysfunction. What is the most likely cause?
o: Portal injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
Compression of the pudendal nerve by the perineal traction post
Sciatic nerve injury from the posterolateral portal
items.e: Pudendal neurapraxia is the classic traction-related nerve injury; risk relates to traction force and duration, so traction time is kept short (often <2 hours) with a well-padded post or post-less distraction. It usually recovers spontaneously.

items.q: A 25-year-old with hip pain has a labral tear on MR arthrography. The lateral centre-edge angle is 16° with an increased Tönnis angle. Why is isolated arthroscopic labral surgery not recommended?
o: The hip is dysplastic, and arthroscopy alone may worsen instability; periacetabular osteotomy is the preferred treatment
A centre-edge angle of 16° indicates pincer impingement needing rim trimming
The labrum cannot be visualised arthroscopically
Arthroscopy is contraindicated in patients under 30
items.e: An LCEA below 20° indicates dysplasia (20–25° borderline). Labral tears are secondary to undercoverage, and capsulotomy or rim resection can destabilise the hip, so a Bernese PAO (with or without arthroscopy) addresses the cause.

items.q: A professional fast bowler has posterior elbow pain at ball release, with pain on forced valgus in terminal extension. Imaging shows a posteromedial olecranon osteophyte and chondromalacia of the posteromedial trochlea. What is the diagnosis?
items.e: Repeated valgus and extension forces wedge the olecranon into the medial olecranon fossa, forming posteromedial osteophytes. Treatment is arthroscopic osteophyte excision, avoiding over-resection, which increases strain on the ulnar collateral ligament.

items.q: A 14-year-old gymnast has lateral elbow pain and locking. MRI shows an osteochondritis dissecans lesion of the capitellum with a fluid line beneath the fragment and a loose body, with the capitellar physis closed. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Activity modification and observation for 6 months
Arthroscopic removal of the loose body with debridement or fixation of the lesion (or osteochondral grafting for large defects)
items.e: Unstable capitellar OCD (fluid behind the fragment, loose body, closed physis) needs surgery; stable lesions with an open physis respond to rest. Panner disease, in children under 10, involves the whole capitellum and resolves with rest.

items.q: A national-level athlete with confirmed inflammatory bowel disease needs a drug that is on the WADA Prohibited List. What should be done before using it in competition?
o: Use it and declare it on the doping control form only
Apply for a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) from the relevant anti-doping organisation
Switch to a herbal supplement with the same action
items.e: A TUE permits a prohibited substance when it is clinically necessary, no permitted alternative exists, it gives no additional performance enhancement and the need is not caused by prior doping. Under strict liability, the athlete is responsible for any substance found.

items.q: Under the World Anti-Doping Code, what combination of whereabouts failures constitutes an anti-doping rule violation?
o: Any 3 missed tests and/or filing failures within a 12-month period
5 missed tests in a calendar year
items.e: Article 2.4 of the Code: any combination of three missed tests and/or filing failures within 12 months by an athlete in a registered testing pool is a violation, regardless of whether a prohibited substance is found.

items.q: A 24-year-old offensive lineman has deep posterior shoulder pain when blocking. With the arm abducted to 90°, axial load on the elevated arm while applying a posteroinferior force produces sudden pain (positive Kim test), and the jerk test is also positive. What lesion is most likely?
items.e: The Kim and jerk tests load the posteroinferior glenoid; combined, they are highly sensitive for a posteroinferior labral lesion, typical of repetitive posteriorly directed force in linemen. MR arthrography confirms and arthroscopic posterior labral repair is performed if rehabilitation fails.

items.q: On a true AP radiograph, the critical shoulder angle (CSA) combines glenoid inclination and lateral acromial extension. A CSA greater than about 35° is associated with:
items.e: Moor et al. showed that a large CSA (>35°) raises superior shear from the deltoid and is associated with cuff tears and retears, whereas a small CSA (<30°) is associated with primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

items.q: In arthroscopic Bankart repair for recurrent anterior shoulder instability, which technical factor is most consistently linked with a higher recurrence rate?
o: Fixation with fewer than three suture anchors
items.e: Using fewer than three anchors (or failing to place anchors low on the glenoid, below 3 o'clock on a right shoulder) increases recurrence. Patient factors such as age under 20, contact sport, hyperlaxity and bone loss (ISIS score) also matter.

items.q: A 12‑year‑old boy presents with delayed growth, muscle weakness, and a classic rachitic rosary at the costochondral junctions. His serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated, calcium is normal, and 1,25‑dihydroxyvitamin D is low. Which deficiency is most likely responsible?
items.e: Low 1,25‑D and high ALP with normal calcium and phosphate point to vitamin D deficiency rickets.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a classic radiographic sign of rickets?
items.e: Sharp, narrow vertebral bodies are seen in osteomalacia, not rickets.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old diabetic patient with sudden onset of foot pain and swelling. X‑ray shows cortical thinning and pseudofractures. Which systemic condition most likely predisposes him to this osteomalacia?
items.e: CKD leads to hypophosphatemia and impaired vitamin D activation, precipitating osteomalacia.

items.q: In vitamin D deficient rickets, the first line therapeutic drug is:
items.e: Alfacalcidol is a synthetic 1α‑hydroxyvitamin D that bypasses the defective hepatic step in deficiency.

items.q: A 9‑year‑old girl with prolonged orthodontic treatment develops pitting on the metaphysis of the tibia and a sponge‑like bone texture on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Sponge bone and metaphyseal pitting are classic X‑ray findings of osteomalacia.

items.q: Which laboratory value is most specific for active vitamin D turnover in osteomalacia?
items.e: Serum 1,25‑D directly reflects active vitamin D; low levels are diagnostic of osteomalacia.

items.q: A 15‑year‑old girl from a rural area presents with bowed legs and a positive Roach sign. Her 25‑hydroxyvitamin D level is 15 ng/mL. Which public health measure would be most effective for her community?
items.e: Vitamin D fortification reduces the risk of rickets in endemic areas.

items.q: A 70‑year‑old woman with CKD Stage 5 is on dialysis. She complains of bone pain. Which therapeutic target should be monitored to prevent dialytic osteodystrophy?
items.e: Controlling serum phosphate is crucial to prevent secondary hyperparathyroidism and osteodystrophy.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman has a painful bunion despite wide shoes. Weight-bearing radiographs show hallux valgus angle 26°, intermetatarsal angle 12°, a congruent first MTP joint and no arthritis. What is the most appropriate operation?
o: Distal chevron osteotomy of the first metatarsal
items.e: Mild-to-moderate hallux valgus (HVA <40°, IMA <15°) without arthritis is corrected by a distal chevron osteotomy; Lapidus suits severe deformity or first-ray hypermobility, and MTP fusion is reserved for arthritis or severe/revision cases.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman has painful plantar callosity under the second metatarsal head with a long second metatarsal and a subluxated second MTP joint. Which osteotomy shortens the metatarsal and decompresses the joint?
items.e: The Weil osteotomy is an oblique distal metatarsal osteotomy parallel to the sole that shortens the lesser metatarsal and decompresses the MTP joint; Akin, Ludloff and Scarf are first-ray osteotomies for hallux valgus.

items.q: A 28-year-old man has a 3-month history of an enlarging painful mass at the proximal tibia. Radiographs show a destructive metaphyseal lesion with sunburst periosteal reaction. What is the most appropriate way to obtain a tissue diagnosis?
o: Image-guided core needle biopsy at the treating sarcoma centre, along the planned resection tract
Frozen-section biopsy through a transverse incision
items.e: Suspected primary bone sarcoma should be biopsied by core needle at the centre that will do the definitive surgery, with the tract placed so it can be excised en bloc; excisional biopsy, FNAC (insufficient tissue) and transverse incisions compromise limb salvage.

items.q: A 16-year-old boy has biopsy-proven high-grade osteosarcoma of the distal femur. Which investigation is essential to detect the most common site of metastasis before planning limb-salvage surgery?
items.e: The lungs are the commonest site of osteosarcoma metastasis, so CT chest is mandatory in staging; a bone scan or PET-CT looks for skeletal spread, and MRI of the whole involved bone detects skip lesions.

items.q: After neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the resected specimen of a conventional osteosarcoma is examined. Poor histological response (an adverse prognostic factor) is defined as tumour necrosis of less than:
items.e: Good response is ≥90% necrosis (Huvos grade III–IV); <90% necrosis (Huvos I–II) is a poor response and is one of the strongest prognostic factors in localised osteosarcoma.

items.q: A spindle-cell tumour arising from the sciatic nerve in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 1 must be distinguished from a cellular schwannoma. Which immunohistochemical finding best supports malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)?
items.e: MPNST shows only patchy S-100/SOX10 in about half of cases, and loss of H3K27me3 (from PRC2 inactivation) is the most useful supportive marker; diffuse strong S-100 and SOX10 favour schwannoma, and MDM2 amplification indicates dedifferentiated liposarcoma.

items.q: Which staging investigation has traditionally been part of the work-up of Ewing sarcoma but NOT of osteosarcoma, reflecting its tendency for marrow spread?
