o: MRI of the whole involved bone
Bilateral bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
items.e: Ewing sarcoma can metastasise to bone marrow, so bilateral marrow aspirate/biopsy has been part of its staging (PET-CT is now often used instead in localised disease); chest CT, whole-bone MRI and bone scan are used for both tumours.

items.q: In secondary (callus) healing of a diaphyseal fracture treated with an intramedullary nail, the main source of osteoprogenitor cells forming the external callus is:
o: The cambium layer of the periosteum
items.e: The inner cambium layer of the periosteum supplies most of the mesenchymal progenitors that form the bridging external callus by endochondral ossification, which is why periosteal stripping impairs healing.

items.q: In the adult bone remodeling cycle, which signaling axis is most directly responsible for the integration of mechanical loading into bone formation?
items.e: Sclerostin, produced by osteocytes, inhibits the Wnt/β‑catenin pathway. Lower mechanical loading increases sclerostin, reducing osteoblastic activity; conversely, loading decreases sclerostin, permitting bone formation via Wnt signalling.

items.q: Schmid-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia is caused by a mutation in COL10A1. Type X collagen is characteristically produced in which zone of the growth plate?
items.e: Type X collagen is a marker of hypertrophic chondrocytes and aids matrix mineralisation in the zone of provisional calcification; resting and proliferative zone chondrocytes produce mainly type II collagen.

items.q: A 45-year-old man on long-term high-dose corticosteroids develops avascular necrosis of the femoral head. What is the histological hallmark of bone death in this condition?
o: Woven bone with mosaic cement lines
Peritrabecular marrow fibrosis with tunnelling resorption
items.e: Death of osteocytes leaves empty lacunae in the trabeculae, the defining feature of osteonecrosis; wide osteoid seams suggest osteomalacia, mosaic pattern Paget disease and tunnelling resorption hyperparathyroidism.

items.q: By weight, approximately what proportion of adult bone is made up of its inorganic (mineral) component?
items.e: Bone is about 60–70% mineral (mainly hydroxyapatite), 20–30% organic matrix (≈90% type I collagen) and about 10% water.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman treated for spinal TB 10 years ago presents with fever and back pain. MRI shows T12 collapse with a large paravertebral abscess. Before starting treatment, which investigation best confirms active disease and detects rifampicin resistance?
o: CT-guided biopsy with CBNAAT (GeneXpert MTB/RIF) and culture
items.e: Tissue diagnosis by CT-guided biopsy with GeneXpert (which also detects rifampicin resistance), culture and histology is essential, particularly in recurrence; MRI shows the extent of disease but cannot confirm activity or drug sensitivity.

items.q: A 60-year-old woman who completed treatment for tuberculosis of the knee 15 years ago now has painful end-stage arthritis of that knee. If total knee arthroplasty is planned, which precaution is recommended?
o: Perioperative antitubercular therapy cover, continued after surgery
Mandatory two-stage arthroplasty with an antibiotic spacer
Knee arthrodesis instead, as arthroplasty is contraindicated
Preoperative radiotherapy to sterilise the joint
items.e: TKA is acceptable in healed tubercular arthritis; most authors give ATT cover starting before surgery and continuing for several months after, with thorough debridement, to lower the risk of reactivation.

items.q: During locking-plate fixation of a three-part proximal humerus fracture through a deltopectoral approach, where should the plate be positioned?
o: At the level of the tip of the greater tuberosity, directly over the bicipital groove
About 5–8 mm below the tip of the greater tuberosity and just lateral to the bicipital groove
items.e: Placing the plate slightly distal to the greater tuberosity tip avoids subacromial impingement, and keeping it lateral to the bicipital groove protects the long head of biceps and the ascending branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery.

items.q: Which is the investigation of choice for diagnosing a suspected occult fracture of the glenoid rim in a patient with persistent shoulder pain after a traumatic shoulder dislocation?
items.e: CT with 3‑D reconstruction accurately demonstrates subtle glenoid rim fractures that are often missed on plain radiographs.

items.q: After a seizure, a patient cannot externally rotate the shoulder. Axillary radiograph shows a posterior dislocation with an impaction fracture of the anteromedial humeral head. This lesion is called:
items.e: In posterior dislocation the anteromedial head impacts on the posterior glenoid rim, producing a reverse Hill-Sachs (McLaughlin) lesion; a Hill-Sachs lesion is posterolateral after anterior dislocation and a Bennett lesion is posterior glenoid ossification in throwers.

items.q: A 65-year-old man with adult degenerative scoliosis has pelvic incidence 55°, lumbar lordosis 20° and SVA 8 cm. Using the PI–LL mismatch rule, what is the minimum lumbar lordosis the surgeon should aim to restore?
items.e: Realignment targets aim for PI–LL within about 10°, so with PI 55° the lordosis should be at least ~45°; 80° would overcorrect beyond PI + 10°.

items.q: In the SRS-Schwab classification of adult spinal deformity, a PI–LL mismatch is graded as marked ('++') when it exceeds:
items.e: The PI–LL modifier is 0 if <10°, + if 10–20° and ++ if >20°; the other sagittal modifiers are SVA (<4 cm, 4–9.5 cm, >9.5 cm) and pelvic tilt (<20°, 20–30°, >30°).

items.q: A 55-year-old man has medial knee pain without locking or giving way. MRI shows a degenerative horizontal tear of the medial meniscus posterior horn with mild osteoarthritis. What is the most appropriate initial management?
items.e: Randomised trials (FIDELITY, METEOR, ESCAPE) showed arthroscopic partial meniscectomy is no better than sham or exercise therapy for degenerative tears without mechanical symptoms, so supervised physiotherapy is first-line.

items.q: Which quantitative cartilage MRI technique uses delayed imaging after intravenous gadolinium to estimate the glycosaminoglycan content of articular cartilage, for example after cartilage repair?
items.e: Negatively charged gadolinium distributes inversely to the negatively charged GAGs, so dGEMRIC T1 maps reflect proteoglycan content; T2 mapping mainly reflects water content and collagen network organisation.

items.q: A 38-year-old rugby player has knee pain. MRI shows a linear high signal within the posterior horn of the medial meniscus that does not reach either articular surface (grade 2 signal). What is the correct interpretation?
o: A horizontal cleavage tear requiring arthroscopy
Intrasubstance (mucoid) degeneration that is not a tear
items.e: Only signal that unequivocally reaches an articular surface (grade 3), ideally on two consecutive images, indicates a tear; grade 1 (globular) and grade 2 (linear, not reaching the surface) signals represent intrasubstance degeneration and are managed by the clinical picture.

items.q: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in children most often starts in the metaphysis of long bones. What is the main anatomical reason?
o: Absence of periosteum over the metaphysis
Direct communication of metaphyseal veins with the joint
Sluggish flow in the looped terminal metaphyseal capillaries and sinusoids next to the physis, with few phagocytes
Higher red marrow content of the diaphysis
items.e: Nutrient artery branches end in hairpin loops beneath the physis and open into venous sinusoids where flow slows and phagocytic activity is low, allowing bacteria to settle; the thick metaphyseal periosteum explains subperiosteal abscess formation, not seeding.

items.q: A 32-year-old woman with generalised ligamentous laxity has recurrent lateral ankle instability after a failed modified Broström–Gould repair, and the remnant ATFL and CFL are attenuated. What is the most appropriate surgical option?
o: Repeat direct ATFL repair with suture anchors
Anatomical reconstruction of the ATFL and CFL with a tendon graft
items.e: Anatomical repair is first-line, but generalised laxity, failed previous repair or poor-quality remnant tissue are indications for anatomical ligament reconstruction with an autograft or allograft tendon; non-anatomical tenodeses sacrifice peroneus brevis and stiffen the subtalar joint.

items.q: Which factor is most strongly associated with secondary malignant transformation of a conventional giant cell tumour of bone?
items.e: Secondary malignant GCT (usually a high-grade sarcoma) occurs mostly years after radiotherapy, though it can follow surgery alone; this is why radiotherapy is reserved for unresectable lesions such as some sacral or spinal GCTs.

items.q: A renal transplant recipient develops acute monoarthritis of the first MTP joint; aspiration shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals. Which of his medications most likely contributed by raising serum urate?
items.e: Calcineurin inhibitors, especially ciclosporin, reduce renal urate excretion and commonly cause hyperuricaemia and gout in transplant patients; note that azathioprine interacts dangerously with allopurinol and febuxostat.

items.q: In a patient with an acute hot, swollen knee, what is the definitive investigation to diagnose crystal arthritis and exclude infection?
o: Joint aspiration for polarised light microscopy, Gram stain and culture
items.e: Identifying crystals in synovial fluid under compensated polarised light is the gold standard, and the same aspirate is cultured because sepsis can coexist; serum urate is often normal during an attack and imaging signs are only supportive.

items.q: Minutes after a lumbar transforaminal epidural injection of particulate methylprednisolone, a patient develops acute paraplegia with a sensory level. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Embolic infarction of the spinal cord after intra-arterial injection into a radiculomedullary artery (artery of Adamkiewicz)
Chemical neurolysis of the injected nerve root
Epidural haematoma from a punctured epidural vein
Acute disc prolapse at the adjacent level
items.e: Particulate steroid injected inadvertently into a radiculomedullary feeder such as the artery of Adamkiewicz can embolise and infarct the cord; using non-particulate dexamethasone and live or digital-subtraction contrast imaging reduces this risk.

items.q: On serial radiographs of a cemented femoral stem, which finding meets the Harris criteria for DEFINITE loosening?
o: A radiolucent line covering 50–99% of the cement–bone interface
A complete radiolucent line around the entire cement–bone interface
Subsidence of the stem or a fracture of the cement mantle
items.e: Harris criteria: definite loosening = migration of the stem or cement, or a cement mantle/stem fracture; probable = a continuous radiolucent line around the whole cement–bone interface; possible = a lucency over 50–99% of the interface.

items.q: On a 3D CT, the intact inferior glenoid diameter is 28 mm and the anterior glenoid bone loss is 5 mm. Using the glenoid track concept (Yamamoto, Itoi; Di Giacomo), what is the width of the glenoid track?
items.e: Glenoid track = 0.83 × D − d = 0.83 × 28 − 5 ≈ 18 mm; a Hill-Sachs interval wider than this is 'off-track' (engaging) and needs a remplissage or a bone-block procedure in addition to Bankart repair.

items.q: A 28-year-old labourer has a scaphoid waist fracture displaced by 2 mm with a lateral intrascaphoid angle of 45°. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Below-elbow thumb spica cast for 12 weeks
Reduction and internal fixation with a headless compression screw
Closed reduction and K-wire fixation of the scaphotrapezial joint
items.e: Displacement over 1 mm or humpback angulation (intrascaphoid angle >35°) carries a high non-union and malunion risk, so the fracture is reduced and fixed with a central headless compression screw; casting is for undisplaced waist fractures.

items.q: Twelve weeks after cast treatment of a scaphoid waist fracture, the patient still has snuffbox tenderness and radiographs are equivocal. Which investigation best establishes whether the fracture has united?
o: Thin-slice CT along the long axis of the scaphoid
items.e: CT along the scaphoid axis best shows trabecular bridging (union is often defined as >50% bridging) and humpback deformity; MRI is better for occult acute fractures and proximal pole vascularity.

items.q: During wrist arthroscopy for suspected scapholunate ligament injury, the probe can be passed between the scaphoid and lunate from the midcarpal portal, but a 2.7 mm arthroscope cannot be passed through the interval. What is the Geissler grade?
items.e: Geissler: I – attenuation seen from radiocarpal side only; II – incongruency/step-off seen from midcarpal side; III – step-off with a gap admitting a probe; IV – gross instability with a 2.7 mm scope passing through the gap ('drive-through' sign).

items.q: A 40-year-old woman has polyostotic fibrous dysplasia of the femur and pelvis together with multiple intramuscular myxomas in the thigh. What is this association called?
items.e: Mazabraud syndrome is fibrous dysplasia (usually polyostotic) with intramuscular myxomas, both linked to activating GNAS mutations; McCune–Albright adds café-au-lait spots and endocrinopathy, and Maffucci is enchondromatosis with haemangiomas.

items.q: After elective primary total hip arthroplasty in a patient without contraindications, extended pharmacological thromboprophylaxis (e.g. LMWH) is recommended by NICE for a total of about:
items.e: NICE recommends about 28 days of LMWH (or 10 days LMWH followed by 28 days aspirin, or a DOAC for 28–35 days) after elective THA, compared with about 14 days after TKA, because VTE risk persists for weeks after hip replacement.

items.q: After a fracture fixation, a patient needs an anti-inflammatory analgesic that will not impair platelet function before a planned second-stage procedure. Which drug fits best?
items.e: Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2 and spares platelet COX-1 thromboxane production, so it does not prolong bleeding; ketorolac and ibuprofen reversibly and aspirin irreversibly inhibit platelet COX-1.

items.q: In the bridge-enhanced ACL restoration (BEAR) technique, how is a complete midsubstance ACL tear treated?
o: Hamstring autograft reconstruction augmented with an internal brace
Suture repair of the torn ends combined with an extracellular-matrix scaffold saturated with the patient's own blood placed in the gap
Primary repair of a proximal avulsion with suture anchors only
Reconstruction with a synthetic LARS ligament
items.e: BEAR bridges the tear with a protein scaffold loaded with autologous blood to promote healing of the native ligament; the BEAR II randomised trial showed patient-reported outcomes and laxity at 2 years comparable to hamstring autograft reconstruction, with better hamstring strength.

items.q: During a Latarjet procedure for anterior glenoid bone loss, where should the coracoid graft ideally be positioned on the anterior glenoid?
o: Below the glenoid equator (about 3 to 5 o'clock on a right shoulder), flush with the glenoid articular surface
Above the equator, 2–3 mm proud of the articular surface
At the equator, 5 mm medial to the articular surface
On the anterior scapular neck 1 cm medial to the rim
items.e: The graft should lie subequatorial and flush with the joint surface; a lateral (proud) graft causes early arthritis, while a medial or high graft leads to recurrent instability.

items.q: A 26-year-old has recurrent anterior instability after a Latarjet procedure; CT shows lysis of the coracoid graft with persistent anterior glenoid bone loss. Which reconstruction is most appropriate?
o: Free bone-block glenoid reconstruction (iliac crest autograft, Eden–Hybinette type, or distal tibial allograft)
items.e: Once the coracoid has been used and lysed, glenoid bone loss is restored with a free bone block such as iliac crest autograft (Eden–Hybinette) or fresh distal tibial allograft; soft-tissue procedures alone fail with significant bone loss and Putti–Platt causes stiffness and arthritis.

items.q: Compared with single-row repair of a full-thickness supraspinatus tear, double-row (including transosseous-equivalent) repair has been shown mainly to:
o: Give consistently superior functional scores at 2 years for all tear sizes
Reduce operating time and implant cost
Eliminate the risk of retear in massive tears
Restore a larger footprint contact area and lower retear rates, especially in larger tears, without a consistent clinical score advantage
items.e: Biomechanically, double-row repairs recreate more of the footprint and improve healing on imaging, particularly for tears over about 3 cm, but randomised trials and meta-analyses show little consistent difference in functional scores.

items.q: A 42-year-old tennis player has a partial articular-sided supraspinatus tear measuring 7 mm deep (more than 50% of tendon thickness) with persistent pain after 6 months of physiotherapy. What is the recommended surgical treatment?
o: Repair of the tendon (completion and repair or transtendon repair)
items.e: In Ellman's classification, grade 3 partial tears are deeper than 6 mm (over half the ~12 mm thickness); these are repaired, whereas grade 1–2 tears (<50%) are usually debrided with or without acromioplasty.

items.q: During hip arthroscopy, which part of the procedure is normally performed WITHOUT traction, with the hip flexed about 30–45°?
o: Peripheral compartment work such as cam osteochondroplasty
Labral repair at the chondrolabral junction
Removal of loose bodies from the acetabular fossa
items.e: The central compartment (labrum seen from the inside, acetabular cartilage, fovea, ligamentum teres) needs traction to distract the joint, whereas the peripheral compartment (head–neck junction for cam resection) is accessed with traction released and the hip flexed.

items.q: A 45-year-old woman has deep buttock pain on long strides and hip extension with adduction. MRI shows oedema in the quadratus femoris and a narrowed space between the lesser trochanter and the ischial tuberosity. Diagnosis?
items.e: Ischiofemoral impingement is entrapment of the quadratus femoris between the ischium and the lesser trochanter, seen as a reduced ischiofemoral distance with quadratus femoris oedema on MRI.

items.q: A 55-year-old woman has lateral hip pain lying on her side and tenderness over the greater trochanter (greater trochanteric pain syndrome). What is the most common underlying pathology?
o: Stress fracture of the greater trochanter
Gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy at their trochanteric insertions
items.e: Imaging and histology show that gluteal (medius/minimus) tendinopathy or tears, often with secondary bursal change, underlie most GTPS; isolated bursitis is uncommon, and education with loading exercise outperforms corticosteroid injection in the medium term (LEAP trial).

items.q: The UK FASHIoN randomised trial (Griffin et al., Lancet 2018) in femoroacetabular impingement syndrome compared hip arthroscopy with personalised hip therapy. What did it show at 12 months?
o: Hip arthroscopy gave a greater improvement in hip-related quality of life (iHOT-33)
No difference between the two treatments
items.e: Both groups improved, but arthroscopic surgery produced a statistically and clinically greater improvement in iHOT-33 at 12 months; the trial was not designed to show any effect on later osteoarthritis.

items.q: After ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction of the elbow in a throwing athlete, which complication is the most frequently reported?
o: Graft rupture within the first year
items.e: Ulnar nerve symptoms are the commonest complication, especially with the original Jobe technique that detached the flexor–pronator mass and routinely transposed the nerve; muscle-splitting approaches (e.g. docking technique) reduced this.

items.q: Under the World Anti-Doping Code, a substance or method may be added to the Prohibited List when it meets at least two of three criteria. Which of the following is NOT one of these criteria?
o: It has the potential to enhance sport performance
It represents an actual or potential health risk to the athlete
Its use violates the spirit of sport
It is not available without a medical prescription
items.e: WADA considers performance enhancement, health risk and violation of the spirit of sport (any two suffice); prescription status is irrelevant, and many over-the-counter products contain prohibited substances.

items.q: A school rugby player has a sport-related concussion and his symptoms have settled. In the graduated return-to-sport strategy, what is the minimum time usually spent at each step before progressing?
items.e: International consensus statements recommend at least 24 hours per stage, progressing only if symptoms do not worsen, and full-contact practice only after medical clearance; children and adolescents usually return more conservatively.

items.q: In the Salter–Thompson classification of Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease, prognosis is predicted from the:
o: Height of the lateral pillar in the fragmentation stage
Extent of the subchondral fracture (crescent sign) in the early stage: less or more than half of the femoral head
Final shape of the femoral head at maturity
items.e: Salter–Thompson group A has a subchondral fracture involving less than half of the head (good prognosis) and group B more than half; it can be applied early but the crescent sign is seen in only about a third of patients.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six clinical signs in the Pirani score for idiopathic clubfoot?
o: Curvature of the lateral border of the foot
items.e: Pirani scores three hindfoot signs (posterior crease, empty heel, rigid equinus) and three midfoot signs (medial crease, curved lateral border, lateral head of talus coverage), each 0, 0.5 or 1, for a maximum of 6.

items.q: In the Dimeglio classification of clubfoot, the foot is scored out of a maximum of:
items.e: Dimeglio scores four reducibility parameters (equinus, varus, derotation, adduction) from 0–4 each plus four additional signs worth 1 point each, total 20; grade IV (16–20) is very severe, teratologic-type stiffness.

items.q: With the patient supine and both hips and knees flexed to 90°, the examiner supports both heels and looks from the side; one tibia drops back relative to the other. This test assesses the:
items.e: This is the Godfrey (posterior sag) test: gravity makes the tibia sag posteriorly in a PCL-deficient knee, and a sag can make a false-positive anterior drawer if the reduced starting position is not recognised.

items.q: Which plain radiographic view best demonstrates an anterosuperior cam deformity at the femoral head–neck junction?
o: AP pelvis with the legs in 15° external rotation
items.e: The 45° (or 90°) Dunn view profiles the anterosuperior head–neck junction where cam lesions lie and is used to measure the alpha angle; the false-profile view assesses anterior acetabular coverage.

items.q: A pitcher with valgus extension overload undergoes arthroscopic removal of a posteromedial olecranon osteophyte. Why should resection of normal olecranon bone be avoided?
o: It risks injury to the radial nerve
It increases strain on the ulnar collateral ligament and may unmask or worsen valgus instability
items.e: The posteromedial olecranon contributes to valgus stability; resecting beyond the osteophyte increases UCL strain, so only the impinging spur is removed and coexisting UCL insufficiency must be assessed.

items.q: After MPFL reconstruction, a patient has medial knee pain and difficulty with flexion; the femoral tunnel is found to be too proximal (anterior–superior to Schöttle's point). Why?
o: The graft is lax in flexion, causing recurrent dislocation
The graft becomes tight in flexion, overloading the medial patellofemoral joint
items.e: A proximal femoral attachment makes the graft non-isometric so it tightens as the knee flexes, raising medial patellofemoral pressure and limiting flexion; a distal tunnel causes tightness in extension and laxity in flexion.

items.q: A 24-year-old has an acute first-time anterior shoulder dislocation. CT shows a displaced anteroinferior glenoid rim fragment involving about 25% of the glenoid width. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Reduction and fixation of the bony Bankart fragment
items.e: A large acute bony Bankart fragment can be reduced and fixed (arthroscopically with anchors/screws or open), restoring the glenoid arc; neglecting it leaves an inverted-pear glenoid with high recurrence.

items.q: What did randomised trials and meta-analyses show about immobilisation in external rotation (Itoi) after a first-time anterior shoulder dislocation?
o: It abolished recurrence in all age groups
It increased the risk of stiffness and rotator cuff tears
It was superior only when used for 12 weeks
It did not significantly reduce recurrence compared with conventional internal rotation sling immobilisation
items.e: Itoi showed that external rotation reduces the Bankart lesion closer to the glenoid on MRI, but subsequent randomised trials and meta-analyses found no significant reduction in recurrence, partly due to poor compliance.

items.q: Compared with bone–patellar tendon–bone autograft, the main advantage of quadriceps tendon autograft for ACL reconstruction is:
o: Faster bone-to-bone healing at both ends
Less anterior knee and kneeling pain with similar stability
No harvest-related weakness of any muscle
It is the only graft suitable for revision surgery
items.e: Quadriceps tendon autograft (with or without a bone block) gives a thick, versatile graft with stability and failure rates comparable to BPTB and hamstrings, but with less donor-site and kneeling pain than BPTB.

items.q: Normally, with the knee flexed to 90°, the medial tibial plateau lies about 1 cm anterior to the medial femoral condyle. In a PCL-injured knee, the tibial plateau is now flush with the femoral condyle. What grade of PCL injury is this?
items.e: Posterior drawer grading uses the tibial step-off: grade I – step-off reduced but plateau still anterior (0–5 mm translation); grade II – flush (5–10 mm); grade III – tibia falls behind the condyles (>10 mm), suggesting an associated posterolateral or posteromedial injury.

items.q: Which statement about load transmission by the menisci is correct?
o: The lateral meniscus carries about 70% of the load in its compartment, more than the medial meniscus does in the medial compartment, so lateral meniscectomy is more harmful
Each meniscus carries less than 10% of the compartmental load
The medial meniscus carries about 90% of the medial compartment load in extension
Load is transmitted mainly through the radial fibres
items.e: The lateral meniscus transmits about 70% and the medial about 50% of compartmental load, and the convex lateral tibial plateau is less congruent, so total lateral meniscectomy leads to faster lateral compartment degeneration; hoop stress is borne by circumferential fibres.

items.q: A 4-week-old girl born breech has a Graf ultrasound alpha angle of 55° with a stable hip on dynamic examination. What is the appropriate management?
o: Repeat ultrasound at about 6–12 weeks of age (physiological immaturity)
items.e: Before 3 months, an alpha angle of 50–59° is Graf type IIa, physiologically immature; most such hips mature spontaneously, so they are re-scanned, and treatment starts if the hip fails to improve (IIb) or is worse.

items.q: A 20-year-old with recurrent anterior shoulder instability is supine with the shoulder abducted 90° and externally rotated, producing apprehension. A posteriorly directed force on the humeral head then relieves the apprehension and allows further external rotation. This is the:
items.e: Relief of apprehension with posterior pressure (relocation) and its return on release (surprise/release test) supports anterior instability; the jerk test assesses posteroinferior instability and the sulcus sign inferior laxity.

items.q: A 24-year-old footballer has anterior hip pain on deep flexion after a previous sprinting injury. 3D CT shows a prominent anterior inferior iliac spine extending down to the acetabular rim. Which diagnosis fits best?
items.e: A low or prominent AIIS (Hetsroni type II reaching the rim, type III extending below it), often after a rectus femoris avulsion, abuts the distal femoral neck in flexion; it is treated by arthroscopic subspine decompression.

items.q: Meldonium, a metabolic modulator found in many positive tests after its inclusion, was added to the WADA Prohibited List in which year?
items.e: Meldonium (mildronate), a cardiac anti-ischaemic drug, was added to the Prohibited List from 1 January 2016 under hormone and metabolic modulators (S4), after monitoring showed widespread use among athletes.

items.q: The International Hip Dysplasia Institute (IHDI) radiographic classification of DDH grades displacement using which landmark, so that it can be used before the femoral head ossific nucleus appears?
o: Centre of the femoral head ossific nucleus
Midpoint of the superior margin of the proximal femoral metaphysis (H-point)
items.e: IHDI grades I–IV by the position of the H-point relative to Hilgenreiner's line, Perkin's line and a 45° diagonal; using the metaphysis avoids dependence on the delayed or asymmetric ossific nucleus that limits the Tönnis grading.

items.q: In the Kalamchi–MacEwen classification of avascular necrosis after treatment of DDH, group III (central physeal damage) typically leads to:
o: Temporary irregular ossification of the nucleus only, with a normal outcome
Lateral physeal tethering with valgus tilt of the femoral head
A short femoral neck with relative overgrowth of the greater trochanter
items.e: Group I – nucleus changes only; II – lateral physeal damage causing valgus tilt; III – central physeal arrest giving a short neck and trochanteric overgrowth (functional coxa vara); IV – total damage to head and physis.

items.q: A 10-year-old with late-stage Perthes disease has painful limitation of abduction. An arthrogram shows that on abduction the lateral part of the enlarged femoral head levers on the acetabular edge and the medial joint space widens. What is the preferred surgical treatment?
o: Valgus (abduction) extension osteotomy of the proximal femur
items.e: Hinge abduction is a contraindication to containment procedures that abduct the head further; a valgus extension osteotomy moves the hinge point out of the joint, improving congruency and pain, sometimes with a shelf procedure.

items.q: During serial casting of idiopathic clubfoot, 'Kite's error' refers to:
o: Abducting the foot with counter-pressure over the calcaneocuboid joint, which locks the calcaneus and blocks hindfoot correction
Correcting the cavus first by supinating the forefoot
Using the lateral head of the talus as the fulcrum
Performing percutaneous tenotomy before full abduction
items.e: Ponseti uses the lateral head of the talus as the fulcrum so the calcaneus can rotate under the talus; Kite placed the thumb at the calcaneocuboid joint, preventing calcaneal abduction and leaving residual varus.

items.q: A 22-year-old weightlifter has recurrent atraumatic posterior shoulder instability despite rehabilitation. CT shows 20° of glenoid retroversion with no glenoid bone loss. Which procedure addresses the underlying bony problem?
items.e: Excessive glenoid retroversion (more than about 10–15°) predisposes to posterior instability and to failure of soft-tissue repair; a posterior opening-wedge glenoid osteotomy corrects version, with posterior bone block reserved for posterior bone loss.

items.q: A 9-year-old with hypothyroidism presents with a unilateral stable SCFE treated by in situ fixation. Why is prophylactic pinning of the contralateral hip recommended in this child?
o: Endocrine-associated slips and onset before 10 years carry a high risk of a contralateral slip
All unilateral SCFEs should have prophylactic contralateral fixation
Pinning prevents avascular necrosis on the treated side
Hypothyroidism is a contraindication to screw fixation of the slipped side
items.e: Prophylactic fixation is advised when contralateral slip risk is high: endocrinopathy or renal osteodystrophy, young age (under ~10 years, open triradiate cartilage) or unreliable follow-up; otherwise practice varies.

items.q: Which infant with hip dislocation is NOT suitable for treatment in a Pavlik harness?
o: A newborn with a teratologic (fixed, irreducible) dislocation associated with arthrogryposis
A 2-month-old with Graf type III hip that reduces on ultrasound in flexion–abduction
items.e: The Pavlik harness needs a reducible hip and normal muscle function; teratologic dislocations (arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele), stiff hips and older infants respond poorly and risk Pavlik disease of the posterior acetabulum.

items.q: The CSAW randomised trial (Beard et al., Lancet 2018) in subacromial pain compared arthroscopic subacromial decompression, investigational arthroscopy only and no treatment. What was its main finding?
o: Decompression was clearly superior to both other groups
Decompression was no better than arthroscopy alone (placebo surgery), though both surgical groups did slightly better than no treatment
No treatment produced the best outcome
items.e: CSAW (and the Finnish FIMPACT trial) found no clinically important benefit of acromioplasty over diagnostic arthroscopy, questioning decompression for subacromial pain without a cuff tear.

items.q: After single-incision anterior repair of an acute distal biceps tendon rupture with a cortical button, which complication is most commonly reported?
items.e: Transient LABCN paraesthesia from retraction is the commonest complication of the anterior single-incision approach; PIN palsy is rarer, and heterotopic ossification or synostosis has been associated more with the two-incision technique.

items.q: In overhead athletes, the 'SICK scapula' syndrome describes all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Scapular malposition with an apparently lower (dropped) scapula
items.e: SICK stands for Scapular malposition, Inferior medial border prominence, Coracoid pain and malposition, and dysKinesis of scapular movement; it reflects tight pectoralis minor and weak scapular stabilisers in throwers.

items.q: In the lever sign (Lelli) test for ACL rupture, the examiner places a fist under the proximal calf of the supine patient and presses down on the distal thigh. In an ACL-deficient knee:
o: The heel rises off the couch
The heel stays on the couch
items.e: With an intact ACL, pressure on the quadriceps lifts the heel as the tibia is levered forward; when the ACL is torn the tibia translates anteriorly over the fulcrum and the heel stays down, a test with high reported sensitivity in acute and chronic tears.

items.q: A 22-year-old competitive swimmer develops sudden swelling, heaviness and bluish discolouration of the dominant arm after intense training. Duplex ultrasound shows thrombosis of the subclavian vein. Diagnosis?
items.e: Effort thrombosis results from repetitive compression of the subclavian vein at the costoclavicular space (venous thoracic outlet syndrome); treatment is anticoagulation, often catheter-directed thrombolysis and later first rib resection.

items.q: The Doha agreement on terminology for groin pain in athletes recommended replacing terms such as 'sports hernia' and 'athletic pubalgia' with which category?
items.e: Doha defined adductor-, iliopsoas-, inguinal- and pubic-related groin pain (plus hip-related and other causes); inguinal-related pain (inguinal canal tenderness without a palpable hernia) replaces vague labels like sports hernia.

items.q: What is the correct sequence of Waldenström stages in Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease?
items.e: The head first becomes dense and smaller (initial), then fragments (when lateral pillar grading is applied), reossifies, and finally remodels to a healed head whose shape is classified by Stulberg.

items.q: Using a KT-1000 arthrometer at 30° of knee flexion, which finding is generally regarded as supporting a complete ACL rupture?
o: A side-to-side difference of at least 3 mm
Posterior translation greater than anterior translation
items.e: A side-to-side difference in anterior tibial translation of 3 mm or more (manual maximum) is the usual threshold for ACL deficiency, and the same measure is used to grade laxity after reconstruction.

items.q: In the Sugaya MRI classification of rotator cuff repair integrity, which types represent a retear?
items.e: Sugaya types I–III describe repaired tendons of sufficient thickness with variable signal or thinning, whereas type IV (small discontinuity) and type V (major discontinuity) indicate retear.

items.q: The rotator cable is a thickening of the capsule and cuff fibres arching from the anterior to the posterior greater tuberosity. What is its proposed biomechanical role?
o: It is the main static restraint to anterior dislocation
It transmits the pull of the long head of biceps to the glenoid
It anchors the acromion to the humeral head
It acts like a suspension bridge, transferring load around a crescent tear so that function can be preserved
items.e: Burkhart's suspension-bridge model explains why a tear confined to the thin avascular crescent lateral to an intact cable may be functionally compensated, whereas tears that disrupt the cable attachments lose force coupling.

items.q: A 5-year-old has a painless waddling gait. Radiographs show a triangular metaphyseal fragment in the inferomedial femoral neck and a Hilgenreiner–epiphyseal angle of 65°. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Observation, as it will resolve spontaneously
Valgus subtrochanteric osteotomy to correct the HE angle to below about 40°
In situ pinning of the physis
items.e: In developmental coxa vara, an HE angle above 60° (or progression, or 45–60° with symptoms) is treated by valgus osteotomy, overcorrecting to below about 35–40°; angles under 45° usually resolve.

items.q: Under the 2021 World Anti-Doping Code, unless an International Federation defines otherwise, the 'in-competition' period begins at:
o: 11:59 pm on the day before a competition in which the athlete is scheduled to participate
The moment the athlete enters the venue
Midnight seven days before the event
The start of the athlete's warm-up
items.e: In-competition runs from 11:59 pm the day before the competition until the end of the competition and its sample collection; substances such as stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids and systemic glucocorticoids are prohibited only in this period.

items.q: Which hip capsular ligament is the strongest, resists extension and external rotation, and is cut during arthroscopic interportal capsulotomy (so it is often repaired in borderline dysplasia)?
items.e: The iliofemoral ligament anterior to the joint is the strongest ligament in the body; unrepaired capsulotomy, particularly with borderline dysplasia or hyperlaxity, can cause iatrogenic microinstability or dislocation.

items.q: An athlete's urine A sample is reported as an adverse analytical finding. What is the athlete's right regarding the B sample?
o: The B sample is always destroyed after the A sample is positive
The B sample can only be analysed in a different country
The athlete may request analysis of the B sample and attend its opening, and the B result must confirm the A finding
A negative B sample leads to a reduced sanction but not exoneration
items.e: The sample is split at collection; if the A sample is positive the athlete may ask for the sealed B sample to be analysed in the same accredited laboratory, attended by the athlete or a representative, and a B sample that does not confirm the A result voids the finding.

items.q: A professional pitcher has medial elbow pain. Which part of the ulnar collateral ligament complex is the primary restraint to valgus stress and is reconstructed in 'Tommy John' surgery?
items.e: The anterior bundle, from the anteroinferior medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle, is the main restraint to valgus from about 30° to 120° of flexion; the posterior bundle is a secondary restraint in deep flexion and the transverse ligament contributes little.

items.q: On a 20° knee-flexion axial (Laurin) view, the lateral patellofemoral angle is formed between a line across the anterior femoral condyles and a line along the lateral patellar facet. Which finding indicates abnormal patellar tilt?
o: The lines are parallel or open medially
The patellar apex lies lateral to the trochlear groove
items.e: Normally the angle opens laterally; parallel lines or a medially opening angle indicate lateral patellar tilt, typical of a tight lateral retinaculum and patellofemoral malalignment.

items.q: A 25-year-old had an isolated arthroscopic lateral retinacular release for anterior knee pain. She now has disabling giving way, and the patella can be displaced medially with apprehension (positive medial Fulkerson relocation test). What is the most likely problem?
o: Patella baja from fat pad scarring
items.e: Excessive or unnecessary lateral release removes the lateral restraint and can cause medial (or multidirectional) patellar instability; it is treated by lateral retinacular repair or reconstruction, and isolated lateral release is not recommended for lateral instability.

items.q: In Wiberg's classification of patellar shape on the axial view, which type is the most common?
o: Type I – medial and lateral facets equal and concave
Type II – medial facet smaller than the lateral and flat or slightly concave
Type III – very small, convex medial facet
Jägerhut (hunter's cap) patella with no medial facet
items.e: Type II is the most common configuration; types III and the Jägerhut variant, with an increasingly small or absent medial facet, are associated with patellar instability and trochlear dysplasia.

items.q: During closed reduction of a dislocated hip from DDH in a 10-month-old, the 'safe zone' of Ramsey describes:
o: The arc of abduction between the angle at which the hip redislocates and the angle of excessive abduction, which a wide arc makes safer
The acetabular index below which no treatment is needed
The position of the femoral head on ultrasound in the Pavlik harness
The degree of external rotation allowed after spica casting
items.e: A hip that stays reduced only in near-maximal abduction risks avascular necrosis; adductor tenotomy widens the safe zone, and a narrow zone (less than about 20–25°) suggests that open reduction is needed.

items.q: Which statement about the medial (Ludloff-type) approach for open reduction of a dislocated hip in DDH is correct?
o: It is best suited to children older than 3 years
It allows a formal capsulorrhaphy and pelvic osteotomy through the same incision
It carries no risk to the femoral head blood supply
It is used in infants under about 12–18 months and approaches the obstacles directly, but capsulorrhaphy is not possible and the medial femoral circumflex artery is at risk
items.e: The medial approach gives direct access to the iliopsoas, transverse acetabular ligament and inferior capsule with little dissection in young infants, but it cannot tighten the capsule and endangers the MFCA; older children need an anterior approach with capsulorrhaphy, often with pelvic or femoral osteotomy.

items.q: Burkhart and De Beer (2000) reviewed recurrence after arthroscopic Bankart repair. Which factor was associated with the highest recurrence rate?
o: Significant bone defects: an inverted-pear glenoid or an engaging Hill–Sachs lesion
Use of three or more anchors
items.e: Recurrence was 67% with significant bone defects versus 4% without (89% versus 6.5% in contact athletes); unrecognised glenoid or humeral bone loss remains the main cause of failed arthroscopic soft-tissue stabilisation.

items.q: Under the 2021 World Anti-Doping Code, an athlete tests positive for cocaine, a designated 'substance of abuse'. If the athlete proves the use was out-of-competition and unrelated to sport performance, the standard period of ineligibility is:
o: 3 months (reducible to 1 month after an approved treatment programme)
items.e: Substances of abuse (cocaine, heroin, MDMA, THC) carry a 3-month ban when out-of-competition use unrelated to performance is established, reducible to 1 month with a treatment programme; otherwise the usual 2–4 year sanctions apply.

items.q: A 3-month-old with idiopathic clubfoot has a short, fat foot with a deep transverse plantar crease across the sole, a hyperextended first MTP joint and a rigid equinus after slipped casts. Which modification of the Ponseti method is recommended for this atypical (complex) clubfoot?
o: Standard abduction to 70° in every cast
Avoiding over-abduction (abducting to about 40°), with the thumb on the talar head and correcting cavus by pushing up both the first and fifth metatarsal heads
Correcting equinus first by forced dorsiflexion
items.e: Ponseti's modified protocol for complex clubfoot limits abduction to about 40°, corrects cavus with simultaneous pressure under all metatarsal heads and uses above-knee casts at 110° knee flexion; over-abduction worsens the deformity.

items.q: Current evidence suggests that cam morphology of the hip in athletes develops mainly because of:
o: High-impact sport during adolescence, before closure of the proximal femoral physis, causing extension of the physis onto the neck
A congenital abnormality present at birth
items.e: Cohort studies of young footballers, basketball and ice-hockey players show cam morphology forms during adolescent growth with intense loading while the capital physis is open, explaining its high prevalence in athletes compared with non-athletes.

items.q: A patient with a failed ACL reconstruction has femoral and tibial tunnels widened to 17 mm in a malpositioned, vertical position. What is the usual approach to revision?
o: Single-stage revision using the existing tunnels with a larger graft
Two-stage revision: bone grafting of the tunnels first, then reconstruction after graft incorporation
items.e: Tunnel enlargement beyond about 15 mm, or tunnels that would overlap new ones and compromise fixation, generally requires staged bone grafting followed by revision reconstruction several months later.

items.q: A 3-year-old treated by the Ponseti method has a corrected clubfoot but walks with dynamic supination, with the tibialis anterior pulling the forefoot into supination during swing. The lateral cuneiform is ossified. What is the recommended procedure?
o: Transfer of the whole tibialis anterior tendon to the lateral cuneiform
items.e: Persistent dynamic supination after age about 2.5–3 years, with passively correctable deformity, is treated by whole tibialis anterior transfer to the lateral cuneiform (often after a few corrective casts); triple arthrodesis is a salvage for rigid adult deformity.

items.q: During arthroscopic repair of a large U-shaped rotator cuff tear, side-to-side sutures are placed between the anterior and posterior leaves before attaching the apex to bone. What is the purpose of this 'margin convergence'?
o: To shift the tear's free margin toward the footprint and reduce strain at the repair
To enlarge the footprint for double-row fixation
To medialise the footprint to the articular margin
items.e: Margin convergence converts a U-shaped tear into a smaller crescent, reducing the gap and strain at the tendon–bone repair (Burkhart); it is used for mobile U- or L-shaped tears that cannot be pulled directly laterally.

items.q: During arthroscopic Bankart repair, where should the suture anchors be placed?
o: 2 cm medial on the scapular neck
On the glenoid articular face at the articular margin (about 1–2 mm onto the face), from about 5:30 upward on a right shoulder
On the humeral neck at the capsular insertion
items.e: Anchors are placed at the edge of the articular surface so the labrum is restored as a bumper; medial anchor placement on the neck heals the labrum in a medialised, ALPSA-like position and increases recurrence, and the most inferior anchor placement is key.

items.q: Which statement about sex differences in Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease is correct?
o: It is more common in girls, who have a better prognosis
It is about four to five times more common in boys, and girls tend to have a worse prognosis
Boys and girls are equally affected
items.e: Perthes disease shows a male predominance of about 4–5:1; girls are often said to fare worse because they mature skeletally earlier, leaving less remodelling time, although this partly reflects their older bone age at onset.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old male sustains an OTA 32‑A3 fracture of the femoral shaft with a transverse mid‑shaft break and an associated contralateral medial femoral condyle epiphyseal injury. The most appropriate definitive fixation in a young active patient is:
o: Locked intramedullary nail with interlocking screws
Plate and screws fixation with a 10‑mm reconstruction plate
Proximal femoral nail anti‑rotation (PFNA) with a distal lock
items.e: Locked intramedullary nailing provides the best biomechanical stability for a transverse shaft fracture while preserving the growth plate and allowing early mobilization.

items.q: Which of the following statements about the "reverse obliquity" (AO/OTA 31‑A3) intertrochanteric fracture is FALSE?
o: It involves a posterior column fracture line extending into the posterior aspect of the lesser trochanter
Closed reduction with a single lag screw is sufficient in all cases
Open reduction is preferred due to the high risk of posterior displacement
items.e: Closed reduction with a single lag screw is inadequate; multiple screws or a sliding caliper plate are required to stabilize the posterior column.

items.q: A 60‑year‑old male undergoes total hip arthroplasty and two weeks later presents with a femoral shaft fracture through the distal 4 cm of the stem. Radiographs show a well‑fixed prosthesis with a normal cortical bone stock. Which fixation principle is most appropriate?
o: Internal fixation with a long proximal buttress plate
Revision arthroplasty with a new femoral component
Cemented intramedullary nail through the existing stem
Proximal femoral replacement with distal locking
items.e: Cemented intramedullary nailing through the existing stem provides a stable construct while preserving the well‑fixed prosthesis.

items.q: A 43‑year‑old man presents with a dislocated trochanteric flip fragment secondary to a high‑energy blunt trauma. Which sign best predicts a displaced comminuted intertrochanteric fracture beyond the anterior cortex?
o: Loss of lateral femoral head prominence on AP hip view
Positive AO‑S/F sign on AP view
Subcapital fracture line on AP view
items.e: The AO‑S/F (Schmeling‑Furie) sign on AP view indicates an anterior flip fragment that is likely displaced and comminuted.

items.q: In a polytrauma patient with isolated Pauwel's type III femoral neck fracture, the best surgical option to reduce the chance of avascular necrosis while allowing early weight bearing is:
o: Closed reduction and internal fixation with multiple cannulated screws
Internal fixation with a single large cancellous screw and dynamic compression plate
items.e: Multiple cannulated screws placed in an inverted triangle provide three‑point fixation, reducing shear and preserving the vascular supply.

items.q: A 50‑year‑old woman falls onto her outstretched hand and is found to have a ‘floating knee’ (femoral shaft and ipsilateral tibial shaft fractures). Which is the single most important factor influencing the decision between a single long intramedullary nail versus a combined fixation (nail for femur, plate for tibia)?
o: The presence of a small distal tibial fragment
The comminution pattern of the femoral shaft
items.e: Severely comminuted femoral shaft fragments often cannot be adequately stabilized by a single nail and require a combined fixation strategy.

items.q: Which of the following is the most reliable radiographic indicator of impending fracture‑to‑implant failure in a periprosthetic femur fracture with a well‑fixed stem?
o: A linear radiolucent zone <5 mm around the stem
Increased cortical thickness distal to the fracture
A narrowing of the medullary canal at the fracture site
An osteolytic bubble in the distal metaphysis
items.e: A radiolucent line <5 mm suggests early loosening and predicts fracture‑to‑implant failure if the fracture progresses.

items.q:
A 72‑year‑old woman falls from standing height and presents with a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture. Her pre‑injury mobility was assisted (walker). Which is the most appropriate surgical option?
A. Closed reduction and percutaneous cannulated screw fixation
B. Cemented bipolar hemiarthroplasty via an anterolateral approach
C. Total hip arthroplasty with a posterior approach
D. Non‑operative management with a hip spica cast
items.e: Elderly patients with low demand and a high operative risk benefit most from a cemented hemiarthroplasty; the anterolateral approach reduces dislocation rates in this cohort.

items.q:
A 60‑year‑old man with a history of hypertension falls and sustains a displaced femoral neck fracture. Which of the following is NOT an absolute contraindication to intramedullary hip nailing in this setting?
A. Severe osteoporosis
B. Active infection at the fracture site
C. Large intracapsular fragment requiring a head‑replacement
D. Fracture extending into the subchondral bone of the femoral head
items.e: Severe osteoporosis is a relative, not an absolute, contraindication; absolute contraindications include infection, need for arthroplasty, and subchondral extension.

items.q:
A 70‑year‑old female falls in her bathroom and sustains a minimally displaced femoral neck fracture. Which of the following best reflects the recent consensus on early weight‑bearing in this group?
A. Non‑weight bearing for 6 weeks
B. Partial weight bearing (50%) for 4 weeks
C. Full weight bearing as tolerated from day one
D. Immediate hip precautions and no weight bearing until union
items.e: Current evidence supports allowing full weight bearing as tolerated in trochanteric fractures, including minimally displaced neck fractures, to promote earlier mobilisation.

items.q:
During an open reduction of a 25‑year‑old male with an AO/OTA 32A3.3 intertrochanteric fracture, the surgeon plans to apply a proximal femoral nail. Which of the following tips best prevents a “tunnel” along the lateral cortex that could lead to a secondary varus?
A. Avoid over‑reaming the entry hole
B. Use a straight drill for the lag screw
C. Place the femoral nail at 10° of ante‑version
D. Secure the distal lock screw 5 mm below joint line
items.e: The entry point and reaming size directly affect lateral cortical integrity; avoiding over‑reaming reduces the risk of a lateral tunnel and varus collapse.

items.q: Why is cobalt–chromium alloy, rather than titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V), used for the articulating femoral component of a total knee arthroplasty?
o: Greater surface hardness and wear resistance against polyethylene
Lower elastic modulus, closer to that of cortical bone
items.e: Titanium alloy has poor wear (abrasion) resistance and notch sensitivity, so as a bearing surface it is scratched and generates debris; CoCr is harder and more wear resistant. Titanium's lower modulus and better osseointegration suit stems, not bearings.

items.q: At the implant–bone interface, stress shielding is most directly related to:
o: The porosity of the ingrowth coating
The surgical approach used for implantation
The surface roughness of the implant
The disparity in Young's modulus (stiffness) between implant and bone
items.e: A stiffer implant carries a greater share of load, so the surrounding bone is under-loaded and resorbs (Wolff's law). Stem stiffness depends on modulus and diameter; surface finish and coating affect fixation rather than load sharing.

items.q: An interbody spinal cage has a titanium-alloy body with a hydroxyapatite coating. What is the main purpose of the hydroxyapatite coating?
o: Increasing surface hardness against endplate wear
Providing radiolucency for assessment of fusion
Bioactive osteoconduction to accelerate bony ongrowth
Reducing the modulus mismatch with the vertebral endplate
items.e: Hydroxyapatite is a bioactive calcium phosphate that is osteoconductive and speeds bone apposition to the implant. The titanium core provides strength; HA does not meaningfully change stiffness or radiolucency.

items.q: In patients with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, which agent produced significantly fewer new vertebral fractures than alendronate in a head-to-head randomised trial (Saag et al., NEJM 2007)?
items.e: Glucocorticoids mainly suppress osteoblast function, so an anabolic agent is logical; teriparatide 20 µg daily increased BMD more and reduced new vertebral fractures compared with alendronate in GIOP.

items.q: By the definition used in most bone-health guidance (Institute of Medicine), vitamin D deficiency is a serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level below:
items.e: A 25(OH)D level below 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) is generally taken as deficiency; many bone societies aim for at least 30 ng/mL in osteoporosis and fracture patients. Levels under 10–12 ng/mL are severe deficiency with risk of osteomalacia.

items.q: Before giving intravenous zoledronic acid for active Paget disease of bone, which condition must be corrected to avoid symptomatic hypocalcaemia?
items.e: Zoledronic acid abruptly suppresses the very high bone turnover of Paget disease and can cause hypocalcaemia, especially if vitamin D is deficient; vitamin D should be replete and calcium given for about 10 days after the infusion. Raised ALP is the disease marker being treated, not a contraindication.

items.q: Which statement about anabolic osteoporosis drugs is correct?
o: Romosozumab acts by inhibiting RANKL on osteoblasts
Teriparatide can be continued indefinitely because its effect does not wane
Romosozumab is given for 12 monthly doses and should be followed by an antiresorptive agent
After stopping teriparatide, BMD gains are maintained without further treatment
items.e: Romosozumab (anti-sclerostin, dual anabolic and antiresorptive action) is limited to 12 months, and teriparatide is usually limited to about 24 months; gains are lost unless followed by an antiresorptive such as a bisphosphonate or denosumab. Denosumab, not romosozumab, inhibits RANKL.

items.q: A 30-year-old has a closed extra-articular distal radius fracture. According to the AAOS clinical guideline, which post-reduction finding favours operative fixation over cast treatment?
items.e: The AAOS guideline suggests operative fixation when post-reduction radial shortening exceeds 3 mm, dorsal tilt exceeds 10°, or intra-articular displacement/step-off exceeds 2 mm. The other values are within acceptable limits.

items.q: A 30-year-old is neurologically intact after a fall. CT shows an L1 burst fracture, and MRI shows an intact posterior ligamentous complex. What is the TLICS score and usual management?
o: 2 – non-operative treatment with early mobilisation, with or without a brace
items.e: TLICS: burst morphology 2, intact PLC 0, neurologically intact 0, total 2. A score of 3 or less is treated non-operatively, 4 is indeterminate, and 5 or more is treated surgically.

items.q: A 35-year-old has a T12 burst fracture after a car crash with partial lower-limb weakness. Which investigation best shows the spinal cord, posterior ligamentous complex and any epidural haematoma?
items.e: MRI is best for soft tissue: cord oedema or contusion, disc and epidural haematoma, and PLC integrity on STIR/T2 sequences. CT is best for bony anatomy and canal compromise; dynamic films are unsafe in acute unstable injuries.

items.q: In the Thoracolumbar Injury Classification and Severity Score (TLICS), which neurological status receives the highest score?
o: Incomplete spinal cord injury or cauda equina syndrome
items.e: Neurological status: intact 0, nerve root injury 2, complete cord injury 2, incomplete cord injury or cauda equina 3. Incomplete injuries score highest because urgent decompression can change the outcome.

items.q: Before a medial mobile-bearing (Oxford) unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, a valgus stress radiograph at about 20° of flexion is obtained mainly to confirm that:
o: The anterior cruciate ligament is intact
The lateral compartment has preserved full-thickness cartilage and the varus deformity is correctable
The posterior tibial slope is below 7°
The patellofemoral joint has no lateral facet wear
items.e: The valgus stress view shows a normal-width lateral joint space (full-thickness lateral cartilage) and that the intra-articular varus corrects, implying a normal-length MCL. ACL integrity is judged clinically/intraoperatively, and the patellofemoral joint is assessed on skyline views.

items.q: In the modified Walch classification of glenoid morphology in primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis, a dysplastic glenoid with retroversion greater than 25°, regardless of erosion, is classified as:
items.e: Walch type C is a dysplastic (developmental) glenoid with more than 25° retroversion. A2 is central erosion, B2 a biconcave glenoid with posterior erosion, and B3 a monoconcave, retroverted glenoid with posterior wear.

items.q: At arthroscopy after a forced-adduction shoulder injury, a superficial anteroinferior labral tear is found together with an adjacent glenoid articular cartilage defect; the shoulder is not unstable. This lesion is a:
items.e: GLAD (glenolabral articular disruption) is a superficial anteroinferior labral tear with an injury to the adjacent glenoid cartilage, typically without instability. Perthes and ALPSA are instability lesions with periosteal sleeve stripping, and HAGL is humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a usual indication for a Latarjet procedure?
o: Recurrent anterior instability after a failed arthroscopic Bankart repair
Recurrent anterior instability in a contact athlete with an off-track Hill–Sachs lesion
Recurrent posterior instability with increased glenoid retroversion
Anterior glenoid bone loss of more than 20–25%
items.e: The Latarjet coracoid transfer treats anterior instability with significant glenoid bone loss, off-track lesions, high-risk athletes and failed soft-tissue repair. Posterior instability with retroversion is managed by posterior bone block or glenoid osteotomy.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy has a painless limp for 4 weeks and restricted hip abduction and internal rotation. Radiographs are normal; gadolinium-enhanced subtraction MRI shows absent perfusion of the femoral capital epiphysis. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: In early Perthes disease radiographs may be normal; MRI (especially perfusion/subtraction sequences) shows epiphyseal ischaemia before collapse. Transient synovitis shows only an effusion, and Meyer dysplasia is a benign irregular ossification in younger children with normal perfusion.

items.q: On the AP pelvis radiograph of an early slipped capital femoral epiphysis, Klein's line drawn along the superior femoral neck fails to intersect the lateral epiphysis. This is called:
items.e: Failure of Klein's line to cut the epiphysis is the Trethowan sign. Steel's blanch sign is a crescent of double density over the metaphysis, Gage sign is a lateral epiphyseal lucency in Perthes disease, and Drehmann sign is obligatory external rotation on hip flexion (a clinical sign).

items.q: A 12-year-old can walk with crutches and has a mild, stable slipped capital femoral epiphysis. The standard treatment is:
o: Closed manipulation to reduce the slip followed by pinning
In situ fixation with a single cannulated screw placed centrally in the epiphysis
items.e: Stable SCFE is treated by in situ fixation with one central-central cannulated screw, without attempting reduction, which carries a risk of avascular necrosis. Osteotomies are reserved for severe deformity, and casting has high rates of slip progression and chondrolysis.

items.q: An infant has an obstetric brachial plexus injury of the Erb (C5–C6) type. Which function is characteristically preserved?
items.e: Erb palsy affects the upper trunk (C5–C6): deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis are weak, giving the waiter's tip posture. Hand muscles and long finger flexors (C8–T1) are spared, unlike Klumpke or total plexus palsy.

items.q: A 48-year-old woman has a painful bunion with a congruent first MTP joint, no arthritis, hallux valgus angle 30° and intermetatarsal angle 12°, with no first-ray hypermobility. The most appropriate procedure is:
o: Distal chevron osteotomy of the first metatarsal
items.e: A distal chevron osteotomy suits mild-to-moderate hallux valgus (HVA up to about 30–35°, IMA up to about 13–15°). Lapidus is chosen for hypermobility or severe IMA, MTP arthrodesis for arthritis or severe/recurrent deformity, and Keller is now largely reserved for low-demand elderly patients.

items.q: The hallux valgus angle is measured on a weight-bearing AP radiograph of the foot between the long axes of:
o: The first metatarsal and the proximal phalanx of the hallux
The proximal and distal phalanges of the hallux
The first metatarsal and the distal phalanx of the hallux
items.e: HVA is the angle between the first metatarsal and proximal phalanx axes (normal under about 15°). The first and second metatarsals form the intermetatarsal angle, and the two phalanges form the hallux valgus interphalangeus angle.

items.q: Avascular necrosis of the first metatarsal head after a distal chevron osteotomy is most strongly linked to:
o: A 60° rather than 90° chevron apex angle
Early weight-bearing in a post-operative shoe
Use of an absorbable pin for fixation
Extensive lateral soft-tissue release through the same approach, damaging the capsular blood supply
items.e: The metatarsal head is supplied largely through capsular branches entering dorsolaterally and plantar-laterally; adding an aggressive lateral capsular release to a distal osteotomy or cutting through the plantar-lateral vessels raises AVN risk. Fixation type and apex angle have little effect.

items.q: When templating for arthroplasty on a plain radiograph, which factor increases the magnification of the bone image?
items.e: Magnification equals source-to-image distance divided by source-to-object distance, so it rises as the bone moves away from the detector (e.g. obese patients) and falls as the tube moves further away. kVp and exposure time affect contrast and density, not geometric magnification.

items.q: During intraoperative fluoroscopy for fixation of a tibial plateau fracture, which set-up most reduces scatter radiation dose to the surgeon?
o: X-ray tube above the table with the image intensifier under it
X-ray tube under the table with the image intensifier close to the patient
Image intensifier kept as far from the patient as possible
Standing on the tube side of the C-arm during lateral images
items.e: Most scatter comes from the beam entry side of the patient, so the tube should be beneath the table and the receptor close to the patient; the surgeon should stand on the image-intensifier side. Moving the receptor away increases dose and magnification.

items.q: A 28-year-old has groin pain. Radiographs show patchy sclerosis of the femoral head without a crescent sign or collapse, and MRI shows a small (under 15% of the head) osteonecrotic lesion. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: Core decompression, with or without bone grafting
items.e: Small, pre-collapse (Ficat II) lesions in young patients do best with joint-preserving core decompression. Once a crescent sign or collapse appears, results of core decompression are poor and grafting, osteotomy or arthroplasty are considered.

items.q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for detecting early osteonecrosis of the femoral head before radiographic changes appear?
items.e: MRI has sensitivity and specificity close to 99% and shows the necrotic segment (double-line sign) before radiographic change. Bone scan is less sensitive and nonspecific, and CT mainly helps show subchondral fracture.

items.q: Which classification of femoral head osteonecrosis adds a grading of the extent of head involvement (mild, moderate or severe) within each stage?
items.e: The Steinberg system stages 0–VI and quantifies lesion size (A <15%, B 15–30%, C >30% of the head), which helps prognosis. Ficat–Arlet is radiographic staging only, and Mitchell classifies the MRI signal of the lesion.

items.q: Which is the most common cause of non-traumatic osteonecrosis of the femoral head?
items.e: Corticosteroids and alcohol together account for most non-traumatic cases, with corticosteroids the single most common. Sickle cell disease, Gaucher disease and dysbarism are recognised but less common causes.

items.q: In an alert patient with a tibial shaft fracture, which is the earliest and most sensitive clinical feature of acute compartment syndrome?
o: Pain out of proportion to the injury, worse on passive stretch
items.e: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch of the compartment muscles appear first. Pulses are usually preserved because compartment pressure rarely exceeds arterial pressure; paralysis and pallor are late signs of established ischaemia.

items.q: A 28-year-old has a flail chest with severe pulmonary contusion and a closed femoral shaft fracture. After resuscitation he remains borderline (lactate rising, needing vasopressors). The best initial management of the femur is:
items.e: Unstable or borderline polytrauma patients, especially with chest injury, risk a "second hit" from reaming and long surgery; damage control with external fixation is followed by conversion to a nail when the patient is stable, ideally within about 2 weeks.

items.q: In suspected chronic periprosthetic joint infection, a key advantage of the synovial alpha-defensin test over synovial culture is that it:
o: Is the only test that is a major criterion in the 2018 ICM definition
Is unaffected by metallosis or adverse reactions to metal debris
Remains accurate in patients who have already received antibiotics
Identifies the causative organism and its sensitivities
items.e: Alpha-defensin is an antimicrobial peptide released by neutrophils, and its accuracy is largely preserved after prior antibiotics. It does not identify the organism, can be falsely positive with metallosis, and is a minor (scored) criterion in the 2018 ICM definition.

items.q: Two years after an uneventful, well-functioning TKA, a patient develops sudden knee pain, swelling and fever 3 days after a urinary infection. The implants are well fixed. In the Tsukayama classification this is:
o: Late chronic infection, treated by two-stage revision
Acute haematogenous infection, usually treated by debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR) with modular exchange
Positive intraoperative cultures, treated with antibiotics alone
Early postoperative infection, treated by two-stage revision
items.e: Tsukayama types are positive intraoperative cultures, early postoperative (<4 weeks), late chronic (>4 weeks, insidious) and acute haematogenous infection in a previously well-functioning joint. Acute haematogenous infection with stable implants and short symptom duration (under about 3 weeks) is suitable for DAIR.

items.q: Which pattern of intra-articular damage is typical of cam-type femoroacetabular impingement?
o: Anterosuperior acetabular cartilage delamination ("carpet" lesion) with labrochondral separation
Isolated central femoral head chondral defect
Circumferential labral ossification with a contrecoup posteroinferior chondral lesion
Ligamentum teres hypertrophy with a medial femoral head cyst
items.e: In cam FAI the aspherical head–neck junction shears into the anterosuperior acetabulum, delaminating cartilage from the outside in and separating it from the labrum. Pincer FAI causes labral crushing and ossification with a contrecoup posteroinferior lesion.

items.q: Which radiographic measurement indicates global acetabular overcoverage (pincer-type impingement)?
items.e: An LCEA above about 40° (with a Tönnis angle of 0° or less, coxa profunda or protrusio) indicates overcoverage. An alpha angle above 55° indicates a cam lesion, while an LCEA under 20° and a Tönnis angle over 10° indicate dysplasia.

items.q: An 8-year-old with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy has a fixed equinus. Ankle dorsiflexion is limited with the knee extended but corrects past neutral with the knee flexed (positive Silfverskiöld test). The preferred procedure is:
o: Botulinum toxin injection into soleus only
items.e: When only the gastrocnemius is contracted, selective gastrocnemius recession corrects equinus without weakening soleus. Over-lengthening the Achilles tendon in diplegia risks calcaneus and crouch gait; split tibialis posterior transfer is for dynamic varus in hemiplegia.

items.q: A non-ambulatory 13-year-old with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy has a 70° thoracolumbar curve with marked pelvic obliquity. The usual extent of posterior spinal fusion is:
o: Upper thoracic spine (T2) to the pelvis
Selective fusion of the main thoracic curve only
items.e: In non-ambulatory neuromuscular scoliosis with pelvic obliquity, fusion from the upper thoracic spine to the pelvis gives balanced sitting and prevents junctional problems. Stopping short of the pelvis leaves the obliquity uncorrected.

items.q: A heterozygous HOXD13 mutation classically causes:
items.e: HOXD13 mutations cause synpolydactyly (syndactyly of the third/fourth fingers with duplication within the web). Holt–Oram is due to TBX5, ulnar–mammary to TBX3 and Apert to FGFR2.

items.q: In the Oberg–Manske–Tonkin (OMT) classification of congenital upper limb anomalies, radial longitudinal deficiency is placed in which category?
o: Malformations – abnormal axis formation/differentiation of the entire upper limb
items.e: OMT groups anomalies into malformations (by the embryological axis affected – proximodistal, radioulnar, dorsoventral), deformations (e.g. constriction ring) and dysplasias (e.g. overgrowth, tumours). Radial longitudinal deficiency is a radial–ulnar axis malformation of the entire limb.

items.q: A 32-year-old rugby player without generalised ligamentous laxity has chronic lateral ankle instability despite 6 months of supervised neuromuscular rehabilitation. The preferred primary operation is:
o: Modified Broström–Gould anatomical repair of the ATFL and CFL
items.e: Anatomical repair (Broström with Gould reinforcement) gives excellent results and preserves subtalar motion. Tendon graft reconstruction is reserved for failed repair, poor tissue or hyperlaxity, and non-anatomical tenodeses stiffen the subtalar joint.

items.q: Why should a transverse incision be avoided for open biopsy of a suspected extremity bone or soft-tissue sarcoma?
o: It contaminates a wider area that is hard to excise en bloc with the later longitudinal resection incision
It increases the risk of a non-diagnostic sample
It is associated with a higher rate of pathological fracture
items.e: The biopsy tract is considered contaminated and must be excised with the tumour, so it should be longitudinal, in line with the planned definitive incision, through a single compartment and away from neurovascular bundles.

items.q: A 60-year-old has a lytic pathological fracture of the femoral shaft. Which biopsy finding indicates metastatic carcinoma rather than a primary bone sarcoma?
o: Cohesive cytokeratin-positive epithelial cells forming glands
Malignant spindle cells producing lace-like osteoid
Sheets of small round blue cells that are CD99 positive
Lobules of atypical hyaline cartilage permeating marrow
items.e: Glands formed by cytokeratin-positive epithelial cells indicate adenocarcinoma metastasis. Malignant osteoid is diagnostic of osteosarcoma, atypical permeative cartilage of chondrosarcoma, and CD99-positive small round cells of Ewing sarcoma.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a normal major component of adult articular (hyaline) cartilage matrix?
items.e: Hyaline cartilage contains mainly type II collagen with minor types IX and XI, and aggrecan as its main proteoglycan. Type I collagen is characteristic of bone, tendon and the fibrocartilage that fills defects after microfracture.

items.q: A 7-year-old from a rural area has bowed legs, delayed dentition with enamel hypoplasia, raised alkaline phosphatase and a low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The most likely cause of the bone changes is:
items.e: Low 25(OH)D with raised ALP and rachitic deformity indicates nutritional vitamin D–deficiency rickets. Hypophosphatasia has a low ALP, and phosphate-wasting rickets has normal 25(OH)D.

items.q: A patient on long-term haemodialysis has bone pain. Hand radiographs show subperiosteal resorption along the radial aspects of the middle phalanges, and serum phosphate and PTH are high. The bone disease is:
o: Osteitis fibrosa (high-turnover renal osteodystrophy) from secondary hyperparathyroidism
items.e: In CKD, phosphate retention and low calcitriol drive secondary hyperparathyroidism, producing high-turnover osteitis fibrosa with subperiosteal resorption, brown tumours and rugger-jersey spine. Adynamic bone disease has a low PTH and low turnover.

items.q: Which serum test best reflects body vitamin D stores in a child with suspected nutritional rickets?
items.e: 25(OH)D has a long half-life and reflects vitamin D stores, so it is the diagnostic test. 1,25(OH)2D may be normal or even high because secondary hyperparathyroidism stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase; ALP shows disease activity, not the cause.

items.q: A child with X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets has persistent bowing despite conventional therapy. Which targeted drug addresses the underlying cause?
items.e: XLH (PHEX mutation) causes excess FGF23, renal phosphate wasting and low calcitriol; burosumab neutralises FGF23 and improves phosphate and rickets more than oral phosphate plus calcitriol. Cholecalciferol alone does not correct phosphate wasting.

items.q: Nine months after statically locked reamed nailing of a closed tibial shaft fracture, a patient has pain on weight-bearing. Radiographs show a hypertrophic non-union with an intact nail; infection markers are normal. The treatment of choice is:
o: Exchange reamed nailing with a larger nail
items.e: Hypertrophic non-union has good biology but lacks stability; exchange nailing (reaming 1–2 mm more, larger nail) adds stiffness and autograft-like reamings and achieves high union rates. Bone grafting alone is chosen for atrophic non-union.

items.q: Which statement best contrasts relative and absolute stability in fracture fixation?
o: Absolute stability is achieved only with plates and relative stability only with intramedullary nails
Relative stability allows controlled motion and healing by callus, whereas absolute stability abolishes interfragmentary motion and gives direct (primary) bone healing
Relative stability requires immobilisation until union, whereas absolute stability allows early weight-bearing
Absolute stability is achieved with absorbable implants and relative stability with metal implants
