items.e: Interfragmentary compression (lag screws, compression plating) gives absolute stability and direct healing without callus. Nails, bridge plates and external fixators give relative stability with secondary (callus) healing; plates can be used in either mode.

items.q: According to the British (BOAST) open fracture standards, if it cannot be done at the first debridement, definitive soft-tissue cover of a Gustilo IIIB tibial fracture should be achieved within:
items.e: BOAST recommends joint orthoplastic care with definitive fixation and soft-tissue coverage ideally at the same time and within 72 hours, as later cover is associated with higher deep infection and flap failure.

items.q: In the early inflammatory phase after a fracture, the local tissue is hypoxic. How does this hypoxia promote healing?
o: It promotes calcium phosphate deposition in the haematoma
It inhibits mesenchymal stem cell recruitment, preventing fibrosis
It stabilises HIF-1α, which upregulates VEGF and drives angiogenesis
items.e: Hypoxia-inducible factor-1α accumulates in hypoxic tissue and induces VEGF, restoring blood supply and coupling angiogenesis with osteogenesis; hypoxia also favours chondrogenic differentiation in the soft callus.

items.q: After volar locking plate fixation of a distal radius fracture, which factor most increases the risk of flexor pollicis longus tendon rupture?
o: Plate placed too proximally on the radial shaft
Repair of the pronator quadratus over the plate
Plate placed distal to the watershed line or prominent volar to it
Use of unicortical distal locking screws
items.e: The FPL glides directly over the watershed line; a plate that is distal to or projects beyond it (Soong grades 1–2) abrades the tendon. Unicortical/short distal screws reduce extensor (not flexor) tendon irritation, and pronator quadratus repair may protect the tendons.

items.q: Bridge plating (bridging osteosynthesis) is best suited to which fracture?
o: A simple transverse forearm fracture in a young adult
A displaced intra-articular tibial plateau fracture needing anatomical reduction
items.e: A bridge plate spans a comminuted zone fixed only to the main proximal and distal fragments, restoring length, alignment and rotation while preserving the fragments' blood supply and giving relative stability. Simple and articular fractures need anatomical reduction and absolute stability.

items.q: A 35-year-old woman has 4 months of back pain with mild right leg weakness. Radiographs show paradiscal destruction of T12–L1 with partial collapse. Which investigation best shows the extent of disease, paravertebral or epidural abscess and cord compression?
o: Contrast-enhanced MRI of the whole spine
items.e: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the imaging of choice in spinal tuberculosis: it shows marrow involvement, abscesses, skip lesions (hence whole-spine imaging) and neural compression. CT shows bony destruction better but not soft-tissue or cord detail.

items.q: A 72-year-old has cuff tear arthropathy: glenohumeral arthritis with a massive irreparable rotator cuff tear, pseudoparalysis and a functioning deltoid. The most appropriate operation is:
items.e: Reverse TSA medialises and lowers the centre of rotation so the deltoid can elevate the arm without a cuff. An anatomic glenoid component fails early by rocking-horse loosening without a cuff, and hemiarthroplasty gives poor elevation.

items.q: In anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty with adequate glenoid bone stock, which glenoid component fixation has the most reliable long-term survival?
o: Metal-backed component with an augmented block and cemented liner
Uncemented hydroxyapatite-coated metal component with a modular sleeve
Uncemented metal-backed component with a polyethylene liner
items.e: Cemented all-polyethylene (keeled or, preferably, pegged) glenoids remain the standard. Metal-backed uncemented designs have had higher failure from polyethylene wear, dissociation and metal-on-metal contact.

items.q: The deltopectoral approach used for anatomic total shoulder arthroplasty exploits the internervous plane between the:
o: Musculocutaneous nerve and the axillary nerve
Axillary nerve (deltoid) and the lateral and medial pectoral nerves (pectoralis major)
Axillary nerve and the suprascapular nerve
items.e: The deltoid (axillary nerve) is retracted laterally and pectoralis major (pectoral nerves) medially along the cephalic vein. Deep, the musculocutaneous nerve lies under the conjoint tendon and the axillary nerve runs along the inferior border of subscapularis.

items.q: A 24-year-old tennis player felt a painful snap behind the lateral malleolus during a forced dorsiflexion–eversion movement, and now has painful clicking there. Which investigation best demonstrates the suspected peroneal tendon subluxation?
o: Dynamic ultrasound during resisted eversion and dorsiflexion
items.e: Dynamic ultrasound can show the peroneal tendons subluxing out of the retromalleolar groove in real time, which static MRI may miss. A lateral malleolar "fleck sign" on radiographs indicates superior peroneal retinaculum avulsion but does not show the tendon dynamically.

items.q: A 24-year-old footballer has groin pain with tenderness at the pubic attachment and pain on resisted adduction and the squeeze test. Under the Doha agreement this is adductor-related groin pain; which muscle is most commonly involved?
items.e: Adductor longus, with its small tendinous pubic origin and high eccentric loads in kicking and change of direction, is the most commonly affected adductor. FADIR-positive pain instead points to intra-articular hip pathology such as FAI or a labral tear.

items.q: Which injectable therapy used for sports injuries is NOT prohibited by WADA?
items.e: PRP was removed from the WADA Prohibited List in 2011, although intravenous infusions above the volume limit remain prohibited. GH, IGF-1 and EPO are peptide hormones/growth factors (class S2) prohibited at all times.

items.q: A 19-year-old competitive swimmer has atraumatic multidirectional shoulder instability with a positive sulcus sign and generalised ligamentous laxity, but has never dislocated. The first-line management is:
o: A structured rehabilitation programme strengthening the rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers
items.e: Atraumatic multidirectional instability (AMBRII) is treated first with at least 6 months of focused rehabilitation; most patients improve. Capsular shift or plication is considered only after failed rehabilitation, and Bankart or Latarjet procedures address traumatic unidirectional instability.

items.q: The haematological module of the WADA Athlete Biological Passport detects blood doping mainly by longitudinal monitoring of:
items.e: The haematological module tracks markers such as haemoglobin, reticulocyte percentage and the OFF-score over time to reveal erythropoiesis-stimulating agents or transfusions. The T/E ratio belongs to the separate steroidal module.

items.q: A 4-month-old girl has a dislocated left hip that reduces with a clunk on the Ortolani manoeuvre; ultrasound confirms a reducible dislocation. The most appropriate initial treatment is:
o: Open reduction through a medial approach
Closed reduction under anaesthesia and hip spica
Observation and repeat ultrasound at 6 months
Pavlik harness with ultrasound monitoring of reduction
items.e: Under about 6 months a reducible dislocated hip is treated with a Pavlik harness, checking reduction by ultrasound. Closed reduction and spica is used when the harness fails or in older infants, and open reduction when closed reduction fails.

items.q: A 3-year-old walking child has a previously undiagnosed dislocated hip from DDH with a high-riding femoral head and a steep, shallow acetabulum. The usual treatment is:
o: Observation until skeletal maturity, then total hip arthroplasty
Open reduction with femoral shortening osteotomy and pelvic (acetabular) osteotomy
Closed reduction and hip spica alone
items.e: After about 2 years, a dislocated hip usually needs open reduction; femoral shortening reduces pressure on the head (lowering AVN risk) and a Salter or Pemberton osteotomy corrects acetabular dysplasia. Harness and closed reduction succeed only in younger children.

items.q: The ossific nucleus of the femoral head normally appears on radiographs at about what age, and its delayed appearance on one side suggests what?
o: 4–6 months; developmental dysplasia of the hip
items.e: The femoral capital ossific nucleus appears between about 4 and 6 months (earlier in girls) and is often delayed or smaller on the dysplastic side. Before it appears, ultrasound is preferred for DDH; after about 4–6 months radiographs become useful.

items.q: After an acute lateral patellar dislocation that has reduced, MRI typically shows bone bruising in which locations?
o: Inferomedial patella and anterolateral (non-articular) lateral femoral condyle
Superolateral patella and medial femoral condyle
Medial tibial plateau and medial femoral condyle
Posterolateral tibial plateau and lateral femoral condyle sulcus
items.e: As the patella relocates from its dislocated position, its medial facet strikes the lateral femoral condyle, producing a "kissing" bruise pattern with a torn MPFL. Lateral femoral condyle sulcus and posterolateral tibial plateau bruising is the ACL pivot-shift pattern.

items.q: Which is an absolute contraindication to sulcus-deepening trochleoplasty for recurrent patellar instability with high-grade trochlear dysplasia?
items.e: Trochleoplasty reshapes the subchondral bone next to the distal femoral physis, so it is avoided in skeletally immature patients. A J sign, a large supratrochlear spur and Dejour B or D dysplasia are the usual indications rather than contraindications.

items.q: A 20-year-old woman has recurrent lateral patellar dislocation, in-toeing, and femoral anteversion of 40° on CT. Besides MPFL reconstruction, which procedure addresses the rotational cause?
items.e: Excess femoral anteversion (more than about 25–30°) internally rotates the trochlea under the patella, increasing the lateral vector; a supracondylar or intertrochanteric external rotation osteotomy corrects it. Tibial tubercle medialisation addresses a raised TT–TG distance, and isolated lateral release does not stabilise the patella.

items.q: Iatrogenic medial patellar instability is most often a complication of:
o: MPFL reconstruction with the femoral tunnel too distal
items.e: Over-release of the lateral retinaculum, including the vastus lateralis obliquus, removes the lateral restraint and can allow medial subluxation, demonstrated by the medial (Fulkerson) relocation test. It is treated by lateral retinacular repair or reconstruction.

items.q: Compared with the TT–TG distance, the TT–PCL distance used in assessment of patellar instability:
o: Is independent of trochlear dysplasia and knee joint rotation, with values of 24 mm or more considered pathological
Is measured on a weight-bearing lateral radiograph
Uses the deepest point of the trochlear groove as its femoral reference
items.e: TT–PCL measures the tibial tubercle relative to the medial border of the PCL on the tibia, so it reflects only tibial tubercle lateralisation and is not affected by trochlear shape or knee rotation; 24 mm or more is abnormal. TT–TG uses the trochlear groove and is considered pathological above about 20 mm.

items.q: On coronal MRI after an anterior shoulder dislocation, the inferior glenohumeral ligament has lost its normal U-shaped axillary pouch and appears J-shaped, drooping inferiorly. This indicates:
o: A humeral avulsion of the glenohumeral ligament (HAGL) lesion
items.e: In HAGL, the IGHL is avulsed from its humeral neck attachment, converting the U-shaped axillary pouch into a J shape. It is an important cause of failed Bankart repair if missed and is repaired open or arthroscopically.

items.q: After a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, which factor most strongly predicts recurrent instability?
o: Younger age at the first dislocation (under about 20 years)
items.e: Recurrence is highest in young patients, especially males under 20 in contact or overhead sport, reaching 50–90% in some series. A greater tuberosity fracture actually lowers the recurrence risk.

items.q: A 65-year-old has a first-time anterior shoulder dislocation. Three weeks after reduction she still cannot actively abduct the arm, although the deltoid contracts and sensation over the lateral arm is normal. The most likely cause is:
o: Persistent glenohumeral subluxation from a Bankart lesion
items.e: In patients over about 40, an anterior dislocation commonly tears the rotator cuff (the "posterior mechanism"); with a contracting deltoid and intact regimental-badge sensation, an axillary nerve palsy is unlikely. Early ultrasound or MRI and repair are recommended.

items.q: In the Stanmore classification of shoulder instability, a patient with atraumatic instability caused by abnormal muscle patterning (polar type III) is best treated with:
o: Specialist physiotherapy with muscle retraining and biofeedback
items.e: Polar type III instability is driven by abnormal muscle activation (often pectoralis major or latissimus dorsi) without structural damage, and surgery has poor results. Type I (traumatic structural) instability is the group that benefits most from surgery.

items.q: In the Thomas and Matsen classification of shoulder instability, the AMBRII group is typically managed by rehabilitation and, if that fails, by which operation?
o: Inferior capsular shift (with rotator interval closure)
items.e: AMBRII stands for Atraumatic, Multidirectional, Bilateral, Rehabilitation, Inferior capsular shift and Interval closure. TUBS (Traumatic, Unidirectional, Bankart, Surgery) is the group treated by Bankart repair.

items.q: In the Ellman classification of partial-thickness rotator cuff tears, surgical repair is generally recommended for:
o: Grade 1 tears – less than 3 mm deep
Any bursal-side tear regardless of depth
Grade 3 tears – deeper than 6 mm (more than 50% of tendon thickness)
items.e: Ellman grades depth as 1 (<3 mm), 2 (3–6 mm) and 3 (>6 mm, over half the roughly 12 mm tendon). Tears involving more than 50% of the thickness are usually completed and repaired or repaired in situ; lower grades are debrided.

items.q: A volleyball player has posterior shoulder pain with isolated wasting and weakness of infraspinatus; supraspinatus is normal. MRI shows a paralabral cyst. Where is the nerve compressed?
o: Suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch
Suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch
Long thoracic nerve at the scalenus medius
Axillary nerve in the quadrilateral space
items.e: Compression at the spinoglenoid notch, often by a ganglion from a posterosuperior labral (SLAP) tear, affects only the infraspinatus branch. Suprascapular notch compression weakens both supraspinatus and infraspinatus; quadrilateral space syndrome affects teres minor and deltoid.

items.q: The examiner holds the patient's arm at 20° of abduction with the elbow flexed 90° and passively rotates the shoulder to near-maximal external rotation; when released, the arm drifts back into internal rotation. This positive external rotation lag sign mainly indicates a tear of:
items.e: The external rotation lag sign detects full-thickness posterosuperior cuff tears involving infraspinatus. Subscapularis tears are detected by lift-off, belly-press and bear-hug tests, and the hornblower sign suggests teres minor insufficiency.

items.q: A 50-year-old has an irreparable, chronic subscapularis tear with anterior shoulder pain and weakness but no glenohumeral arthritis. A recognised tendon transfer is:
o: Latissimus dorsi transfer to the greater tuberosity
Teres major transfer to the infraspinatus footprint
Pectoralis major transfer (sternal head or split, ideally under the conjoint tendon)
items.e: Pectoralis major (or latissimus dorsi to the lesser tuberosity) transfers substitute for the internal rotation and anterior stabilising function of subscapularis. Lower trapezius and latissimus dorsi to the greater tuberosity are used for irreparable posterosuperior tears.

items.q: During hip arthroscopy, which nerve is most at risk when the anterior portal is created?
items.e: Branches of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve lie within a few millimetres of the anterior portal, which is why only the skin is incised there. The superior gluteal nerve is closest to the anterolateral portal, and the sciatic nerve to the posterolateral portal.

items.q: The most common neurological complication of hip arthroscopy performed with a perineal post for traction is:
items.e: Compression by the perineal post during traction causes transient pudendal neurapraxia (perineal numbness, sexual or urinary symptoms); risk rises with traction force and time. Keeping traction time short and using a well-padded or post-less system reduces it.

items.q: During arthroscopic femoral osteochondroplasty for cam impingement, resection of more than about what proportion of the femoral neck diameter significantly increases the risk of femoral neck fracture?
items.e: Cadaveric work (Mardones et al.) showed that resecting up to 30% of the anterolateral head–neck junction does not significantly reduce load to fracture, while larger resections do. Protected weight-bearing is often advised after large resections.

items.q: Which preoperative finding most predicts a poor outcome and early conversion to total hip arthroplasty after arthroscopic surgery for femoroacetabular impingement?
o: Tönnis grade 2 or higher osteoarthritis (joint space under about 2 mm)
items.e: Established arthritis, with joint space narrowing to 2 mm or less (Tönnis grade 2–3), strongly predicts failure of hip preservation. A raised alpha angle, labral tear and positive FADIR are the expected features of FAI that arthroscopy aims to treat.

items.q: A 24-year-old with borderline hip dysplasia (lateral centre-edge angle 22°) and a cam lesion undergoes hip arthroscopy. Which step is most important to prevent postoperative instability?
o: Repair or plication of the capsule at the end of the procedure
items.e: In borderline dysplasia the capsule and labrum are key stabilisers; careful labral preservation and capsular closure or plication reduce the risk of iatrogenic microinstability or dislocation. Rim trimming further reduces coverage and is contraindicated.

items.q: The moving valgus stress test for an ulnar collateral ligament injury of the elbow is positive when medial elbow pain is reproduced:
o: Only at full elbow extension with varus stress
Between about 70° and 120° of elbow flexion while the elbow is extended from full flexion under valgus load
At 90° of flexion with the forearm fully supinated and no valgus load
Only at full flexion with the shoulder adducted
items.e: O'Driscoll's moving valgus stress test applies valgus torque with the shoulder abducted and externally rotated while the elbow is extended from full flexion; pain in the 70–120° "shear angle" arc, corresponding to the late cocking and early acceleration phases, is positive.

items.q: On MR arthrography of a pitcher's elbow, contrast tracks along the undersurface of the anterior bundle of the ulnar collateral ligament at its insertion, forming a "T sign". This indicates:
o: A partial undersurface tear of the UCL at the sublime tubercle
items.e: The anterior bundle of the UCL inserts on the sublime tubercle of the ulna; contrast leaking between the ligament and bone without extending through it produces the T sign of a partial undersurface tear. A full-thickness tear allows contrast to leak beyond the ligament.

items.q: In ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction of the elbow (Jobe or docking technique), the most commonly used autograft is:
items.e: Palmaris longus is the usual graft because it is expendable and of suitable size; its presence must be confirmed preoperatively because it is absent in about 15% of people, in which case gracilis or plantaris is used.

items.q: An adolescent baseball pitcher has posterior elbow pain during the deceleration phase. MRI shows oedema and a transverse lucency across the olecranon, and the pain persists despite rest. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: Internal fixation with an intramedullary compression screw
items.e: Olecranon stress fractures in throwers result from repetitive triceps traction and valgus extension forces; if rest fails, compression screw fixation reliably achieves union and return to throwing. Excision would disrupt the triceps insertion.

items.q: A professional pitcher has glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) of 30° in the throwing shoulder compared with the other side. The usual first-line treatment is:
o: Posterior capsular stretching such as the sleeper stretch
items.e: GIRD is caused by posteroinferior capsular contracture and shifts the humeral head posterosuperiorly in late cocking, predisposing to SLAP lesions and internal impingement. Most respond to posterior capsular stretching (sleeper and cross-body stretches); posterior capsular release is reserved for failures.

items.q: In the overhead thrower, internal (posterosuperior) impingement occurs when, in maximal abduction and external rotation, the:
o: Articular surface of the posterosuperior rotator cuff is pinched between the greater tuberosity and the posterosuperior glenoid and labrum
Long head of biceps subluxes medially out of the groove
Subscapularis impinges between the coracoid and lesser tuberosity
Bursal surface of the supraspinatus impinges on the coracoacromial arch
items.e: Internal impingement produces articular-side partial cuff tears and posterosuperior labral lesions in throwers. Classic Neer (external) impingement affects the bursal side under the acromion, and coracoid impingement involves subscapularis.

items.q: After the age of about 3 months, which examination finding is the most reliable sign of a dislocated hip in DDH?
items.e: As soft tissues tighten, the Ortolani and Barlow tests become negative, and limitation of abduction (with apparent femoral shortening) becomes the most reliable sign. Asymmetric skin folds are common in normal infants and are unreliable.

items.q: An infant with a dislocated hip has been in a Pavlik harness for 3–4 weeks, but ultrasound shows the hip is still not reduced. The next step is:
o: Tighten the posterior straps to increase abduction beyond 70°
Add a night abduction brace while continuing the harness
Stop the harness and proceed to closed reduction and spica casting
Continue the harness for another 3 months
items.e: Persisting with the harness when the hip stays dislocated risks "Pavlik harness disease", erosion of the posterior acetabular wall that makes later reduction harder. Excessive abduction risks avascular necrosis, and excessive flexion femoral nerve palsy.

items.q: In a Salter innominate osteotomy for DDH, the distal acetabular fragment rotates through which hinge?
items.e: Salter's complete transverse iliac osteotomy above the acetabulum rotates the whole acetabulum anterolaterally, hinging on the symphysis pubis; it requires a concentrically reduced hip with good motion. The Pemberton incomplete osteotomy hinges on the triradiate cartilage.

items.q: After closed reduction of a dislocated hip in DDH, the hip spica is applied in the "human position". This means:
o: About 100° of hip flexion with abduction kept within the safe zone (under about 60°)
Full hip extension with 45° of abduction
90° of flexion with 20° of adduction and internal rotation
30° of hip flexion with maximal (frog-leg) abduction
items.e: The human position (Salter) maintains reduction with deep flexion and moderate abduction within Ramsey's safe zone, between the angle of redislocation and maximal abduction. Extreme abduction (frog-leg) compresses the medial circumflex vessels and causes AVN.

items.q: Which obstacle to concentric closed reduction in DDH is extra-articular?
o: A tight iliopsoas tendon constricting the capsule (hourglass constriction)
items.e: The iliopsoas tendon crosses the anteromedial capsule and creates an hourglass constriction; it is released during open reduction. The inverted limbus, pulvinar, ligamentum teres and transverse acetabular ligament are intra-articular obstacles.

items.q: A 10-year-old with late-stage Perthes disease has painful limited abduction. An abduction arthrogram shows the deformed femoral head levering on the lateral acetabular edge and widening of the medial joint space. The appropriate procedure is:
items.e: Hinge abduction means the hip can no longer be contained; further abduction worsens it. A valgus (extension) osteotomy brings the congruent part of the head under the acetabulum in the adducted position, relieving pain. Varus osteotomy and abduction casting are containment methods, contraindicated here.

items.q: The Herring lateral pillar classification in Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease is assigned during which stage of the disease?
items.e: Lateral pillar height is graded on the AP radiograph early in the fragmentation stage (A: normal, B: more than 50% height preserved, B/C border, C: less than 50%). The Stulberg classification is applied in the healed stage to predict long-term outcome.

items.q: Which child presenting with a slipped capital femoral epiphysis should be investigated for an underlying endocrine disorder?
o: A 9-year-old whose weight is below the 50th centile
A 14-year-old boy with a stable slip after sport
items.e: Typical SCFE occurs in obese adolescents (girls about 12, boys about 13–14). Onset under 10 or over 16 years, or a weight below the 50th centile, suggests hypothyroidism, growth hormone therapy, panhypopituitarism or renal osteodystrophy, which also raise the risk of bilateral slips.

items.q: During in situ screw fixation of a stable SCFE, which technical error is most associated with chondrolysis?
o: Engaging at least five threads in the epiphysis
Placing the screw in the centre of the epiphysis
Using a single rather than two screws
Unrecognised penetration of the screw into the hip joint
items.e: Persistent intra-articular screw penetration damages the articular cartilage and is the main iatrogenic cause of chondrolysis; the "approach–withdraw" fluoroscopic technique and keeping the tip at least about 5 mm from subchondral bone avoid it. A single central screw with adequate threads across the physis is the standard.

items.q: A newborn has a rigid rocker-bottom foot. A forced plantarflexion lateral radiograph shows that the navicular remains dorsally dislocated on the talar neck. The diagnosis and usual initial treatment are:
o: Congenital vertical talus; serial reverse-Ponseti casting followed by talonavicular pinning and percutaneous Achilles tenotomy (Dobbs method)
items.e: In congenital vertical talus the talonavicular dislocation does not reduce on plantarflexion, distinguishing it from oblique talus, which reduces. The minimally invasive Dobbs method has largely replaced extensive one-stage release; calcaneovalgus is a flexible positional deformity.

items.q: After Ponseti correction of unilateral idiopathic clubfoot, the foot abduction brace holds the shoes at approximately:
o: 90° of external rotation on the clubfoot side and neutral on the normal side
60–70° of external rotation on the clubfoot side and 30–40° on the normal side, with the bar shoulder-width apart
Neutral rotation on both sides with 10° of dorsiflexion
20° of external rotation on both sides with feet together
items.e: The brace maintains the abduction achieved in casting: about 60–70° external rotation on the affected side (40° on a normal foot), with the bar at shoulder width and slight dorsiflexion bend. It is worn full-time for 3 months, then at night and nap times until about 4 years.

items.q: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) compared two physical‑therapy protocols after ankle fracture fixation. The authors reported a mean difference in functional score of 4.5 points (SD = 7.2) favoring protocol A, with a p-value of 0.04. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Protocol A is clinically superior to protocol B.
Protocol A shows a statistically significant but possibly trivial benefit.
The study is underpowered and the result is unreliable.
The difference is clinically insignificant because the SD exceeds the mean.
items.e: p = 0.04 shows the difference is unlikely to be chance, but statistical significance says nothing about size: a 4.5-point difference may be below the score's minimal clinically important difference (MCID). Judge clinical relevance against the MCID, not the p-value.

items.q: In evidence‑based orthopaedics, the GRADE system classifies the quality of evidence. Which statement best describes the starting level for a cohort study?
items.e: Cohort studies begin as low‑quality evidence in GRADE, though they can be upgraded with large effect sizes or dose‑response gradients.

items.q: Why is the confidence interval (CI) width an important consideration when interpreting registry data on postoperative complications?
o: Narrow CIs always indicate better outcomes.
Wide CIs may reflect small sample sizes or high variability.
CIs are irrelevant for registry studies.
Wide CIs confirm the superiority of one treatment.
items.e: A wide CI suggests imprecision, often due to limited events or heterogeneity, which limits the certainty of the estimate.

items.q: A systematic review of analgesic protocols after hip arthroscopy ended with an odds ratio of 0.62 (95% CI 0.45–0.85) for postoperative opioid use with multimodal regimen versus standard care. What does the CI imply?
o: The odds of opioid use are reduced by somewhere between about 15% and 55%
The odds of opioid use are reduced by at least 38%
The result is not statistically significant
The multimodal regimen increases opioid use
items.e: An OR of 0.62 with a 95% CI of 0.45–0.85 means the true odds reduction plausibly lies between 15% (OR 0.85) and 55% (OR 0.45); because the whole interval lies below 1, the result is statistically significant.

items.q: Which is a correct description of the ‘intention‑to‑treat’ (ITT) principle in orthopaedic RCTs?
o: Patients are analyzed only if they complete the intervention.
Dropouts are excluded from the analysis to avoid bias.
All randomized patients are included in the group they were assigned.
The outcome is measured only after the full intervention course.
items.e: ITT includes every randomized patient in their assigned group regardless of adherence, preserving the benefit of randomization and preventing attrition bias.

items.q: A radiograph of a young adult with chronic bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia shows an 'Erlenmeyer flask' expansion of the distal femoral metaphyses. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Marrow infiltration by glucocerebroside-laden macrophages in Gaucher disease causes failure of metaphyseal remodelling (Erlenmeyer flask femur), with hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bone crises and osteonecrosis. Erlenmeyer flask deformity is also seen in osteopetrosis and Pyle disease, not in rickets.

items.q: A 67-year-old woman has generalised bone pain. Which single blood test best reflects her total body vitamin D stores?
items.e: 25(OH)D has a long half-life and is the accepted measure of vitamin D status. 1,25(OH)2D is misleading because secondary hyperparathyroidism keeps it normal or even high in deficiency.

items.q: Regarding raloxifene in postmenopausal osteoporosis (MORE trial), which statement is correct?
o: It increases the risk of invasive breast cancer
It reduces vertebral but not hip fractures
It reduces the risk of venous thromboembolism
items.e: Raloxifene, a SERM, reduces vertebral fracture risk by about 30–50% but has not been shown to reduce hip or non-vertebral fractures. It increases VTE risk and hot flushes and lowers the risk of ER-positive invasive breast cancer.

items.q: A 12-year-old girl has an undisplaced, stable transverse fracture of the distal femoral metaphysis just above the physis. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: Long-leg cast with close radiographic follow-up
Open reduction and transphyseal screw fixation
items.e: An undisplaced, stable fracture can be treated in a long-leg cast with weekly radiographs to detect displacement. Fixation is kept for displaced or unstable fractures, and screws across the physis should be avoided.

items.q: A 70-year-old osteoporotic woman has an AO/OTA 31A3 (reverse-obliquity) intertrochanteric fracture with a comminuted lateral wall. The implant of choice is:
items.e: In A3 fractures and fractures with an incompetent lateral wall, a sliding hip screw allows uncontrolled lateral sliding and medialisation of the shaft; an intramedullary nail acts as a buttress and has lower failure rates. Proximal femoral locking plates have high rates of varus collapse and implant failure.

items.q: On CT, which feature distinguishes a thoracolumbar burst fracture from a simple wedge compression fracture?
o: Loss of anterior vertebral body height
Retropulsion of a posterior vertebral wall fragment into the canal
items.e: A burst fracture involves the middle column (posterior vertebral body wall), often with a retropulsed fragment narrowing the canal and widening of the interpedicular distance. A compression fracture fails only the anterior column, so the posterior wall stays intact.

items.q: A 45-year-old man has unilateral leg pain radiating to the lateral foot, with a reduced ankle jerk. MRI shows a posterolateral (paracentral) disc herniation at L5–S1. Which nerve root is compressed?
items.e: A paracentral herniation compresses the traversing root, which at L5–S1 is S1 (lateral foot pain, weak plantarflexion, absent ankle jerk). A far-lateral (foraminal) herniation at L5–S1 would compress the exiting L5 root.

items.q: Two years after a long posterior instrumented thoracolumbar fusion for adult deformity, a 68-year-old osteoporotic woman has increased kyphosis of 15° between the upper instrumented vertebra and two levels above it. This is:
items.e: PJK is defined as a proximal junctional angle (UIV to UIV+2) of at least 10° and at least 10° greater than before surgery. Risk factors include older age, osteoporosis, large sagittal corrections and long constructs.

items.q: In TKA, the most commonly used anatomical landmark for setting tibial component rotation is:
o: Medial third of the tibial tubercle
Posterior condylar line of the tibia
items.e: The tibial component is usually aligned to the junction of the medial and middle thirds of the tibial tubercle (Akagi line). Internal rotation of the tibial component is a common cause of patellar maltracking and anterior knee pain. The transepicondylar axis and Whiteside's line are femoral references.

items.q: Which statement best describes kinematic alignment TKA?
o: The tibia is cut perpendicular to its mechanical axis
Bone and cartilage are resected to equal the implant thickness so the pre-arthritic joint lines are restored
The femoral component is set in 3° external rotation to the posterior condylar axis
Routine collateral ligament releases achieve a neutral hip-knee-ankle angle
items.e: Kinematic alignment resurfaces the knee by removing the thickness of the implant (after allowing for cartilage wear), restoring the patient's own pre-arthritic joint lines and limb alignment with few or no ligament releases. Mechanical alignment uses a neutral tibial cut and femoral rotation referenced to fixed axes.

items.q: A 24-year-old tennis player has groin pain with a positive FADIR test. Radiographs show a cam lesion at the anterosuperior femoral head–neck junction with an alpha angle of 70°, Tönnis grade 0 and a repairable labral tear on MR arthrography. After failed physiotherapy, the best option is:
o: Arthroscopic femoral osteochondroplasty with labral repair
Core decompression of the femoral head
items.e: Symptomatic cam FAI without arthritis is treated by resecting the cam (femoral osteochondroplasty) and repairing the labrum. Debridement alone leaves the cause behind, and PAO is for acetabular dysplasia.

items.q: A 32‑year‑old soccer player with FAI symptoms relapses after a partial arthroscopic osteoplasty. Which postoperative imaging is most useful to rule out residual cam morphology?
o: CT with 3D reconstruction and radial reformats of the head–neck junction
items.e: CT with 3D/radial reformats best shows the bony head–neck contour and quantifies residual cam (alpha angle around the clock face); under-resection of the cam is the commonest cause of revision hip arthroscopy.

items.q: Which finding is the strongest predictor of a poor outcome, and hence a relative contraindication, for arthroscopic treatment of symptomatic FAI?
o: Tönnis grade 0 hip with a cam lesion
Joint space width less than 2 mm on the AP pelvis
items.e: Established arthritis (Tönnis grade 2 or more, joint space under 2 mm) predicts failure and early conversion to THA after hip arthroscopy. Labral tears and mixed morphology are routine indications.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy has a closed, displaced Salter-Harris type II fracture of the distal tibia with an intact neurovascular status. The most appropriate initial management is:
o: Open reduction with a transphyseal screw
items.e: Displaced SH II distal tibial fractures are usually treated by gentle closed reduction and casting. Interposed periosteum preventing reduction (residual gap over 3 mm) is an indication for open reduction, and any metaphyseal (Thurston-Holland) screw should avoid the physis.

items.q: A 9-year-old has a Salter-Harris type II fracture of the proximal humerus with 40° angulation and 50% displacement. The best management is:
o: Closed reduction and percutaneous K-wire fixation
items.e: The proximal humeral physis provides about 80% of humeral length and the shoulder has a wide range of motion, so remodelling is excellent: in children under about 10 years almost any angulation and displacement is accepted. Reduction and fixation are considered in adolescents near skeletal maturity with severe displacement.

items.q: Which of the following supracondylar humerus fractures in a child can routinely be treated without reduction or fixation?
o: Gartland type II fracture with medial column comminution and varus
Gartland type I fracture with only a posterior fat pad sign
items.e: Gartland type I (undisplaced) fractures are treated in an above-elbow cast at about 90°. Type III, type II with rotation or medial comminution (risk of cubitus varus), and displaced flexion-type fractures need reduction and pinning.

items.q: A 13-year-old girl has a Salter-Harris type III fracture of the distal femoral epiphysis with 3 mm articular displacement. The best treatment is:
o: Open (or arthroscopically assisted) reduction and screw fixation parallel to the physis within the epiphysis
Crossed smooth K-wires across the physis
items.e: SH III/IV fractures are intra-articular and cross the physis, so anatomical reduction (displacement no more than about 2 mm) is needed to protect both the joint surface and the physis. Fixation uses epiphyseal screws parallel to the physis, avoiding it.

items.q: Ten days after fixation of an open distal radius fracture, a patient has fever, a hot swollen wrist and painful restricted motion. The most important investigation to confirm septic arthritis of the wrist is:
o: Joint aspiration for Gram stain, cell count and culture
items.e: Aspiration of synovial fluid (white cell count usually above 50,000/mm³, Gram stain, culture) confirms septic arthritis and identifies the organism. Imaging and inflammatory markers support the diagnosis but cannot confirm it.

items.q: Which of the following organisms is most commonly implicated in a culture‑positive pyogenic infection of the hand?
items.e: Staphylococcus aureus accounts for the majority of acute pyogenic hand infections, especially following trauma or penetrating wounds.

items.q: The standard open approach for drainage of a septic radiocarpal joint is:
o: Dorsal arthrotomy through the interval between the third and fourth extensor compartments
Volar approach through the flexor carpi radialis sheath
Ulnar approach between ECU and FCU
Radial approach through the first extensor compartment
items.e: The radiocarpal joint is drained through a dorsal longitudinal incision between the 3rd (EPL) and 4th (EDC) compartments, opening the capsule just distal to Lister's tubercle; arthroscopic lavage is an alternative.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old marathon runner presents with a sudden sharp pain behind the heel while running and a palpable ‘gap’ on the posterior aspect of the ankle. The most likely diagnosis is
items.e: An acute Achilles rupture presents with a sudden ‘snap’ and a palpable defect. Mid‑portion tendinopathy is a chronic process, not a discrete gap. The other options are unrelated to the described presentation.

items.q: The first-line investigation for an isolated mid‑portion Achilles tendinopathy suspected clinically in a patient with non‑traumatic posterior heel pain is
items.e: Ultrasound is quick, inexpensive and sensitive for detecting tendon thickening, fiber disruption or inflammatory changes in mid‑portion tendinopathy. MRI is reserved for equivocal or atypical cases.

items.q: Which principle of biopsy for a suspected primary bone sarcoma of the distal femur is correct?
o: The tract should pass through the knee joint for easier access to the lesion
A transverse incision gives the best cosmetic result
The tract should lie in line with the planned resection incision, through a single muscle compartment, avoiding the joint and neurovascular bundle
The biopsy should be done at a hospital other than the treating sarcoma centre
items.e: The biopsy tract is contaminated and must be excised en bloc with the tumour, so it is placed along the line of the definitive incision, through one compartment, away from the joint and neurovascular structures. Ideally it is done at the treating centre (Mankin).

items.q: After a needle biopsy of a proximal humeral osteosarcoma, what is the implication of the biopsy tract for definitive surgery?
o: Immediate adjuvant radiotherapy to the tract is mandatory
The tract upstages the tumour to stage III
The tract must be excised en bloc with the tumour at definitive surgery
No change: the tract is an unavoidable artefact
items.e: A biopsy tract is considered a potential seed line; definitive surgery should excise the tract en bloc to reduce local recurrence risk, but it does not up‑stage the tumour itself.

items.q: A 32-year-old man has 3 months of thoracic back pain, evening fever and weight loss. MRI shows paradiscal involvement of T6–T7 with mild collapse and a subligamentous paravertebral abscess. The investigation to confirm the diagnosis is:
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thoracic spine
CT-guided core biopsy for histopathology, culture and CBNAAT (GeneXpert)
items.e: Tissue diagnosis by CT-guided biopsy (caseating granulomas, AFB culture, CBNAAT that also detects rifampicin resistance) confirms spinal tuberculosis. Imaging and Mantoux are only suggestive.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT one of Rajasekaran's 'spine-at-risk' radiological signs predicting progressive kyphosis in children with spinal tuberculosis?
o: Posterior retropulsion of the diseased segment
items.e: The four spine-at-risk signs are facet separation, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation and toppling of the superior vertebra. Two or more signs predict kyphosis progression during growth and favour early surgical stabilisation; abscess size is not one of them.

items.q: According to WHO and Indian (INDEX-TB) guidance, the recommended total duration of antitubercular therapy for drug-sensitive osteoarticular tuberculosis is:
items.e: Bone and joint TB is treated for about 12 months (2 months HRZE intensive phase plus 10 months HRE continuation), extended case by case on clinical and radiological response. Six months is the pulmonary standard.

items.q: All of the following are features of spinal tuberculosis EXCEPT:
items.e: Spinal TB characteristically shows paradiscal involvement, subligamentous spread with skip lesions, and cold abscesses with caseating granulomas. Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis suggests ankylosing spondylitis; tuberculous sacroiliitis is usually unilateral.

items.q: A high-energy pelvic injury shows symphysis diastasis with complete disruption of the posterior sacroiliac complex and 2 cm cranial displacement of the hemipelvis. The Tile classification is:
items.e: Tile C injuries are rotationally and vertically unstable (complete posterior arch disruption); C1 is unilateral. Tile B1 is open-book (rotationally unstable, vertically stable) and B2 is lateral compression.

items.q: For an isolated posterior wall acetabular fracture, the indication for ORIF through a Kocher–Langenbeck approach is:
o: A fragment under 20% of the wall with a stable hip on examination under anaesthesia
Hip instability on stress examination, or incongruity from an intra-articular fragment or marginal impaction
Any posterior wall fracture in a patient over 60 years
A posterior wall fracture associated with a sciatic nerve palsy only
items.e: Posterior wall fractures are fixed when the hip is unstable (usually fragments over 40–50% of the wall, or instability on EUA) or incongruous. Small stable fragments with a congruent joint can be treated non-operatively.

items.q: A 28-year-old farmer from a TB-endemic region has mid-lumbar pain, low-grade fever and night sweats with normal radiographs. The most sensitive imaging modality for early diagnosis of spinal tuberculosis is:
o: CT scan of the lumbar spine
MRI of the lumbar spine with contrast
items.e: Contrast MRI detects marrow oedema, paradiscal enhancement, subligamentous spread and abscesses weeks before radiographic changes (which need about 30–40% bone loss). CT shows bone destruction but is less sensitive early.

items.q: In thoracolumbar tuberculosis with anterior vertebral body destruction and cord compression, which procedure is contraindicated as an isolated operation?
o: Anterior radical debridement and strut grafting
items.e: In Pott's disease the anterior column is destroyed; laminectomy removes the only intact column, worsening kyphosis and neurological deficit. Anterior or posterolateral decompression, with stabilisation, is the accepted approach.

items.q: In Pott’s disease, the presence of a ‘Gibbus’ deformity is most commonly associated with which of the following patterns of vertebral involvement?
o: Involvement of only the posterior elements
Anterior column destruction with sparing of the disc space
Anterior column and disc destruction with collapse of one or more vertebral bodies
Bilateral facet joint erosion without vertebral body collapse
items.e: A gibbus results from anterior column collapse; the disc is usually destroyed, leading to a sharp angular kyphosis characteristic of TB.

items.q: Three weeks after an L4–L5 microdiscectomy, a 32-year-old woman has severe back pain, fever and a rising CRP. The investigation of choice is:
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the lumbar spine
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the lumbar spine
items.e: Contrast MRI is the most sensitive and specific test for postoperative spondylodiscitis and epidural abscess (disc and endplate enhancement, marrow oedema, rim-enhancing collection). Bone scan is non-specific after recent surgery.

items.q: A patient with pyogenic spondylodiscitis was started on empirical antibiotics without a microbiological diagnosis and has not improved after 7 days. The most appropriate next step is:
o: CT-guided percutaneous biopsy (repeat or open biopsy if negative) for culture
Change to oral antibiotics and repeat MRI in 4 weeks
items.e: Without an organism, treatment is guesswork: CT-guided biopsy (ideally before antibiotics, or after a washout period) gives culture and sensitivities, with open biopsy if it is non-diagnostic. Surgery is reserved for neurological deficit, instability, abscess or failure of targeted therapy.

items.q: Twelve years after a cemented THA, a 68-year-old man has groin pain and radiographs show superior migration of the cup with a progressive radiolucent line. The first step in his evaluation is:
o: ESR and CRP (with aspiration if raised) to exclude periprosthetic infection
CT with 3-D reconstruction to assess acetabular bone stock
Paprosky classification of acetabular bone loss
items.e: Every painful or loose arthroplasty is presumed infected until proven otherwise: serum ESR/CRP, then aspiration if abnormal (ICM/MSIS criteria). Only after infection is excluded is bone stock assessed (CT, Paprosky) to plan an aseptic revision.

items.q: In a patient with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing, the recommended screening test for systemic metal ion release is:
items.e: Whole-blood cobalt and chromium levels quantify ion release; levels above about 7 ppb (MHRA) are a concern and prompt cross-sectional imaging. MARS MRI is used to detect pseudotumours (adverse reaction to metal debris), not to measure ions.

items.q: A 2-year-old has a mildly painful swollen knee with low-grade fever and a modestly raised CRP after a recent upper respiratory infection. Routine cultures of joint fluid are negative, but PCR identifies a Gram-negative coccobacillus. The organism is:
items.e: Kingella kingae is the commonest cause of osteoarticular infection between 6 months and 4 years. It is fastidious, so it is best detected by blood-culture bottle inoculation or PCR, and it causes a milder illness. It is a Gram-negative coccobacillus usually sensitive to beta-lactams.

items.q: A febrile, irritable 6-month-old holds the right hip flexed and externally rotated. CRP is raised and ultrasound shows a hip effusion. The best next step is:
o: Urgent ultrasound-guided hip aspiration, proceeding to arthrotomy if purulent
MRI under sedation before any intervention
Observation and repeat ultrasound in 48 hours
items.e: Suspected septic hip in an infant is a surgical emergency: aspiration confirms it and urgent arthrotomy with washout prevents femoral head destruction (avascular necrosis, Tom Smith arthritis). Delaying for imaging or observation risks permanent damage.

items.q: For the diagnosis of acute osteomyelitis in a child under 6 years, which imaging modality is considered the investigation of choice?
items.e: MRI has the highest sensitivity and specificity for early osteomyelitis, showing marrow oedema, subperiosteal abscess and physeal involvement within days; radiographs lag by 10–14 days. Bone scan is useful when the site cannot be localised.

items.q: In a 2‑year‑old with a septic joint of the hip, which of the following is the most reliable laboratory marker for monitoring response to therapy?
items.e: CRP responds more rapidly and reflects acute inflammation, making it the preferred marker for serial monitoring.

items.q: Eight weeks after an undisplaced distal radius fracture, a 45-year-old carpenter suddenly cannot extend the thumb IP joint. The most appropriate treatment is:
o: Extensor indicis proprius to EPL transfer
Free graft from flexor carpi ulnaris
items.e: Attritional EPL rupture at Lister's tubercle after (often undisplaced) distal radius fractures leaves frayed ends that cannot be repaired directly. EIP transfer is the standard reconstruction; palmaris longus intercalary grafting is an alternative.

items.q: A 42-year-old woman has a painful bunion with a hallux valgus angle of 32°, an intermetatarsal angle of 15°, a congruent joint, no arthritis and no first-ray hypermobility. The most appropriate procedure is:
o: Scarf osteotomy of the first metatarsal
items.e: Moderate deformity (HVA about 20–40°, IMA about 13–20°) is corrected with a shaft (scarf) or proximal osteotomy plus Akin as needed. Distal chevron suits mild deformity (IMA under about 13°), Lapidus is chosen for hypermobility or severe IMA, and Keller is for elderly low-demand patients.

items.q: For first MTP joint arthrodesis in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, the biomechanically strongest commonly used construct is:
o: Dorsal (locking) plate combined with an interfragmentary lag screw
items.e: A dorsal plate combined with an interfragmentary compression screw is the stiffest construct and gives high union rates. The joint is fused in about 10–15° of valgus and slight dorsiflexion relative to the floor.

items.q: A 10-year-old has pain in the arm. Radiographs show an eccentric, expansile, lytic metaphyseal lesion of the proximal humerus, and MRI shows multiple fluid–fluid levels with thin enhancing septa and no solid nodular component. The most likely diagnosis is:
items.e: Primary ABC is eccentric, expansile and metaphyseal, with multiple fluid–fluid levels and thin septa; USP6 rearrangement is characteristic. Thick nodular enhancing tissue would raise the possibility of telangiectatic osteosarcoma, and a unicameral cyst is central with at most a single fluid level after fracture.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding giant cell tumor of bone is FALSE?
o: It most commonly occurs in skeletally mature adults
It presents with night pain relieved by NSAIDs
It has a 5‑year local recurrence rate of around 20 % after curettage
It can metastasise to the lungs despite being histologically low‑grade
items.e: Night pain relieved by NSAIDs is classic for osteoid osteoma, not GCT. GCT occurs in skeletally mature patients (epiphyseal–metaphyseal), recurs in about 15–25% after extended curettage, and gives benign pulmonary metastases in about 2–5%.

items.q: In skeletal muscle excitation–contraction coupling, the voltage sensor in the T-tubule that is mechanically linked to calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum is the:
items.e: T-tubule depolarisation changes the shape of the dihydropyridine receptor, which directly opens RyR1 in the sarcoplasmic reticulum; the released Ca²⁺ binds troponin C to allow cross-bridge cycling. RyR1 mutations cause malignant hyperthermia and central core disease.

items.q: Which statement about muscle spindles is correct?
o: They lie in series with extrafusal fibres and mainly sense tension
Their intrafusal fibres are supplied by group Ia afferents that signal changes in muscle length
Their intrafusal fibres are innervated by alpha motor neurons
They signal through group Ib afferents to inhibit the agonist
items.e: Muscle spindles lie in parallel with extrafusal fibres; their intrafusal fibres (gamma-motor innervated) carry Ia and II afferents that sense length and rate of stretch, mediating the stretch reflex. Golgi tendon organs lie in series, sense tension and signal through Ib afferents (autogenic inhibition).

items.q: A 55-year-old man with gout has an acutely hot, swollen first MTP joint. Serum urate is normal. Aspirate shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals and no organisms on Gram stain. Which statement is correct?
o: A negative Gram stain excludes septic arthritis
This is acute gout; serum urate is often normal during an acute attack
The crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition
The normal urate level makes gout unlikely
items.e: Monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid confirm gout; serum urate falls during an acute flare in up to 40% of cases. Fluid should still be cultured because the Gram stain is often falsely negative and sepsis can coexist with crystals. CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.

items.q: Which finding is diagnostic of calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) arthritis?
o: Chondrocalcinosis of the knee menisci on radiographs
Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals in synovial fluid on polarised microscopy
items.e: Definitive diagnosis rests on identifying CPP crystals (rhomboid, weakly positive birefringence) in synovial fluid. Chondrocalcinosis supports but does not confirm it, since it is common in the asymptomatic elderly; screen for haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and hypomagnesaemia in young patients.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman falls from a bicycle and cannot bear weight. Radiographs show a closed, displaced spiral fracture of the mid-shaft femur with 10 mm shortening. The definitive treatment of choice is:
items.e: Statically locked reamed antegrade nailing is the gold standard for adult femoral shaft fractures, with union rates above 95% and early mobilisation. Plating has more soft-tissue stripping and implant failure, and non-operative treatment is obsolete in adults.

items.q: A 45-year-old construction worker falls from 5 m. Radiographs show a displaced Pauwels type III femoral neck fracture. The treatment of choice is:
o: Urgent anatomical reduction and fixation with a fixed-angle device (sliding hip screw with derotation screw or femoral neck system)
Three parallel cannulated screws without reduction
items.e: In young adults the femoral head is preserved: urgent anatomical (open if needed) reduction and stable fixation. For vertical, high-shear Pauwels III fractures, fixed-angle devices (sliding hip screw/FNS, with or without a medial buttress plate) resist shear better than parallel screws. Arthroplasty is reserved for older or low-demand patients.

items.q: A 68-year-old man has chronic low back pain and cannot stand upright for long. Standing full-length lateral radiographs show a sagittal vertical axis of 10 cm and a pelvic incidence–lumbar lordosis (PI–LL) mismatch of 20°. His symptoms are best explained by:
o: Lumbar canal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Sagittal imbalance from loss of lumbar lordosis
Isolated degenerative disc disease without malalignment
items.e: SRS–Schwab thresholds for disabling adult deformity are SVA above 5 cm, PI–LL above 10° and pelvic tilt above 20°. These patients compensate with pelvic retroversion and knee flexion, causing fatigue and pain when standing.

items.q: Regarding spinopelvic parameters, which statement is FALSE?
o: Pelvic tilt increases as a compensation for sagittal imbalance
Pelvic incidence equals pelvic tilt plus sacral slope
Pelvic incidence changes between sitting and standing
About two-thirds of lumbar lordosis lies between L4 and S1
items.e: Pelvic incidence is a fixed morphological parameter after skeletal maturity, and PI = PT + SS. Posture changes PT and SS reciprocally: retroversion raises PT and lowers SS. The L4–S1 segments contribute roughly two-thirds of total lumbar lordosis.

items.q: In a patient undergoing uncemented THA, proximal femoral stress shielding is most effectively minimized by:
o: Using a large, heavily coated cobalt‑chromium stem
Employing a proximally coated, titanium low‑modulus stem
Choosing a proximally coated large‑diameter stainless steel stem
items.e: A proximally coated, low‑modulus (titanium) stem allows physiological loading of the metaphyseal bone, reducing the incidence of stress shielding.

items.q: In the direct lateral (Hardinge) approach to the hip, the split in gluteus medius should not extend more than about 5 cm above the tip of the greater trochanter to protect the:
items.e: The inferior branch of the superior gluteal nerve runs between gluteus medius and minimus about 3–5 cm above the trochanter; injury denervates the anterior abductors and tensor fasciae latae, causing a Trendelenburg limp.

items.q: The Mankin score is used to evaluate which of the following?
items.e: The Mankin score grades articular cartilage based on histological structure, cellularity, matrix staining, and tidemark integrity.

items.q: A ramp lesion of the knee is most commonly associated with which injury?
o: Grade III medial collateral ligament tear
items.e: A ramp lesion is a meniscocapsular separation of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus, found in about 15–25% of ACL-injured knees. It is easily missed on MRI and through standard portals, so look via a trans-notch view or posteromedial portal.

items.q: In the ICRS classification, a cartilage lesion extending deeper than 50% of cartilage depth, down to the calcified layer but not through the subchondral bone, is:
items.e: ICRS grade 1 is superficial (softening, fissures), grade 2 is under 50% depth, grade 3 is over 50% depth down to the calcified layer or subchondral bone without penetrating it, and grade 4 is an osteochondral lesion through the subchondral plate.

items.q: A 35‑year‑old male presents with fever, left knee pain and swelling. Aspiration yields cloudy, straw‑yellow fluid; Gram‑positive cocci in chains are seen. He has a history of a penetrating knee injury 10 days ago. Which initial investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
o: MRI of the knee with contrast
items.e: Synovial fluid culture (with sensitivities) confirms septic arthritis and directs antibiotic choice; imaging and blood cultures are adjuncts. Gram-positive cocci in chains suggest streptococci, whereas staphylococci form clusters.

items.q: The classic radiographic appearance of subacute osteomyelitis (Brodie abscess) in a child is:
o: Well-circumscribed metaphyseal lucency with a sclerotic rim, which may cross the physis
items.e: A Brodie abscess is a walled-off metaphyseal lucency with reactive sclerosis, often with a serpiginous tract that may cross the physis (unlike most tumours). Onion-skin periosteal reaction suggests Ewing sarcoma, and sunburst suggests osteosarcoma.

items.q: A 28-year-old woman develops fever and a painful swelling at the operative site after shoulder arthroscopy; cultures grow MRSA. Along with surgical washout, the most appropriate antibiotic is:
items.e: MRSA is resistant to all beta-lactams, including cefazolin and ampicillin–sulbactam. IV vancomycin (or daptomycin/linezolid) with surgical debridement is standard; adding Gram-negative cover is unnecessary once the organism is known.

items.q: A 62-year-old woman with dementia who walks only within her home sustains a Garden IV femoral neck fracture after a low-energy fall. The most appropriate treatment is:
items.e: Displaced intracapsular fractures in older patients are treated by arthroplasty; fixation has high rates of non-union and AVN. THA is offered to active, independently mobile, cognitively intact patients (NICE), so cemented hemiarthroplasty suits this low-demand patient with cognitive impairment.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognised complication of a closed intertrochanteric femoral fracture treated with a sliding hip screw?
items.e: Tibial nerve palsy is unrelated to hip fixation; the other three are established postoperative concerns.

items.q: A 35-year-old man sustains a closed, extra-articular distal femoral (AO/OTA 33-A) fracture in a road traffic accident. A preferred definitive fixation is:
items.e: Extra-articular distal femoral fractures are treated with a retrograde IM nail or a lateral locked plate. Both give relative stability and allow early motion; K-wires and a DHS are biomechanically inadequate.

items.q: All of the following are indications for surgical intervention in spinal tuberculosis EXCEPT:
o: No clinical or radiological response to 3–6 months of ATT
items.e: Surgery in spinal TB is indicated for neurological deficit (especially if worsening or not responding to ATT), instability or progressive kyphosis, failure of medical treatment and diagnostic uncertainty. Coexisting active pulmonary TB is treated medically.

items.q: In a conventional metal-on-polyethylene THA, periprosthetic osteolysis is mainly caused by macrophage response to:
o: Polyethylene particles about 0.1–1 µm in size
items.e: Submicron polyethylene particles (0.1–1 µm) are phagocytosed by macrophages, which release TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 and RANKL, activating osteoclasts. Particles larger than about 10 µm cannot be phagocytosed and are less biologically active.

items.q: A child of normal length at birth with a normal face develops short-limbed dwarfism after age 2, with marked ligamentous laxity and early-onset arthritis. Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by a mutation in:
items.e: Pseudoachondroplasia (and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia) results from cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP) mutations, with retained protein in chondrocyte rough endoplasmic reticulum. Achondroplasia (FGFR3) is evident at birth with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia.

items.q: All of the following are stages in Luck's classification of Dupuytren's disease EXCEPT:
items.e: Luck described three histological stages: proliferative (myofibroblast-rich nodules), involutional (myofibroblasts align along tension lines) and residual (relatively acellular, collagen-dense cords). Type III collagen increases relative to type I.

items.q: In the WHO 2020 classification, a grade 1 central cartilaginous malignancy of the long bones of the appendicular skeleton is termed:
items.e: Low-grade central cartilage tumours of the limb long bones are called atypical cartilaginous tumours because they almost never metastasise; extended intralesional curettage with adjuvant is acceptable. The same histology in the pelvis, scapula or skull base is still called chondrosarcoma grade 1 and needs wide resection.

items.q: The corrosion resistance of titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) implants in vivo is mainly due to:
o: A spontaneously formed passive titanium dioxide surface layer
items.e: Titanium instantly forms a stable, self-repairing TiO2 passive film, which gives excellent corrosion resistance and osseointegration. Stainless steel and cobalt-chrome rely on a chromium oxide layer; mixing dissimilar metals promotes galvanic corrosion.

items.q: A 68‑year‑old woman with postmenopausal osteoporosis has sustained a compression fracture of the 5th thoracic vertebra. Which drug is preferred as first‑line therapy to increase BMD and reduce future fracture risk?
items.e: Oral bisphosphonates (alendronate) are first-line for most postmenopausal osteoporosis because they are effective against vertebral, non-vertebral and hip fractures and are inexpensive. Anabolic agents (teriparatide, romosozumab) are preferred for very high-risk patients, and calcitonin is no longer recommended.

items.q: Zoledronic acid reduces bone resorption by:
o: Inhibiting farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway of osteoclasts
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates bind hydroxyapatite and, once taken up by resorbing osteoclasts, inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, preventing protein prenylation and causing osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis. Denosumab targets RANKL, teriparatide the PTH-1 receptor, and romosozumab sclerostin.

items.q: In a woman with severe postmenopausal osteoporosis and recent vertebral fractures, which agent produces the greatest increase in lumbar spine BMD in the first 12 months?
items.e: Romosozumab (anti-sclerostin, monthly SC for 12 months) has a dual effect, increasing formation and reducing resorption, and gave about 13% spine BMD gain at 1 year, outperforming alendronate in ARCH. It must be followed by an antiresorptive and is avoided after recent MI or stroke.

items.q: A 70-year-old woman who has taken alendronate for 8 years has aching thigh pain. Radiographs show focal lateral cortical thickening ('beaking') of the subtrochanteric femur with a transverse lucent line. The diagnosis is:
items.e: Atypical femoral fractures (ASBMR criteria) start at the lateral cortex as transverse stress fractures with localised periosteal or endosteal thickening, linked to long-term bisphosphonates. Stop the drug, check the other femur, and nail prophylactically if there is pain or a lucent line.

items.q: A 22-year-old man has a closed Schatzker V bicondylar tibial plateau fracture with severe swelling and fracture blisters. The most appropriate strategy is:
o: Immediate dual plating through a single midline incision
Spanning external fixator, then delayed ORIF (dual plating) once the soft tissues recover
items.e: High-energy bicondylar plateau fractures with compromised soft tissues are managed in stages: a knee-spanning fixator restores length and alignment, and definitive fixation (often dual-incision plating) waits for the wrinkle sign at 1–3 weeks. This markedly reduces wound complications and infection.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with a pilon fracture graded as a Gustilo–Anderson type IIIB. Which of the following is the best initial management step?
o: Immediate internal fixation with posterior plating
Debridement, temporary external fixation, and antibiotics
items.e: Type IIIB requires thorough debridement, stabilization with a temporary external fixator, and broad‑spectrum antibiotics to control contamination before definitive fixation.

items.q: Which of the following imaging modalities is the gold standard for evaluating articular step‑off in a tibial plateau fracture?
o: CT scan with 1 mm coronal slices
items.e: Thin‑slice CT provides precise measurement of articular step‑off and fragment geometry, guiding surgical planning.

items.q: When planning a medial opening-wedge high tibial osteotomy for medial compartment osteoarthritis with varus, the weight-bearing line is usually aimed to pass through a point about:
o: 50% of the tibial plateau width from medial (centre of the knee)
62% of the tibial plateau width from medial (Fujisawa point)
At the lateral edge of the tibial plateau (100%)
items.e: Fujisawa showed that slight overcorrection, with the mechanical axis passing about 60–62.5% across the plateau from medial, gives the best results; this is planned with the Miniaci method. Neutral correction risks recurrent varus, and excessive correction overloads the lateral compartment.

items.q: In an Oxford mobile-bearing medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, flexion and extension gaps are balanced by comparing feeler-gauge measurements at:
items.e: The Oxford technique measures the extension gap at 20° (not full extension, where the tight posterior capsule gives a falsely small gap) and the flexion gap at 110°, then mills the distal femur until they match. This prevents bearing dislocation and preserves normal ligament tension.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old marathon runner presents with medial knee pain localized to the posterior horn of the medial meniscus. Arthroscopy reveals a longitudinal tear limited to the vascular zone. Which of the following is the most appropriate intra‑operative management for this tear?
o: Rasping of the tear edges and meniscal repair (all-inside or inside-out sutures)
items.e: Longitudinal vertical tears in the peripheral vascular (red–red or red–white) zone of a young patient have the best healing potential and should be repaired after freshening the tear edges, preserving the meniscus' load-sharing role.

items.q: Which statement best describes the correlation between the meniscal tear pattern seen on MRI and the likelihood of successful arthroscopic meniscal repair?
o: Horizontal flaps have the highest repair potential compared to longitudinal tears
A vertical tear involving the vascular zone has a better prognosis than a radial tear in the avascular zone
Any tear confined to 50% of the meniscus thickness can be repaired successfully
The presence of concomitant ACL injury guarantees successful meniscal healing
items.e: Repair success depends mainly on tear location; vertical tears in the vascular zone show the best healing potential, whereas radial tears in the avascular zone have poorer outcomes.

items.q: In slipped capital femoral epiphysis, which factor is the strongest predictor of avascular necrosis?
o: Unstable slip by Loder's classification (unable to bear weight even with crutches)
items.e: Loder found AVN in about 47% of unstable slips and almost none of the stable ones, so stability is the key prognostic factor. Slip severity (Southwick angle) affects deformity and impingement more than AVN risk.

items.q: A 6-year-old boy with Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease has radiographs showing fragmentation of the femoral epiphysis. In Waldenström's staging, this is:
items.e: Waldenström stages are initial (dense, smaller epiphysis), fragmentation, reossification and healed. The lateral pillar (Herring) classification is applied in the fragmentation stage, whereas Stulberg's classification grades the final outcome at maturity.

cmvvzbs1rd63ru.q: Module 1: Memory-Based Previous Year MCQs, High-Yield Concepts & Analytical Explanations Section A: Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA) Biomechanics & Surgery Q1. During an Anterior Approach (Hueter) to the hip joint, bleeding is encountered in the intermuscular plane between the Tensor Fasciae Latae (TFL) and Sartorius. Which vessel is most vulnerable to injury at this stage?
o: Ascending Branch of Lateral Femoral Circumflex Artery (LFCA)
First Perforating Artery of Profunda Femoris
cmvvzbs1rd63ru.aText: Ascending Branch of Lateral Femoral Circumflex Artery (LFCA)
cmvvzbs1rd63ru.e: [Ascending Branch of LFCA] The internervous plane for the direct anterior approach is between the TFL (Superior Gluteal N.) and Sartorius (Femoral N.). Deep in this interval, the ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery crosses horizontally and must be identified, ligated, or cauterized to prevent brisk arterial bleeding and postoperative hematoma formation.

cmvvzbs2afemhj.q: According to Lewinnek's defined "Safe Zone" for acetabular cup positioning in THA to minimize post- operative dislocation, which pair of angles represents the exact standard target?
cmvvzbs2afemhj.e: [Inclination: 40° ± 10°, Anteversion: 15° ± 10°] Lewinnek's classic safe zone defined acetabular cup inclination as 40° ± 10° (30° – 50°) and anteversion as 15° ± 10° (5° – 25°). Combined anteversion (femoral + acetabular) generally targets 25° – 45° to optimize stability and avoid impingement. High-Yield Reference Metric Master Table Anatomical / Surgical Parameter Standard Range / Target Value Clinical Significance Neck-Shaft Angle (NSA) 125° – 135° <125° causes Coxa Vara (increases femoral stem bending moment); >135° causes Coxa Valga. Hip Joint Reaction Force (Walking)

cmvvzbs2n4r1qb.q: 5× to 4× Body Weight Increases up to 7 – 8× Body Weight during high-impact activities or stumbling. Lewinnek Cup Anteversion 15° ± 10° Malpositioning increases risks of anterior (excessive version) or posterior dislocation. Q-Angle (Females vs. Males) Females: ~14° – 17° | Males: ~10° – 14° Increased Q-angle increases lateral patellar tracking forces and patellofemoral arthritis. Section B: Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA) & Revision Protocols Q3. A 68-year-old male with a history of primary TKA presents 4 years later with persistent knee pain, a felt "patellar clunk" when extending the knee from 60° to 30° flexion, and no systemic signs of infection. What is the underlying cause?
o: Loose Tibial Component with Anterior Subsidence
Fibrovascular Nodule Entrapment at the Superior Pole of the Patella
Excessive External Rotation of the Femoral Component
Patellar Tendon Rupture with Patellar Baja
cmvvzbs2n4r1qb.aText: Fibrovascular Nodule Entrapment at the Superior Pole of the Patella
cmvvzbs2n4r1qb.e: [Fibrovascular Nodule Entrapment] Patellar clunk syndrome is caused by a fibrous/ fibrovascular nodule that forms at the junction of the superior pole of the patella and the quadriceps tendon. During knee flexion, the nodule lodges into the intercondylar notch of the posterior-stabilized (PS) femoral component, and during extension (around 30° – 45°), it abruptly pops out with a painful "clunk."

cmvvzbs30vobtm.q: In Total Knee Arthroplasty, what is the consequence of placing the femoral component in excessive Internal Rotation?
o: Flexion gap asymmetry leading to lateral laxity and patellar maltracking
Flexion gap asymmetry leading to medial tightness and anterior impingement
Symmetric tightness in both extension and flexion gaps
Improved Q-angle leading to reduced patellar wear
cmvvzbs30vobtm.aText: Flexion gap asymmetry leading to lateral laxity and patellar maltracking
cmvvzbs30vobtm.e: [Flexion gap asymmetry leading to lateral laxity & patellar maltracking] Internal rotation of the femoral component narrows the medial flexion space and widens the lateral flexion space. It shifts the trochlear groove medially, thereby increasing the Q-angle and lateral forces, leading to patellar subluxation/maltracking, tilt, or polyethylene failure.

cmvvzbs3cd0diw.q: According to the MSIS (Musculoskeletal Infection Society) / ICM criteria for Periprosthetic Joint Infection (PJI), which of the following is considered a MAJOR criterion for diagnosis?
o: Elevated Synovial Fluid WBC Count > 3,000 cells/μL
Sinus Tract Communicating directly with the Prosthesis
cmvvzbs3cd0diw.aText: Sinus Tract Communicating directly with the Prosthesis
cmvvzbs3cd0diw.e: [Sinus Tract Communicating directly with the Prosthesis] The two MAJOR criteria for PJI (where presence of either one is diagnostic) are: 1) Two positive operative synovial/tissue cultures with identical organisms, OR 2) A sinus tract communicating with the joint/prosthesis. Elevated CRP, high synovial WBC, or a single positive culture are minor criteria. High-Yield Exam Pearl: Vancouver Classification of Periprosthetic Femoral Fractures • Type A: Peritrochanteric region (AG = Greater Trochanter; AL = Lesser Trochanter). • Type B: Around or just distal to the stem. B1: Well- fixed stem (ORIF needed); B2: Loose stem, good bone stock (Revision with long stem); B3: Loose stem, poor bone stock (Revision with stem + allograft/strut). • Type C: Well distal to the stem tip (Treated independently with ORIF). Section C: Biomaterials, Wear Mechanisms & Tribology

cmvvzbs3tvcb7g.q: A 62-year-old female undergoes THA with a Ceramic-on-Ceramic (CoC) bearing couple. 3 years postoperatively, she reports a loud, audible "squeaking" sound during gait. Which surgical parameter is most strongly correlated with this complication?
o: Micro-separation caused by steep cup inclination (> 50°) leading to edge loading
Incomplete seat engagement of the polyethylene liner
Use of a 28mm ceramic head size instead of 36mm
cmvvzbs3tvcb7g.aText: Micro-separation caused by steep cup inclination (> 50°) leading to edge loading
cmvvzbs3tvcb7g.e: [Micro-separation caused by steep cup inclination (> 50°) leading to edge loading] Squeaking in Ceramic-on-Ceramic bearings is associated with fluid film breakdown and stripe wear caused by edge loading. Steep cup inclination (>50°), mal-anteversion, component mismatch, or pelvic tilting leads to micro-separation during heel-strike, stripe wear, and acoustical squeaking.

cmvvzbs462tdlt.q: Which of the following is considered an ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION for fixed-bearing Unicondylar Knee Arthroplasty (UKA) in medial compartment osteoarthritis?
o: Deficiency or chronic tear of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)
cmvvzbs462tdlt.aText: Deficiency or chronic tear of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)
cmvvzbs462tdlt.e: [Deficiency or chronic tear of the ACL] An intact ACL is vital for UKA kinematics. ACL deficiency allows anterior tibial translation and shifted contact stress to the posterior tibial plateau, leading to rapid disease progression in the unreplaced lateral compartment and early implant loosening.

cmvvzbs4efb7tv.q: In Reverse Total Shoulder Arthroplasty (RTSA), moving the center of rotation (COR) medially and inferiorly alters shoulder biomechanics primarily by doing what?
o: Restoring supraspinatus tension and increasing subscapularis leverage
Lengthening the deltoid moment arm and recruiting deltoid fibers for elevation
Decreasing shear forces at the glenosphere-glenoid baseplate interface
Increasing external rotation power by pre-tensioning Teres Minor
cmvvzbs4efb7tv.aText: Lengthening the deltoid moment arm and recruiting deltoid fibers for elevation
